title: The Sūtra of Individual Liberation
explainer: The Prātimokṣa Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Sosor Tharpa'i Do (སོ་སོར་ཐར་པའི་མདོ་), or in English as the Sūtra of Individual Liberation, is one of the most foundational texts of Buddhist monastic life, setting out the rules of conduct and training that govern the lives of fully ordained monks. It belongs to the Vinaya, the broad category of canonical literature concerned with monastic discipline, and takes the form of a sūtra whose verses and injunctions are traditionally recited at communal confession ceremonies held twice monthly within the monastic community. Opening with a homage to the Buddha as the Omniscient One who discovered the treasury of the Three Jewels and crossed the ocean of suffering, the text frames its detailed disciplinary code within a devotional and doctrinal vision of the Buddha's incomparable wisdom and compassion. This text is Toh 2 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the Vinaya scriptures.

title: The Sūtra of Individual Liberation for Fully Ordained Nuns
explainer: Toh 4 in the Kangyur is the Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Dge slong ma'i so sor thar pa'i mdo, or in English as the Sūtra of Individual Liberation for Fully Ordained Nuns. It is a Vinaya text — a code of monastic discipline — setting out the rules of individual liberation, the prātimokṣa, specifically for fully ordained Buddhist nuns, the bhikṣuṇīs. The text opens with verses of homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha before proceeding to enumerate the precepts that govern the conduct and spiritual life of nuns within the monastic community. As one of the foundational disciplinary scriptures, it belongs to the Vinaya section of the Kangyur, the collection of texts attributed to the Buddha himself.

title: The perfection of wisdom in one hundred thousand lines
The perfection of wisdom in twenty five thousand lines
The perfection of wisdom in eighteen thousand lines

The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Verse Condensation
explainer: Toh 13 in the Kangyur is the Āryaprajñāpāramitāsaṃcayagāthā, known in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa sdud pa tshigs su bcad pa, and rendered in English as The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Verse Condensation. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras, one of the most important groupings in the Kangyur, and presents the profound teachings on prajñāpāramitā — the wisdom gone beyond — in metrical verse form rather than the extended prose dialogues characteristic of longer works in this cycle. As its title indicates, the text functions as a poetic summary or condensation of the Perfection of Wisdom teachings, covering themes such as omniscience, the nature of emptiness, and the path of the bodhisattva. It is among the earliest and most studied verse formulations of prajñāpāramitā doctrine and has been widely used across Buddhist traditions as a concise yet comprehensive expression of these teachings.

title: The perfection of wisdom teachings the questions of suvikrantavikramin
The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Five Hundred Lines
explainer: Toh 15 in the Kangyur is the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Five Hundred Lines, known in Sanskrit as the Āryapañcaśatikāprajñāpāramitā and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lnga brgya pa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras, a body of canonical Buddhist scripture that explores the nature of emptiness and the transcendent wisdom cultivated on the bodhisattva path. Like others in this genre, it takes the form of a discourse delivered by the Buddha — here on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha — in which he instructs the Venerable Subhūti on the insubstantial nature of the aggregates, sense bases, and all conditioned phenomena. As one of the shorter Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, it distills these profound themes concisely, sitting within the broader collection of Perfection of Wisdom texts that forms a central section of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom Called the Diamond Cutter
explainer: The Diamond Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa rdo rje gcod pa, is one of the most celebrated texts in the Mahāyāna Buddhist tradition. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras and teaches the nature of emptiness and non-attachment, famously using the image of a diamond or thunderbolt that cuts through illusion to convey how wisdom severs all conceptual clinging, including attachment to the very teachings themselves. The text is structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and his disciple Subhūti, set in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada near Śrāvastī, and unfolds through a series of penetrating questions and answers about the nature of bodhisattvas, merit, and ultimate reality. It is Toh 16 in the Kangyur, preserved among the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, and has been among the most widely studied and revered scriptures across the Mahāyāna world for well over a millennium.

title: The Noble One Hundred and Fifty Modes of the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 17 in the Kangyur is a Perfection of Wisdom sūtra known in English as "The Noble One Hundred and Fifty Modes of the Perfection of Wisdom," in Sanskrit as the Āryaprajñāpāramitānayaśatapañcāśatikā, and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i tshul brgya lnga bcu pa. It belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā class of canonical Buddhist texts, which expound the doctrine of the perfection of wisdom and the nature of emptiness as the foundation of the bodhisattva path. The text opens in the traditional sūtra style with the Buddha as its central figure, described in richly elaborated terms as the sovereign of great yogins, the mother of all Tathāgatas, and the embodiment of omniscient primordial wisdom. As one of the shorter Perfection of Wisdom sūtras preserved in the Kangyur, it presents the teaching of transcendent wisdom through a structured enumeration of its modes or aspects, situating it within the broader tradition of texts that systematically analyze the nature and practice of prajñāpāramitā.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom of the Blessed Lady in Fifty Lines
explainer: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom of the Blessed Lady in Fifty Lines, known in Sanskrit as the Āryabhagavatī-prajñāpāramitā-pañcāśatikā and in Tibetan as Phags pa bcom ldan 'das ma shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lnga bcu pa, is a short Prajñāpāramitā sūtra belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom class of Mahāyāna scriptures. As its title indicates, the text is a condensed teaching on the perfection of wisdom, delivered by the Buddha at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha to an assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and various divine and worldly beings, with the venerable Subhūti as the primary interlocutor. The discourse addresses those wishing to train at the levels of śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva, offering a succinct distillation of prajñāpāramitā doctrine. It is catalogued as Toh 18 in the Kangyur, where it forms part of the collection of Perfection of Wisdom sūtras.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom Called Kauśika
explainer: Toh 19 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in English as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom Called Kauśika, in Sanskrit as the Ārya Kauśika Prajñāpāramitā, and in Tibetan as Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa kau shi ka. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts and presents the Buddha teaching Śakra, lord of the gods — whose epithet Kauśika gives the text its name — on the nature of the Perfection of Wisdom as beyond duality, signs, and all conceptual elaboration. The setting is Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, and the text unfolds as a direct discourse on the ineffable character of wisdom that transcends taking up or casting aside. As a relatively concise Prajñāpāramitā sūtra, it sits within the broader collection of Perfection of Wisdom scriptures in the Kangyur.

title: The Twenty-Five Gateways of the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 20 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-pañcaviṃśatika-prajñāpāramitā-mukha, in Tibetan as the Shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i sgo nyi shu rtsa lnga pa, and in English as The Twenty-Five Gateways of the Perfection of Wisdom. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom genre, a major class of Mahāyāna scripture concerned with the nature of prajñāpāramitā, or transcendent wisdom, and the path of the bodhisattva. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling on the summit of Mount Meru, surrounded by a vast assembly of bodhisattvas, gods, and other beings within a great maṇḍala, and proceeds to expound the perfection of wisdom through twenty-five thematic gateways or modes of entry. As its catalog number indicates, it is Toh 20 in the Kangyur, placed among the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras that form one of the most extensive and central sections of that collection.

title: Heart of the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 21 in the Kangyur is the Heart Sūtra, known in Sanskrit as the Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya and in Tibetan as the Bcom ldan 'das ma shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i snying po, meaning "The Heart of the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom." It is one of the most celebrated and widely recited texts in all of Buddhist literature, belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom, class of sūtras, and it distills the vast teachings on emptiness and wisdom into a remarkably compact form. The text presents the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara's insight into the emptiness of the five aggregates, culminating in the famous mantra that encapsulates the path to liberation. As a sūtra attributed to the speech of the Buddha, it belongs to the Kangyur, the Tibetan canonical collection of translated words of the Buddha, and sits within the broader Prajñāpāramitā section of that canon.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables
explainer: Toh 22 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryasvalpaakṣaraprajñāpāramitā and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa yi ge nyung ngu, meaning in English the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables. As its name suggests, it is a brief prajñāpāramitā scripture — one of the shorter texts belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom class — that distills the essence of the vast prajñāpāramitā literature into a compact teaching on the nature of emptiness and awakening. The sūtra opens with the Buddha residing on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rises to deliver its core instruction. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom section of the Kangyur, standing within a rich tradition of sūtras that range from enormously expansive to highly condensed formulations of the same profound insight.

title: The Perfection of Wisdom in a Single Syllable, the Mother of All Tathāgatas
explainer: Toh 23 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Perfection of Wisdom in a Single Syllable, the Mother of All Tathāgatas," in Sanskrit as the Eka Akṣarī Mātā Nāma Sarva Tathāgata Prajñāpāramitā, and in Tibetan as the Deshyin shekpa thamché kyi yum yigé chungngü shyejawa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom, or Prajñāpāramitā, class of texts — a body of Mahāyāna literature concerned with the nature of wisdom and emptiness as the path to awakening. This remarkably concise sūtra takes the form of a teaching given by the Buddha on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha, addressed to his attendant Ānanda, in which the entirety of the Perfection of Wisdom is distilled into a single syllable for the benefit of all sentient beings. As Toh 23 in the Kangyur, it is counted among the canonical scriptures preserved in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, sitting within the broader Prajñāpāramitā section of that collection.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines
explainer: Toh 24 in the Kangyur is the Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-saptaśatikā-prajñāpāramitā-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa bdun brgya pa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of Mahāyāna sūtras and, like others in this genre, expounds the doctrine of prajñāpāramitā — the perfection of wisdom that perceives the empty nature of all phenomena. The text opens in the familiar sūtra style, with the Buddha residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove accompanied by a great assembly of monks and a vast gathering of bodhisattvas including Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, pointing to the dialogical treatment of wisdom that characterizes the Perfection of Wisdom literature. As one of the shorter prajñāpāramitā scriptures, it distills key insights of the tradition in a relatively compact form, situating it within the rich spectrum of Perfection of Wisdom texts preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Text of One Hundred and Eight Names
explainer: Toh 25 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical scripture known in English as "The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Text of One Hundred and Eight Names," corresponding to the Sanskrit Āryaprajñāpāramitānāmāṣṭaśatakaṃ and the Tibetan Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i mtshan brgya rtsa brgyad pa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts and takes the form of a devotional hymn enumerating one hundred and eight names and epithets of the Perfection of Wisdom, personified as the mother of all buddhas across past, present, and future. Opening with a verse of homage to this "Blessed Lady," the text then proceeds to enumerate her names in rapid succession, covering qualities such as omniscience, suchness, emptiness, and signlessness. As part of the Kangyur, it sits within the vast Prajñāpāramitā scriptural tradition and reflects the deeply devotional as well as philosophical dimensions of that literature.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom, Vajrapāṇi, Great Vehicle Sūtra
explainer: Toh 29 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom, Vajrapāṇi Sūtra, in Sanskrit as the Ārya-prajñāpāramitā-vajrapāṇi-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lag na rdo rje theg pa chen po'i mdo. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts and is set at Rājagṛha, where the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi poses questions to the Buddha about how a bodhisattva should train in the Perfection of Wisdom. The Buddha's central teaching in response is that such training rests on understanding all phenomena as without arising. The text immediately follows Toh 28, the Noble Samantabhadra Great Vehicle Sūtra, and together these short sūtras form part of the broader Prajñāpāramitā section of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Vajra Victory Banner
explainer: Toh 30 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom, the Vajra Victory Banner, in Sanskrit as the Ārya-prajñāpāramitā-vajra-ketu-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་རྒྱལ་མཚན. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts, a large body of Mahāyāna scriptures concerned with the nature and practice of prajñāpāramitā, the transcendent wisdom that perceives the emptiness of all phenomena. This particular sūtra takes the form of a dialogue in which the bodhisattva Vajra Victory Banner, seated among an assembled retinue at Rājagṛha, questions the Buddha about the qualities that constitute the Perfection of Wisdom. It is one of the shorter works within the Perfection of Wisdom section of the Kangyur, presenting the teaching in a concise and direct exchange between the Buddha and the inquiring bodhisattva.

title: The Sūtra of the Thoroughly Turning of the Wheel of Dharma
explainer: The Dharmacakrapravartana Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Chos kyi 'khor lo rab tu bskor ba'i mdo and in English as the Sūtra of the Thoroughly Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, is one of the most revered and historically significant discourses in the entire Buddhist canon. It records the Buddha's first teaching following his enlightenment, delivered at the Deer Park near Vārāṇasī to his five former companions, in which he sets out the Middle Way between asceticism and sensual indulgence and introduces the Four Noble Truths — the foundational framework of the Buddhist path. This event, traditionally known as the first turning of the wheel of Dharma, marks the very beginning of the Buddha's teaching career and the establishment of the Sangha. The text is catalogued as Toh 31 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the sūtra literature, and its central place in Buddhist tradition across all schools has made it a touchstone for understanding the origins and core doctrines of the Buddha's teaching.

title: Account of the previous lives of the buddha
The Sūtra of the Palace of Āṭānāṭā
explainer: The Āṭānāṭiya Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Sūtra of the Palace of Āṭānāṭā (Lcang lo can gyi pho brang gi mdo), is a protective discourse in which the four great kings — the guardian deities of the cardinal directions — visit the Buddha on Vulture Peak Mountain and recite a powerful dhāraṇī intended to ward off malevolent spirits and safeguard Buddhist practitioners. The text belongs to the genre of rakṣā or protection literature, drawing on the cosmology of yakṣas, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, and nāgas who serve under the four kings and whose names are invoked throughout the sūtra. It is one of the most widely used ritual protection texts in Buddhist traditions across Asia, recited to this day as a safeguard against harm. This sūtra is Toh 33 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the general sūtra literature.

title: The Sūtra of the Great Assembly
explainer: The Sūtra of the Great Assembly, known in Sanskrit as the Mahāsamayasūtra and in Tibetan as Düpa Chenpo'i Do (འདུས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་མདོ), is a canonical Buddhist sūtra recounting a vast celestial gathering in which the gods of ten world-systems converge to behold the Buddha and his community of five hundred arhats in the Śākya land. The text celebrates this great assembly by enumerating the many divine beings who come to pay homage, making it a remarkable panoramic vision of the Buddhist cosmos and its inhabitants. It belongs to the genre of sūtra literature and is catalogued as Toh 34 in the Kangyur, the Tibetan canon of texts attributed to the Buddha himself.

title: The Sūtra of Maitreya
explainer: The Sūtra of Maitreya, known in Sanskrit as the Maitrīsūtra and in Tibetan as Byams pa'i mdo, is a canonical Buddhist sūtra concerning the future buddha Maitreya, the successor to the present buddha Śākyamuni. In the text, the venerable Śāriputra addresses the Blessed One at the Nyagrodha pleasure grove beside the Rohiṇī river, asking him to describe the qualities and nature of the coming buddha, and the Blessed One responds by extolling Maitreya's immeasurable merit and boundless renown. It is Toh 35 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general class of sūtra literature, and was translated into Tibetan by Zangpo at the great temple of Palthaling.

title: The Sūtra on Cultivating Loving-Kindness
explainer: The Sūtra on Cultivating Loving-Kindness, known in Sanskrit as the Maitrī Bhāvanā Sūtra and in Tibetan as Byams pa bsgom pa'i mdo, is a canonical Buddhist discourse in which the Buddha, while residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, instructs his monks on the practice of loving-kindness as a method for liberating the mind. The text belongs to the sūtra literature and centers on the enumeration of eleven benefits that arise from cultivating loving-kindness diligently, presenting it as a foundational meditative quality to be steadied, developed, and thoroughly familiarized. It is Toh 36 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the general sūtras of the collection.

title: The benefits of the five precepts
The Noble Sūtra of Ānanda of the Mountain
explainer: The Noble Sūtra of Ānanda of the Mountain, known in Sanskrit as the Giri Ānanda Sūtra and in Tibetan as Ri'i Kun dga' bo'i mdo, is a short sūtra belonging to the class of noble discourses attributed to the Buddha himself. It recounts an episode in which the venerable Ānanda falls gravely ill and approaches the Blessed One at Śrāvastī, prompting the Buddha to offer teachings connected with contemplation and the relief of suffering. The text is Toh 38 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical scriptures regarded as the word of the Buddha, and sits within the sūtra section of that canon. It was translated into Tibetan at the great temple of Dpal Thar pa Gling, where it was edited and finalized for transmission to Tibetan readers.

title: Sūtra on Taming the Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda
explainer: The Sūtra on Taming the Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda, known in Sanskrit as the Nandopananda-nāgarāja-damana-sūtra and in Tibetan as Klu'i rgyal po dga' bo nyer dga' gdul ba'i mdo, is a Buddhist sūtra recounting the legendary taming of two powerful nāga kings by the Buddha and his disciples. The text belongs to the narrative sūtra genre and centers on a dramatic episode in which the serpentine nāga lords Nanda and Upananda are subdued through the miraculous powers of the Buddha's retinue, illustrating themes of conversion, the supremacy of the Buddha's wisdom, and the protective role of the Dharma. The story unfolds from the familiar setting of Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove, grounding it within the broader biographical and legendary literature surrounding Śākyamuni Buddha. It is catalogued as Toh 39 in the Kangyur, where it falls among the general sūtra literature of that collection.

title: The Sūtra of the Great Kāśyapa
explainer: The Sūtra of the Great Kāśyapa, known in Sanskrit as the Mahākāśyapa Sūtra and in Tibetan as Ösung Chenpo'i Do (འོད་སྲུང་ཆེན་པོའི་མདོ), is a Buddhist sūtra recounting a direct encounter between the Buddha and his senior disciple Mahākāśyapa. The text opens with Mahākāśyapa lying gravely ill in the Pippalī cave near Rājagṛha, whereupon the Buddha himself comes to visit him, setting the stage for teachings arising out of that compassionate exchange. As a sūtra, it belongs to the discourses attributed to the historical Buddha and preserved in narrative form, centering on themes of illness, spiritual endurance, and the relationship between teacher and disciple. It is Toh 40 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts regarded as the word of the Buddha in the Tibetan tradition, and it falls within the general category of sūtras.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra from the Great Heap of Jewels: The Dharma Exposition in One Hundred Thousand Verses, the Chapter on the Teaching of the Three Vows
explainer: Toh 45 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Mahāratnakūṭa-dharma-paryāya-śatasāhasrika-grantha-trisaṃvara-nirdeśa-parivarta, and in Tibetan as part of the collection called the Noble Great Heap of Jewels, or Ratnakūṭa. This text is a chapter — specifically the section entitled "The Teaching on the Three Vows" — drawn from an enormous dharma-exposition said to span one hundred thousand verses, and it belongs to the celebrated Ratnakūṭa collection, one of the major groupings of Mahāyāna sūtras in the Kangyur. Set on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, the sūtra opens in the classic narrative frame of the Buddha dwelling amid a richly described assembly of human and non-human beings, before proceeding to expound the nature and observance of the three vows. As Toh 45 in the Kangyur, it sits within the Ratnakūṭa section of that canon, which gathers together some of the most influential Mahāyāna scriptural teachings on bodhisattva ethics, discipline, and the path to awakening.

title: The teaching on clearing the boundless gates

The Noble Ten Dharmas
explainer: Toh 53 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Noble Ten Dharmas," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-daśadharma-nāma-mahāyānasūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa chos bcu pa. It forms the ninth chapter of the vast collection known as the Great Ratnakūṭa, a compendium of one hundred thousand chapters organized around the theme of the "Heap of Jewels," and it belongs to the Ratnakūṭa section of the Kangyur. Set on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha, the text opens with the Buddha surrounded by a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, and centers on a bodhisattva named Pure Virtue, Stainless and Immaculate, King of Jewel Moonlight, suggesting that its teaching will concern a set of ten dharmas or spiritual qualities of particular importance for the bodhisattva path.

Toh 66 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-mahā-pra
explainer: Toh 66 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-mahā-pratihārya-nirdeśa-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as "The Noble Demonstration of the Great Miracle" (འཕགས་པ་དཀོན་མཆོག་བརྩེགས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ལེའུ་). It forms a chapter — specifically the twenty-second chapter, concerning the demonstration of a great miraculous display — within the vast scriptural collection known as the Great Jewel Heap (Mahāratnakūṭa), a compendium spanning one hundred thousand chapters and gathering together numerous Dharma categories. The text is set in the familiar canonical scene of the Buddha residing in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, surrounded by a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. It was translated into Tibetan by the abbot Jinamitra, Prajñāvarman, and the editor-translator monk Yeshé Dé, and belongs to the Ratnakūṭa section of the Kangyur.

title: Ascertaining the discipline the sutra of upalis questions
The inquiry of the girl sumati
The Questions of Vimaladatta
explainer: The Questions of Vimaladatta, known in Sanskrit as the Āryavimaladattatāparipṛcchā and in Tibetan as Drimé Kyijinpé Zhüpa, is a Mahāyāna sūtra presented as a discourse given by the Buddha in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī before a great assembly of monks. The text belongs to the genre of "questions" sūtras, in which a named figure poses inquiries that occasion the Buddha's teaching, and it concerns the dharma as transmitted through the interlocutor Vimaladatta. It is Toh 77 in the Kangyur, where it appears not as a standalone work but as Chapter Thirty-Three of the vast compendium known as the Great Jewel Heap, the Ratnakūṭa collection, which gathers one hundred thousand chapters of dharma synonyms under a single canonical heading.

title: The sutra teaching the unfathomable sphere of a buddha
The sutra of the devaputra susthitamatis questions
Chapter Thirty-Eight of the Noble Great Jewel Heap: The Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Requested by the Bodhisattva Sublime Gnosis, Skilled in the Great Secret Skillful Means of All Buddhas
explainer: Toh 82 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryasarvabuddhamahārahasyopāyakauśalyajñānottarabodhisattvaparipṛcchā and in Tibetan as the chapter requested by the bodhisattva Sublime Gnosis, skilled in the great secret skillful means of all buddhas. It forms Chapter Thirty-Eight of the vast collection known as the Great Jewel Heap, or Ratnakūṭa, a compendium of one hundred thousand chapters of Dharma teachings, and is itself classified as a Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to that broader canonical grouping. The text is set in the familiar scene of the Buddha residing in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī among a great assembly, and its teachings are framed as a dialogue prompted by the bodhisattva Sublime Gnosis, whose particular concern is the profound and secret dimension of skillful means common to all buddhas. As part of the Ratnakūṭa collection, it belongs to one of the most important sutra groupings in the Kangyur, bringing together a wide range of Mahāyāna doctrinal perspectives under the theme of the precious heap of Dharma.

title: The sutra of the girl vimalasraddhas questions
Question of maitreya on eight qualities
The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called the Chapter of Kāśyapa
explainer: The Kāśyapaparivarta, known in Sanskrit as the Āryakāśyapaparivarta and in Tibetan as འཕགས་པ་འོད་སྲུང་གིས་ཞུས་པ (Pakpa Ösung gi Zhüpa), is a Mahāyāna sūtra in which the venerable Mahākāśyapa poses questions to the Buddha on Vulture Peak Mountain before a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. The text is notable as the forty-third chapter of the great Mahāratnakūṭa collection, a compendium of one hundred thousand chapters, and it contains a prophecy delivered in response to Kāśyapa's inquiries, touching on themes central to Mahāyāna practice and understanding. It is catalogued as Toh 87 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtra literature, and its standalone transmission under the title "Chapter of Kāśyapa" reflects the enduring importance this particular discourse held as an independent scripture across the Buddhist traditions of India and Tibet.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called 'The Heap of Jewels'
explainer: Toh 88 in the Kangyur is the forty-fourth chapter of a vast Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-ratnārāśi-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa rin po che'i phung po, rendered in English as "The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called 'The Heap of Jewels.'" This chapter, titled "The Prophecy of the Noble Heap of Jewels," belongs to the broader collection known as the Great Jewel Heap, a massive compendium of Dharma teachings comprising one hundred thousand chapters, and it takes the form of a canonical Mahāyāna discourse set on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, where the Buddha addresses an assembly of thousands of monks and bodhisattvas gathered from many buddha-fields. As its title suggests, the chapter is concerned with prophetic teachings, delivered to an audience of highly advanced bodhisattvas who stand only a single lifetime away from perfect awakening. Situated within the Kangyur's collection of Mahāyāna sūtras, this text represents one section of a sprawling scriptural corpus that was preserved and transmitted as part of the Tibetan Buddhist canonical tradition.

title: The Prophecy Requested by the Noble Inexhaustible Intelligence
explainer: Toh 89 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Akṣayamati-paripṛcchā and in Tibetan as "Phags pa blo gros mi zad pas zhus pa," rendered in English as "The Noble Sūtra of the Questions of Inexhaustible Intelligence." The text records teachings given by the Buddha on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, framed as a dialogue initiated by the bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intelligence, and belongs to a tradition of inquiry-centered Mahāyāna scriptures in which a bodhisattva's questions draw forth profound doctrinal exposition. It forms the forty-fifth chapter of the vast collection known as the Great Heap of Jewels, the Ratnakūṭa, a compendium of one hundred thousand chapters gathering numerous independent sūtras under a single organizing title. The translation into Tibetan was carried out and finalized by the great translator-monk Yeshé Dé, one of the most prolific and revered translators of the early period of Buddhist textual transmission in Tibet.

title: Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines
explainer: Toh 90 in the Kangyur is the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Verses, known in Sanskrit as the Āryasaptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་བདུན་བརྒྱ་པ. It is a Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom family of texts, presenting teachings on prajñāpāramitā — the wisdom that transcends ordinary understanding and lies at the heart of the bodhisattva path. The text is set at Śrāvastī, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, and its content is framed as a prophetic discourse concerning the Perfection of Wisdom in seven hundred verses. Within the Kangyur, it forms the forty-sixth chapter of the Noble Great Jewel Heap, a vast collection containing one hundred thousand chapters of Dharma categories, placing this sūtra within one of the most expansive groupings of canonical Buddhist scripture.

title: The Questions of the Noble Ratnacūḍa: A Mahāyāna Sūtra
explainer: The Questions of the Noble Ratnacūḍa, known in Sanskrit as the Āryaratna-cūḍa-paripṛcchā and in Tibetan as Phags pa gtsug na rin po ches zhus pa, is a Mahāyāna sūtra in which the bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa poses questions to the Buddha, who is depicted teaching on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha before a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. The text belongs to the celebrated Great Jewel Heap collection, the Ratnakūṭa, a large anthology of Mahāyāna sūtras, of which this discourse forms the forty-seventh chapter. It is catalogued as Toh 91 in the Kangyur, where it is preserved among the sūtra texts of that collection.

title: Noble Lion's Roar of Queen Śrīmālā
explainer: The Lion's Roar of Queen Śrīmālā, known in Sanskrit as the Āryaśrīmālādevīsiṃhanāda and in Tibetan as འཕགས་པ་ལྷ་མོ་དཔལ་ཕྲེང་གི་སེང་གེའི་སྒྲ, is a Mahāyāna sūtra centered on the teachings of the noble queen Śrīmālā, who delivers a celebrated discourse on the nature of the tathāgatagarbha, the one vehicle, and the path to liberation. The text takes the form of a dialogue set at Śrāvastī, in which Queen Śrīmālā, daughter of King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā, expounds profound doctrines before the Buddha, who affirms and praises her understanding. It is one of the most influential Indian Buddhist scriptures on buddha-nature theory, widely studied across Mahāyāna traditions. This text is Toh 92 in the Kangyur, where it appears as the forty-eighth chapter of the vast sūtra collection known as the Great Jewel Heap, and belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras.

The Noble Saṅghāṭī Sūtra, a Synonym of the Dharma
explainer: The Noble Saṅghāṭī Sūtra, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Saṅghāṭī Sūtra Dharma Paryāya and in Tibetan as Phakpa Zung gi Do chö kyi Namgrang, is a Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the general sūtra literature of the Buddhist canon. It takes the form of a discourse delivered by the Buddha at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha before a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, and it is renowned for its emphasis on the extraordinary merit generated simply by hearing, reciting, or venerating the text itself. The sūtra is Toh 102 in the Kangyur, where it is classed among the general sūtras, and it has been particularly influential in Tibetan Buddhist practice as a text whose very recitation is held to purify negative karma and plant the seeds of future awakening.

The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'The Dense Array of Ornaments'
explainer: Toh 110 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Ghanavyūha Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Gyen Tukpo Köpa (འཕགས་པ་རྒྱན་སྟུག་པོ་བཀོད་པ), rendered in English as "The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called The Dense Array of Ornaments." It belongs to the sūtra section of the Kangyur and presents a visionary scene in which the Buddha abides in a magnificent, densely adorned buddha-field together with an assembly of great bodhisattvas who are masters of the highest yoga. The text concerns the qualities and powers of the Buddha and the advanced bodhisattvas surrounding him, unfolding against a cosmological backdrop that encompasses the form realm, the formless realm, and beyond. As a Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra, it is addressed to practitioners of the Great Vehicle and reflects the elaborate visionary and doctrinal richness characteristic of that tradition.

The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the King Who Arrays the Qualities of All Phenomena
explainer: Toh 114 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarvadharmaguṇavyūharāja and in Tibetan as the Chö tamché kyi yönten köpé gyalpo, rendered in English as the Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the King Who Arrays the Qualities of All Phenomena. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and is set in Rājagṛha, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, each accomplished in dhāraṇī and devoted to the welfare of all beings. The text's title suggests a concern with the display and enumeration of the qualities inherent in all phenomena, a theme characteristic of sūtras that illuminate the nature of reality through the lens of Mahāyāna doctrine. As with many sūtras of its kind, it opens with the standard proclamation of the teaching's direct transmission through the words "Thus did I hear," situating it firmly within the received scriptural tradition of the Buddha's discourses.

title: Display of pure land of sukhavati
The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called 'The Jewel Casket'
explainer: Toh 117 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-ratnakaraṇḍa-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Könchok gi Zamatok Chéjawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do, rendered in English as "The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called The Jewel Casket." It belongs to the sūtra section of the Kangyur and takes the form of a discourse delivered by the Buddha to a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī. The text features the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī as a prominent interlocutor, arriving alongside thousands of bodhisattvas and divine beings, and unfolds as a teaching on Mahāyāna principles framed within this richly described gathering. The title's image of a jewel casket suggests a treasury of precious Dharma, pointing to the text's character as a repository of important Buddhist teachings intended for those pursuing the bodhisattva path.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra)
explainer: Toh 119 in the Kangyur is the Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow, known in Sanskrit as the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa yongs su mya ngan las das pa chen po'i mdo. It is a major Mahāyāna sūtra recounting the final hours and teachings of the Buddha Śākyamuni as he approaches his passing into nirvāṇa between two śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī river near Kuśinagara, surrounded by a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. The text expounds on themes of central importance to Mahāyāna Buddhism, including the nature of nirvāṇa, the eternity and qualities of the Buddha, and the presence of buddha-nature in all sentient beings. As one of the most celebrated and extensive Mahāyāna sūtras, it belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur.

title: The mahayana sutra of the great parinirvana
The Noble Sūtra of the Great Complete Nirvāṇa
explainer: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and in Tibetan as 'Phags pa yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo, is a major Mahāyāna sūtra centered on the final days and passing into nirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha, set dramatically in the grove of paired śāla trees near Kuśinagara as the Buddha addresses his disciple Ānanda. The text unfolds as a sweeping prophecy of the ages following the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, describing the successive conditions of the Dharma and its practitioners across the centuries to come. It belongs to the sūtra literature of the Mahāyāna, a genre concerned with the Buddha's final teachings and the enduring nature of buddhahood, and shares broad thematic territory with other recensions of the Mahāparinirvāṇa tradition while carrying its own distinctive emphases. This text is Toh 121 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the Mahāyāna sūtras of that great collection of translated Buddhist scriptures.

The Text of the Dharma of Vajra Absorption
explainer: Toh 135 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in Tibetan as Dorjé Ting ngé dzin gyi chö kyi yige, and in Sanskrit as the Vajrasamādhisūtra, commonly rendered in English as the Sūtra of Vajra Absorption or the Scripture of Diamond Concentration. It is a Mahāyāna discourse set on Vulture Peak Mountain, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks, arhats, bodhisattvas, and noble beings, expounding teachings centered on the nature of vajra-like meditative absorption and the profound principles of the Dharma. The text is structured in named chapters, opening with a formal introductory summary in the style of classical Indian sūtra literature, and its assembly scene — featuring celebrated disciples such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Subhūti alongside prominent bodhisattvas — places it firmly within the tradition of the great Mahāyāna sūtras. As Toh 135 in the Kangyur, it belongs to the general sūtra section of the Tibetan Buddhist canon and has historically attracted commentary across both East Asian and Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

title: The Noble Supreme and Sublime Meditative Absorption
explainer: Toh 137 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist sūtra known in English as "The Noble Supreme and Sublime Meditative Absorption," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Samādhi-Agra-Uttama, and in Tibetan as the Phags pa ting nge 'dzin mchog dam pa. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and centers on the theme of meditative absorption, presenting the Buddha entering into a profound samādhi known as the Samādhi of Light Rays before a vast assembly gathered at Rājagṛha, including thirty thousand monks, thousands of great bodhisattvas, and numerous classes of celestial and worldly beings. The text opens in the classic sūtra style, establishing the setting and retinue before turning to the teaching that unfolds from the Buddha's silent entry into meditation. It is preserved as a single fascicle within the Kangyur.

title: The great collection sutra of the incantations of ratnaketu

The Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Accomplisher of Boundless Gates
explainer: Toh 140 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Anantamukhasādhaka Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Accomplisher of Boundless Gates. As a dhāraṇī text, it belongs to the broader class of sūtra literature and centers on a powerful dhāraṇī — a sacred formula of spiritual accomplishment — presented within a narrative setting in which the Buddha resides in Vaiśālī and, in the context of announcing his approaching final nirvāṇa, imparts this teaching to a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. The text thus weaves together themes of the Buddha's passing and the efficacy of dhāraṇī practice, situating the teaching at a moment of profound significance in the Buddha's life. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian master Śīlendrabodhi together with the great editor-translator the monk Ye shes sde and their colleagues.

title: The Dhāraṇī of Two Verses
explainer: Toh 143 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Gāthādvayadhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Dhāraṇī of Two Verses. It belongs to the dhāraṇī literature of the Kangyur and presents a brief verse teaching on the spiritual obstacles that impede beings — including disrespect toward the Buddha and Dharma, laziness, attachment, and doubt — followed by a dhāraṇī mantra offered as their antidote. The text was translated into Tibetan by the Indian scholars Jinamitra and Dānaśīla together with the renowned Tibetan editor-translator Kawa Paltsek, and despite its compact form it carries the characteristic structure of canonical dhāraṇī scriptures, combining doctrinal verse with a ritual mantra formula.

title: The sutra on cultivating faith in the mahayana
The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the Dhāraṇī of the Jewel Meteor
explainer: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the Dhāraṇī of the Jewel Meteor, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-ratnolkā-nāma-dhāraṇī-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa dkon mchog ta la la'i gzungs zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī sūtra centering on a powerful dhāraṇī — a sacred formula for protection and spiritual accomplishment — associated with the image of a radiant jewel meteor. The text opens in the classic sūtra style, with the Buddha dwelling on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha in the company of a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, establishing the authoritative setting from which the teaching flows. As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it belongs to that genre of Mahāyāna literature in which the recitation and preservation of sacred formulas is presented as a central vehicle for liberation and merit. It is catalogued as Toh 145 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the general sūtra collections of the Mahāyāna.

explainer: Toh 161 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Questions of the Son of the Gods, Suvikrāntacinta," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Suvikrāntacintādeva-putra-paripṛcchā, and in Tibetan as the Lha'i bu rab rtsal sems kyis zhus pa. As a paripṛcchā, or "questions" sūtra, it belongs to a well-established genre in which a divine or noble interlocutor poses questions to the Buddha, prompting teachings of broad doctrinal scope. The text is set at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, where the Buddha is surrounded by a vast assembly including monks, bodhisattvas drawn from many world-systems, gods of the desire and form realms, nāgas, and yakṣas, reflecting the cosmic grandeur typical of Mahāyāna scriptural settings. It is classified among the sūtras of the Kangyur and represents the tradition of canonical discourse addressed to an audience spanning both human and supramundane beings.

The Questions of the Noble King of Magical Transformations
explainer: The Questions of the Noble King of Magical Transformations, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-vikurvana-rāja-paripṛcchā and in Tibetan as Phags pa rnam par 'phrul pa'i rgyal pos zhus pa, is a Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the genre of texts structured around questions posed to the Buddha by a distinguished interlocutor. The text opens in the familiar setting of Śrāvastī's Jeta Grove, where the Buddha is gathered with a large assembly of monks and an array of advanced bodhisattvas — including Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta — all said to be beings bound by only a single further birth, signaling the exalted spiritual register of the discourse. As its title indicates, the sūtra centers on the inquiries of a royal figure associated with miraculous or magical transformation, a theme that likely unfolds through exchanges exploring the nature and powers of advanced bodhisattva practice. It is catalogued as Toh 167 in the Kangyur, where it stands among the general Mahāyāna sūtras.

title: The Questions of Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light)
explainer: The Questions of Vimalaprabha, known in Sanskrit as the Vimalaprabhaparipṛcchā and in Tibetan as Dri ma med pa'i 'od kyis zhus pa, is a sūtra in which the bodhisattva or deity Vimalaprabha — Stainless Light — poses questions to the Buddha in the context of a grand celestial assembly. The text opens with the Buddha teaching the Essence of the Moon sūtra on Vulture Peak, summoning gods and yakṣa kings including the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, situating the discourse within a cosmologically rich setting that suggests connections to lunar and calendrical themes found in related tantric literature. As a question-and-answer sūtra framed around divine interlocutors and protective deities, it belongs to the broader sūtra literature of the Kangyur. It is catalogued as Toh 168 in the Kangyur, where it appears among the general sūtra collections.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called Instructions on the Great Vehicle
explainer: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called "Instructions on the Great Vehicle," known in Sanskrit as the Āryamahāyānopadeśa and in Tibetan as Pakpa Tekpa Chenpo'i Men Ngak (འཕགས་པ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་མན་ངག), is a Mahāyāna sūtra presenting the Buddha's teachings on the path and practices of the Great Vehicle. Set at Rājagṛha in a magnificent celestial assembly hall adorned with precious things and described as the domain of the Tathāgatas, the text opens with an elaborate evocation of a sacred space perfected through the merit and miraculous powers of the buddhas, suggesting a discourse of considerable scope directed toward bodhisattvas and great beings. It is Toh 169 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the Mahāyāna sūtras, and its organization into fascicles indicates it is a text of substantial length.

explainer: The Noble Teaching on the Inconceivable Qualities of the Dharma of the Buddhas, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-buddha-dharma-acintya-nirdeśa and in Tibetan as Phags pa sangs rgyas kyi chos bsam gyis mi khyab pa bstan pa, is a Mahāyāna sūtra exploring the inconceivable and transcendent qualities of the buddhas and their dharma. The text unfolds as a teaching prompted by the reflections of a great assembly of bodhisattvas, each contemplating a different aspect of the buddhas' inexhaustible qualities — from their purified buddha-fields and aspirations to their lineage, arising, and bodies — suggesting a wide-ranging meditation on the nature of awakening that lies beyond ordinary conceptual grasp. It belongs to the genre of discourses in which the wonders of the buddhas serve as the occasion for doctrinal elaboration directed at the bodhisattva path. This text is Toh 187 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the Mahāyāna sūtras.

The Noble Prophecy of the Great Goddess Śrī
explainer: Toh 193 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Śrī-Yamahādevī-vyākaraṇa and in Tibetan as the Pakpa Lhamo Chenmo Pal Lungtenpа, rendered in English as The Noble Prophecy of the Great Goddess Śrī. It belongs to the class of vyākaraṇa, or prophecy texts, in which a buddha foretells the future spiritual attainments or destiny of a particular being — in this case the great goddess Śrī, a prominent divine figure in both Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The sūtra is set in the realm of Bliss, the pure land of Amitābha, where the Blessed One addresses a vast assembly of celebrated bodhisattvas including Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Kṣitigarbha, and Samantabhadra, among others. As a canonical Mahāyāna sūtra, it sits within the Kangyur, the Tibetan Buddhist collection of texts regarded as the word of the Buddha.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called the Offering of Lamps
explainer: Toh 204 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryapradīpadānīya and in Tibetan as the Phags pa mar me 'bul ba, meaning in English "The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle called The Offering of Lamps." It belongs to the general sūtra section of the Kangyur and is presented as a discourse delivered by the Buddha to his disciple Śāriputra while residing at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī. The text concerns the spiritual merit and qualities arising from the offering of lamps, situating this devotional practice within a broader Mahāyāna framework that encompasses the four immeasurables, moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, and liberation. As a relatively concise sūtra, it reflects the widespread Buddhist tradition of expounding the virtues of light-offering as a vehicle for accumulating merit and cultivating qualities conducive to awakening.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'The Proclamation of the Lion's Roar'
explainer: Toh 209 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Proclamation of the Lion's Roar," in Sanskrit as the Ārya Siṃhanādikā Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra, and in Tibetan as the Pakpa Sengé Dra Zhesya Pa Tekpa Chenpo Do. As a sūtra, it belongs to the class of canonical texts that record the teachings of the Buddha, here presented as a discourse delivered by the Blessed One in the celestial Palace of the Sun and Moon, the Abode of Complete Victory, before a vast assembly of monks and arhats. The text opens with the Buddha addressing the bodhisattva Heap of Complete Victory, pointing beyond innumerable world-systems, suggesting a teaching of cosmic scope characteristic of the Mahāyāna tradition. It was translated into Tibetan by a scholar named Dpal and subsequently revised and finalized by the Indian abbot Viryākarasiṃha together with the great translator monk Debtsan Dra.

title: Sutra teaching fundamental exposition and detailed analysis of dependent arising
The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'Dependent Origination'
explainer: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called "Dependent Origination," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Pratītyasamutpādanāma Mahāyānasūtra and in Tibetan as 'Phags pa rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, is a Mahāyāna sūtra devoted to the teaching of dependent origination, one of the most fundamental doctrines in Buddhist thought. The text presents the Buddha discoursing on this principle — the chain of conditioned arising through which existence unfolds — along with a classification of its aspects, set against the backdrop of the Buddha dwelling among the gods of the Thirty-Three in the company of great śrāvakas, bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and Avalokiteśvara, and celestial figures including the great Brahmā. It is Toh 212 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras, and its opening homage and framing narrative follow the conventions characteristic of that tradition.

title: The sutra for the benefit of angulimala
Putting an end to karmic obscurations
Counsel to a King
explainer: Toh 221 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "Counsel to a King," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-rāja-avavādaka-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as the Phags pa rgyal po la gdams pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and presents teachings that the Buddha delivers in the context of a royal visit, with Prasenajit, King of Kosala, traveling to the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī to pay homage, make offerings, and receive the Dharma. The setting — a great assembly of monks gathered around the Blessed One — frames what is evidently a discourse addressed to a monarch, exploring themes of guidance and instruction suited to one who holds worldly power. As its title suggests, the text is concerned with counsel given to a king, situating it within a broader tradition of Buddhist literature that reflects on the relationship between spiritual teaching and royal life.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'The Chapter on Bearing the Great Drum'
explainer: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called "The Chapter on Bearing the Great Drum," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Mahābherī-hāraka-parivarta-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Ngabo Chenpo Chenpö Leu Shyejawa Tekpa Chenpo Do, is a Mahāyāna sūtra set in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monastics, bodhisattvas, gods, nāgas, and laypeople. The text's evocative title centers on the image of a great drum, which in Buddhist literature often serves as a metaphor for the far-reaching and awakening power of the Dharma. It is Toh 222 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general category of Mahāyāna sūtras, and is preserved in both its Sanskrit title and Tibetan translation, attesting to its transmission through the classical Indian and Tibetan canonical traditions.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'The Chapter of the Thirty-Three'
explainer: Toh 223 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Trayastriṃśat-parivarta-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa sum cu rtsa gsum pa'i le'u zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, rendered into English as "The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'The Chapter of the Thirty-Three.'" The text takes its name from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the realm of the Thirty-Three gods, where the Buddha is depicted as dwelling beside the Pārijāta tree out of loving concern for the mother who gave birth to his form-body. It belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur and is set in the Mahāyāna literary tradition, opening with a vast assembly that includes eight thousand arhat monks and seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas. As with many sūtras of this class, it frames its teachings within a richly described celestial setting, connecting the Buddha's compassionate presence in the divine realm to the spiritual instruction that follows.

title: The sutra on the threefold going for refuge
The sutra on transmigration through existences
The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called the Compendium of All Knowledge
sanskrit: Ārya Sarva Vidyā Saṃgraha Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra
explainer: Toh 227 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called the Compendium of All Knowledge, in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarva Vidyā Saṃgraha Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa rnam par 'thag pa. It belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur and presents itself as a discourse delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, set dramatically at the time of his approaching final nirvāṇa, in the presence of a vast assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, gods, and laypeople. As its title suggests, the text is concerned with the gathering or synthesis of knowledge, situating this theme within the solemn context of the Buddha's last rains retreat and his imminent passing.

title: The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra: Gathering of Buddhas
explainer: The Noble Discourse on the Harmonious Gathering of Buddhas, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Buddhasaṅgīti Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangyé Drowa Zhéjawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do, is a Mahāyāna sūtra set during a time of five great worldly degenerations, in which the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and gods gathered at a mountain cave near a mango grove in the Middle Country. The text takes its name from the theme of a harmonious gathering or concert of buddhas, and its opening situates this teaching amid the challenges of a degenerate age, suggesting a concern with how beings may find guidance and refuge when the world has declined. It is Toh 228 in the Kangyur, classified among the Mahāyāna sūtras.

title: The sutra on the splendid commitments of the tathagatas
The Chapter Called 'The Great Festival in Which the Ocean of Bodhisattvas from the Ten Directions Gathers and Takes Delight,' from the Noble Sūtra of the Great Cloud
explainer: Toh 233 in the Kangyur is a chapter from the Noble Sūtra of the Great Cloud, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-mahāmegha-sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa sprin chen po'i mdo, with this particular section bearing the title "The Great Festival in Which the Ocean of Bodhisattvas from the Ten Directions Gathers and Takes Delight." It is a Mahāyāna sūtra set on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, where the Buddha is depicted addressing an enormous assembly of monks, nuns, bodhisattvas, and laypeople. The text belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur and is presented as a discrete named chapter, or parivarta, of the larger Great Cloud collection. As suggested by both its title and its vast assembly scene, the work is concerned with the gathering and rejoicing of bodhisattvas from across the ten directions, situating it within the tradition of grand Mahāyāna scriptures that celebrate the scope and splendor of the bodhisattva path.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra: The Chapter on the Maṇḍala of the Wind of the Great Cloud, the Heart-Essence of All Nāgas
explainer: Toh 234 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Mahāmegha-vāyu-maṇḍala-parivarta-sarvanāgahṛdaya and in Tibetan as Phags pa sprin chen po rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi le'u klu thams cad kyi snying po, rendered in English as "The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra: The Chapter on the Maṇḍala of the Wind of the Great Cloud, the Heart-Essence of All Nāgas." The text belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur and centers on the world of the nāgas, serpentine beings associated with rain, water, and the natural elements, presenting the Buddha teaching in a jeweled ocean palace before a vast assembly of nāga kings possessed of great miraculous power. It is concerned with esoteric heart-essences or dhāraṇīs connected to nāgas and the wind-maṇḍala of the great cloud, themes that link it to both the sūtra and dhāraṇī literature of the Mahāyāna tradition. The text thus sits at the intersection of narrative sūtra and ritual-protective literature, reflecting a widespread Indian and Tibetan interest in harnessing the power of nāgas for rain, fertility, and spiritual protection.

title: The Noble Great Cloud
explainer: Toh 235 in the Kangyur is known in English as The Noble Great Cloud, in Sanskrit as the Ārya Mahāmegha, and in Tibetan as the འཕགས་པ་སྤྲིན་ཆེན་པོ (Phakpa Trin Chenpo). It is a Mahāyāna sūtra centered on the teachings and blessings associated with rain-clouds, nāgas, and the power of the Buddha's compassion to bring spiritual and worldly benefit, much as great clouds bring life-giving rain to the earth. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling in a magnificent jeweled cloud palace alongside a vast assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and an extensive gathering of nāga kings — beings traditionally associated with water, rainfall, and the fertility of the natural world — signaling that the sūtra addresses themes of cosmic abundance, protection, and the Buddha's sovereign influence over both human and non-human realms. As Toh 235, it belongs to the sūtra section of the Kangyur, the collection of canonical teachings attributed to the Buddha himself.

title: The Sūtra on Manifestly Attaining the Aim of Accomplishing the Great Uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed One, the Secret of the Tathāgata
explainer: Toh 236 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in English as "The Sūtra of the Courageous Conduct of All Bodhisattvas," concerned with manifestly attaining the aim of accomplishing the great uṣṇīṣa — the cranial protuberance — of the Blessed One, described as the secret of the Tathāgata. The text presents itself as the tenth chapter of a larger ten-thousand-verse sūtra, opening with the Tathāgata addressing his retinue, including Ānanda, from a lion throne, and belongs to the broader class of Mahāyāna sūtra literature focused on bodhisattva practice. The Tibetan title begins with a phrase indicating it concerns the accomplishment of the tathāgata's great uṣṇīṣa, and while precise Sanskrit and Tibetan short-form titles are not fully determinable from the available material, the text is clearly situated within the sūtra division of the Kangyur. It was translated into Tibetan by the monk Yeshe De, who also revised and finalized it in accordance with the royal editing decree standardizing Tibetan Buddhist translations.

title: The sutra of the ten wheels of ksitigarbha
The sutra of the wheel of no reversions
The sutra of the wheel of meditative concentration
The sutra of the wheel of dedication
The Sūtra of the Great Vehicle, King of the True Dharma
explainer: The Sūtra of the Great Vehicle, King of the True Dharma, known in Sanskrit as the Saddharmarāja Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as Dampé Chökyi Gyalpo Tekpa Chenpo'i Do, is a Mahāyāna sūtra set at the most solemn of moments: the Buddha's imminent passing into final nirvāṇa beneath the two śāla trees. In it, the Buddha emits a great radiance that directly reveals all phenomena to an assembled multitude, and the bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, the Treasury of Space, rises among the gathered beings to receive and engage with these final teachings. The text belongs to the class of Mahāyāna sūtras concerned with the Buddha's parinirvāṇa and the profound Dharma he imparts in those last moments. It is catalogued as Toh 243 in the Kangyur, preserved among the general Mahāyāna sūtras of that collection.

title: The sutra of the victory of the ultimate dharma
Distinguishing phenomena and what is meaningful
The accomplishment of the sets of four qualities the bodhisattvas pratimoksa
The noble mahayana sutra on the four factors
The Sūtra Called 'The Three Dharmas'
explainer: Toh 253 in the Kangyur is a brief Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Tri-dharma-nāma-sūtra and in Tibetan as Chos gsum pa zhes bya ba'i mdo, meaning "The Sūtra Called 'The Three Dharmas.'" It belongs to the general class of sūtra literature and records a teaching delivered by the Buddha at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, addressed to an assembly of monks. The discourse identifies three qualities — attachment, miserliness, and heedlessness — that obstruct foolish persons from giving gifts, making merit, and maintaining moral discipline, and it contrasts these with the three corresponding virtues that enable practitioners to flourish in the Dharma. The text appears in the Kangyur as part of a sequence of short Mahāyāna sūtras and is notable for its concise, practical focus on the ethical foundations of Buddhist practice.

title: The Great Ocean of Dharma: Ten Chapters on the Abiding of the Bodhisattva Mind as Taught by the Buddha Vairocana
explainer: Toh 256 in the Kangyur is a Mahayana scripture known in English as "The Great Ocean of Dharma," spoken by the buddha Vairocana and organized into ten chapters on the abiding of the bodhisattva mind; its Tibetan title is Chos kyi rgya mo. The text opens with a solemn call to assembly in which all children of the buddha are urged to join their palms, confess any transgressions wholeheartedly, and listen as the great moral discipline of all buddhas is expounded. It addresses a broad audience — those of great virtue alongside laymen and laywomen — and its emphasis on confession, purification, and the cultivation of the bodhisattva mind marks it as a work concerned with both ethical conduct and the awakening aspiration central to the Mahayana. The text belongs to the general class of Mahayana sutras within the Kangyur.

title: The sutra of the quintessence of the sun
The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called 'Buddha-Nature'
explainer: Toh 258 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryatathāgatagarbha-nāma-mahāyānasūtra, in Tibetan as the Phags pa de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, and in English as the Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called "Buddha-Nature." It belongs to the class of tathāgatagarbha literature, which concerns the teaching that all sentient beings possess within them an innate buddha-nature — the seed or essence of awakening — and it is one of the earliest and most foundational texts to articulate this doctrine explicitly. The sūtra is set at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, where the Buddha, ten years after his enlightenment, addresses a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas and uses a series of vivid similes to illustrate how buddha-nature is present in all beings even while obscured by adventitious defilements. As Toh 258 in the Kangyur, it is classified among the general Mahāyāna sūtras and has exercised a profound and lasting influence on Buddhist thought across Tibet, China, and East Asia.

title: The sutra on the quintessence that illuminates the basket without words
The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called Skillful Means
explainer: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called Skillful Means, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Upāyakauśalya-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa thabs mkhas pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, is a Mahāyāna sūtra devoted to the theme of skillful means, the Buddha's capacity to adapt his teachings and conduct to the needs and conditions of beings. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling at Śrāvastī amid an enormous assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, setting the stage for teachings that explore how compassionate wisdom may express itself through seemingly unconventional or even transgressive actions for the ultimate benefit of others. It is catalogued as Toh 261 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha himself, and belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras.

title: The five thousand four hundred and fiftythree names of the buddha
The acceptance that tames beings with the sky colored method of perfect conduct
From the Sūtra Called 'The Noble Great Realization Fully Expansive': The Chapter on the Ritual of Homage
explainer: Toh 265 in the Kangyur is a sūtra excerpt known in English as "The Ritual of Homage from the Noble Great Realization Fully Expansive," drawn from the larger Tibetan canonical work sometimes identified in Sanskrit as the Mahābodhi-vistara-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa rtogs pa chen po yongs su rgyas pa'i mdo. It is a devotional and liturgical text that brings together several thematic chapters: a ritual of homage, the names and praises of the Tathāgatas of the three times, the twelve divisions of scripture, homage to bodhisattvas by name, and a chapter on confession. The text is addressed by bodhisattvas assembled from the ten directions to the Buddha and takes the form of reverent address, praise, and purification practice. As the opening makes clear, what survives here is a condensed and edited translation of select portions from that larger sūtra, rather than the complete work.

title: The sutra of king of the inconceivable
Dispelling the darkness of the ten directions
The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called 'The Seven Buddhas'
explainer: Toh 270 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Seven Buddhas," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-sapta-buddha-ka-nā-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangyé Dünpa Shéjawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do. It belongs to the general class of sūtra literature and recounts a teaching delivered by the Buddha on the summit of Mount Kailāsa, in the company of a vast assembly of monks and advanced bodhisattvas including Maitreya, Ākāśagarbha, and Samantabhadra. As its title suggests, the text centers on the theme of the seven buddhas, situating this teaching within a rich cosmological and devotional context characteristic of Mahāyāna scripture.

title: The Sūtra of the Ten Buddhas
explainer: The Ten Buddhas, known in Sanskrit as the Daśabuddhaka and in Tibetan as Sangyé Chupa, is a Mahāyāna sūtra concerned with the veneration and qualities of ten buddhas. It is Toh 272 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general category of Mahāyāna sūtras. The text opens with a familiar canonical setting — the Buddha dwelling on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha — and is prompted by the bodhisattva Qualities-Precious-Blossoming-Flower, a young Licchavi from Vaiśālī, who rises to address the Blessed One before an assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. The sūtra thus unfolds as a teaching delivered in response to a question or entreaty from this bodhisattva, centering on the significance and invocation of ten buddhas.

title: The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra Called 'The Twelve Buddhas'
explainer: Toh 273 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Twelve Buddhas," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-dvādaśabuddhika-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangye Chunyi Shyewa Zhejawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and takes the form of a teaching delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, addressed to the bodhisattva Maitreya, in which the Buddha describes buddha-fields and the buddhas presiding over them in the eastern direction and beyond. The text was translated into Tibetan by the great editor-translator, the monk Yeshé Dé, together with the Indian scholar Varma and others.

title: The Noble Crown of the Buddhas: A Great Mahāyāna Sūtra, a Great Dharma Teaching
sanskrit: Ārya Buddhamakuṭa Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra Mahādharmaparyāya
explainer: The Noble Crown of the Buddhas, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Buddhamakuṭa Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangyé Tsukgyen Zhéjawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do, is a Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the great class of Dharma teachings. The text opens in the classic sūtra style, with the Buddha residing on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha in the company of a vast assembly of monks, bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and Mañjuśrī, and multitudes of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and other beings. It is catalogued as Toh 274 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha himself. The translation was carried out by the Indian preceptors Jinamitra and Dānaśīla together with the great Tibetan editor-translator, the monk Ye shes sde, who also revised and finalized the text.

title: The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra Called 'The Ground of the Buddhas'
explainer: Toh 275 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Ground of the Buddhas," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-buddhabūmi-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa sangs rgyas kyi sa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and concerns the exalted domain or ground of a fully awakened buddha — the qualities, purified consciousness, and transcendent abode that characterize buddhahood itself. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling in a resplendent palace blazing with the seven precious substances, radiating light throughout immeasurable world-systems, and proceeds to describe the nature of that ground as utterly pure, sovereign awareness completely beyond the three realms. As one of the shorter but doctrinally significant sūtras in the Kangyur, it provided foundational material for later scholastic treatises on the attributes of buddhahood, most notably the Buddhabūmisūtra-śāstra tradition.

title: The sutra on not rejecting the buddha
The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called the Eight Maṇḍalas
explainer: Toh 277 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-aṣṭa-maṇḍalakaṃ nāma mahāyānasūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Kyil Khor Gyé pa Shyejawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do, rendered in English as The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle called The Eight Maṇḍalas. The text belongs to the sūtra class of canonical Buddhist scripture and opens in the customary manner, with the Buddha residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, attended by a large assembly of monks and an extensive gathering of bodhisattvas. As its title suggests, the sūtra centers on the subject of maṇḍalas — sacred ritual or contemplative circles — treated within a Mahāyāna doctrinal framework. It was translated into Tibetan by Jñānasena and his collaborators, then edited and finalized in accordance with standard translation conventions of the period.

title: The Noble Recollection of the Buddha
explainer: The Noble Recollection of the Buddha, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-buddha-anusmṛti and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangyé Drénpa, is a short devotional text belonging to the broader tradition of buddhānusmṛti, or mindful recollection of the Buddha's qualities. It enumerates the sublime attributes of the buddhas and serves as a support for contemplative practice centered on calling the Buddha to mind. The text is Toh 279 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the general class of dhāraṇī and ritual texts, and it was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian preceptor Surendrabodhi together with the great editor-translator the monk Yeshé Dé.

title: Recollection of the Dharma
explainer: Toh 280 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical text known in Sanskrit as the Dharma-anusmṛti and in Tibetan as Chos rjes su dran pa, meaning "Recollection of the Dharma" in English. It belongs to the traditional series of recollection practices — anusmṛti — in which the practitioner meditates upon and praises the qualities of the Three Jewels, and this particular text is devoted to extolling the virtues of the Dharma as proclaimed by the buddhas. The text describes the sublime Dharma as well proclaimed, wholesome throughout, perfectly pure, and directly knowable by the wise, drawing on formulations found widely across Buddhist tradition. As the opening lines indicate, it follows immediately after the Recollection of the Buddhas in the canonical sequence, situating it within a broader collection of devotional recollection texts in the Kangyur.

title: Recollection of the Saṅgha
explainer: Toh 281 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical text known in Sanskrit as the Saṅghānusmṛti and in Tibetan as Dge 'dun rjes su dran pa, meaning "Recollection of the Saṅgha." It belongs to a traditional set of devotional recollections — which also include the recollection of the Buddha and the Dharma — and enumerates the noble qualities of the ārya saṅgha, praising the community of noble practitioners as having entered the path well, rightly, harmoniously, and straightforwardly, and as being supremely worthy of homage, reverence, and generosity. As a brief praise and recollection text, it functions both as a devotional practice and as a concise doctrinal statement of what makes the saṅgha a refuge and a field of merit. It is classified among the sūtra-related works of the Kangyur and would traditionally be recited alongside its companion recollection texts as part of foundational Buddhist practice.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Entitled 'The Three Aggregates'
explainer: Toh 284 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryatriskandhaka-nāma-mahāyānasūtra and in Tibetan as the Phung po gsum pa, meaning "The Three Aggregates" or, as an alternate rendering suggests, "The Three Bodies." It is a relatively concise scripture in which the Buddha, dwelling at the Dharma-grove hermitage, sets forth a practice centered on paying homage to the buddhas of past, present, and future, confessing misdeeds, and rejoicing in virtue — the three "aggregates" or collections of meritorious action that give the text its name. The sūtra is notable for its devotional orientation and its vision of the buddhas as endowed with boundless wisdom, the dharmakāya, and the dharmadhātu. It belongs to the general sūtra section of the Kangyur and has been widely used in Tibetan Buddhism as a liturgical confession and purification text.

title: The Great Sūtra Called the Reception by Bimbisāra of Solid Form
explainer: The Great Sūtra Called the Reception by Bimbisāra, known in Sanskrit as the Pimpisāra Pratyungamana Mahāsūtra and in Tibetan as Mdo chen po gzugs can snying pos bsu ba, is a canonical Buddhist sūtra recounting the famous meeting between the Buddha and King Bimbisāra of Magadha. The text opens with the Buddha travelling through Magadha accompanied by a great assembly of a thousand monks — all former matted-hair ascetics and accomplished arhats — as he makes his way toward the bamboo grove of Supratișṭhita, setting the scene for the royal reception that gives the sūtra its name. This narrative belongs to a well-known episode in early Buddhist literature in which the king, having previously pledged to welcome the Buddha upon his attainment of awakening, fulfills that vow. It is Toh 289 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the general sūtras of the canon.

title: The Great Sūtra Called Emptiness
explainer: Toh 290 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in English as The Great Sūtra Called Emptiness, in Sanskrit as the Śūnyatā-nāma-mahāsūtra, and in Tibetan as Mdo chen po stong pa nyid ces bya ba. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and takes as its central concern the Buddha's direct teaching on emptiness, presented through a dialogue between the Buddha and his attendant Ānanda at the Eastern Park in Śrāvastī. The exchange is prompted by Ānanda's recollection of a statement the Buddha had once made among the Śākyas — that he dwells repeatedly in emptiness — and his wish to understand its deeper meaning. As a "great sūtra" dedicated entirely to this theme, the text offers a sustained and focused exposition of emptiness as a meditative reality and a fundamental characteristic of experience.

title: The Great Sūtra Called Great Emptiness
explainer: Toh 291 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Mahāśūnyatā-nāma-mahāsūtra and in Tibetan as the Mdo chen po stong pa nyid chen po zhes bya ba, rendered in English as "The Great Sūtra Called Great Emptiness."
