As its title suggests, this is a Mahāyāna sūtra concerned with the theme of great emptiness, one of the profound philosophical pillars of Buddhist thought. The text opens with the Buddha residing at Kapilavāstu, the city associated with his own Śākyan clan, where he goes on an alms round before making his way to a Śākyan temple, setting the stage for the teachings that follow. It belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur, the collection of texts attributed to the word of the Buddha himself.

title: The Great Sūtra Called The Five-and-Three
explainer: The Great Sūtra Called The Five-and-Three, known in Sanskrit as the Pañcatriyanāma Mahāsūtra and in Tibetan as Mdo chen po lnga gsum pa zhes bya ba, is a Buddhist sūtra in which the Buddha addresses a gathering of monks at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove. The text concerns the various metaphysical positions held by ascetics and brahmins regarding perception, non-perception, annihilation, and liberation, systematically examining the views through which such thinkers make declarations about existence and the self. Its title appears to reflect a structural arrangement of five and three categories that organize the discourse. It is Toh 294 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general class of sūtra literature.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Hurled Stone
explainer: Toh 295 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-śilākṣipta-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa rdo 'phangs pa'i mdo, rendered into English as The Noble Sūtra of the Hurled Stone. It belongs to the general class of canonical sūtra literature and recounts an episode in which the Buddha, wandering through the territory of the Mallas and resting in a dense grove of sal trees, instructs the Venerable Ānanda to accompany him toward the city of Kuśa. The narrative unfolds against the backdrop of a large assembly of Malla warriors gathered in council, suggesting the text is concerned with teachings or events arising from this dramatic social and political setting. As a canonical sūtra attributed to the direct speech of the Buddha, it is preserved among the sūtra collections of the Kangyur.

title: Sūtra of the Youth Similes
explainer: The Sūtra of the Youth Similes, known in Sanskrit as the Kumāradṛṣṭānta Sūtra and in Tibetan as the Gzhon nu dpe'i mdo, is a discourse in which the Buddha responds to the skepticism of King Prasenajit of Kosala, who doubts that so young a teacher could have attained the highest awakening. The Buddha addresses this doubt through a series of similes illustrating that youth is no barrier to greatness or danger, gently but firmly establishing the authenticity of his enlightenment in dialogue with the king at Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī. It belongs to the sūtra literature of the Kangyur and is classified as Toh 296, placed among the individual discourses that make up the general collection of canonical teachings attributed directly to the Buddha.

title: The sutra on timings for the gandhi
The sutra on having moral discipline
Sūtra Examining the Virtuous and Non-Virtuous Results of the Five Classes of Transgressions
explainer: The Sūtra Examining the Virtuous and Non-Virtuous Results of the Five Classes of Transgressions, known in Sanskrit as the Pañcapātanikāyaśubhāśubhaphalapārīkṣāsūtra and in Tibetan as the Ltung ba sde lnga'i dge ba dang mi dge ba'i 'bras bu brtag pa'i mdo, is a canonical Buddhist sūtra in which the Buddha, speaking to an assembly of monks at Śrāvastī, examines the karmic fruits — virtuous and non-virtuous — associated with the five classes of transgressions recognized in Buddhist ethical and vinaya thought. The text proceeds by elaborating the cosmological framework of divine realms and their lifespans, situating the consequences of moral conduct within a vast vision of cyclic existence. It is Toh 304 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general category of sūtra literature.

title: Exposition of the Qualities Refined through the Path of Liberation
explainer: Toh 306 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Vimuktamārgadhutaguṇanirdeśa and in Tibetan as the Exposition of the Qualities Refined through the Path of Liberation. It is a discourse on the ascetic or "dhūta" qualities — a set of refined spiritual practices cultivated through disciplined renunciation — presented as essential virtues for yogic practitioners who aspire to liberation through perfectly pure moral conduct. The text enumerates qualities such as few desires, contentment, modest requisites, diligent effort, and the thorough cutting off of attachment, framing these as the foundation for guarding and deepening ethical practice. It belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur and opens with a homage to Mañjuśrī, suggesting a connection to that bodhisattva's association with wisdom and spiritual instruction.

title: Sutra on the limits of lifes duration
The Great Sūtra of Entering the Noble City of Vaiśālī
explainer: Toh 312 in the Kangyur is a large sūtra known in English as The Great Sūtra of Entering the Noble City of Vaiśālī, in Sanskrit as the Ārya Vaiśālī Praveśa Mahāsūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa yangs pa'i grong khyer du 'jug pa'i mdo chen po. It belongs to the general class of Mahāyāna sūtras and recounts teachings given by the Buddha as he journeyed to and dwelt in the celebrated city of Vaiśālī, a place of great significance in early Buddhist history, arriving at the mango grove of Ambapālī in the company of his attendant Ānanda. The text opens with the Buddha setting out from a resting place among the reeds of a marsh, suggesting a narrative connected to the final period of his life and perhaps to events associated with his last testament. As part of the Kangyur, it preserves canonical teachings attributed directly to the Buddha and transmitted through the traditional formula of dependent witnessing.

title: The Noble Auspicious Night Sūtra
explainer: Toh 313 in the Kangyur is a short sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Bhadrakatrī Nāma Sūtra and in Tibetan as "The Noble Auspicious Night." The text belongs to the general sūtra literature of the Kangyur and takes the form of a nocturnal encounter in which a radiant deity descends to the bank of the Tapotā river near Rājagṛha and addresses a monk seated there in the night, prompting a teaching connected to auspicious conduct and the Dharma. The setting at Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, places it within the classic framework of the Buddha's discourses, and the celestial visitor's appearance lends the text a luminous, devotional character. Though brief, the sūtra conveys an emphasis on practicing loving-kindness and the Dharma day and night, virtues celebrated as the hallmarks of the truly auspicious life.

title: The sutra of the entry into the gloomy forest
The sutra on ones father and mother
The Noble Sūtra of the Four Truths
explainer: The Noble Sūtra of the Four Truths, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Catuḥsatya Sūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Denpa Shyi'i Do (འཕགས་པ་བདེན་པ་བཞིའི་མདོ།), is a sūtra in which the Buddha expounds the Four Noble Truths to an assembly of monks, emphasizing that ignorance of these truths is the very cause of beings' continued wandering in saṃsāra. The teaching is set at a royal residence between the cities of Campā and Rājagṛha, where the Buddha addresses his monastics directly in the first person, underscoring the shared journey of teacher and disciples through cycles of existence. This text is Toh 316 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the general class of sūtra literature.

title: The Noble Dharma Teaching Called 'The Vast Meaning'
explainer: The Noble Synonym of Dharma Called "The Vast Meaning," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-arthavistara-nāma-dharmaparyāya and in Tibetan as Pakpa Dön Gyépa Zhéjawa'i Chö Kyi Rgyacher Röpa, is a sūtra in which the Venerable Śāriputra, at the Buddha's residence in Jeta Grove near Śrāvastī, expounds to the assembled monks a teaching described as wholesome throughout — in its beginning, middle, and end — and that illuminates the holy life through an extended enumeration of synonyms for the Dharma. The text belongs to the genre of dharmaparyāya, or Dharma discourse, a form concerned with conveying the Buddha's teaching in richly elaborated terms. It is Toh 318 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha, and was translated into Tibetan by the monk Yeshé Dé, one of the foremost translators of the early transmission period.

title: The dharma discourse describing the benefits of establishing representations of the tathagatha
The Collection of Purposeful Utterances
explainer: Toh 326 in the Kangyur is a canonical Buddhist scripture known in Sanskrit as the Udānavarga and in Tibetan as the Cheddu Jöpé Tsom, meaning The Collection of Purposeful Utterances. It is a collection of inspired or solemn verses attributed to the Buddha, organized into topical chapters, and represents an expanded Indic compilation related to the Pali Udāna and Dhammapada traditions, gathering pithy sayings and verse teachings spoken by the Buddha on various occasions. The text opens with homage to the Omniscient One and moves swiftly into verses on impermanence, the urgency of spiritual practice, and the nature of suffering, setting a tone of earnest moral and contemplative instruction aimed at motivating practitioners. As a verse anthology of the Buddha's direct speech, it belongs to the broader class of sūtra literature within the Kangyur.

title: The sutra of nandas going forth
Sūtra of the Terraced House
explainer: The Sūtra of the Terraced House, known in Sanskrit as the Kūṭāgārasūtra and in Tibetan as the Khang bu brtsegs pa'i mdo, is a short sūtra in which the venerable Ānanda asks the Buddha about the fruits of various meritorious acts — including making offerings of flowers, creating a maṇḍala, taking refuge, and observing the precepts of training. The Buddha's replies offer guidance on the karmic results of these foundational practices, making the text a practical teaching on the accumulation of virtue and the path of devotion. It is Toh 332 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general collection of sūtras, and is set in the familiar framing of the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, one of the most common settings for the Buddha's discourses.

title: The rite of the commitment to bear the mendicants staff
The sutra of the wise and foolish
The questions of dirghanakha the wandering mendicant
The hundred accounts of noble deeds beginning with that of purna
The exemplary tale about a sow
The account of the noble deeds of sumagadha
The Narrative of the Deeds of Moonlight
explainer: The Candraprabha Avadāna, known in Tibetan as the Narrative of the Deeds of Moonlight, is a canonical Buddhist narrative belonging to the avadāna genre — a class of text that recounts legendary deeds and their karmic consequences, typically to illustrate the workings of cause and effect across lifetimes. This particular text opens at Rājagṛha, where the Buddha's monks, troubled by the passing into nirvāṇa of the two great disciples Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, seek the Blessed One's guidance on matters of doubt. It is catalogued as Toh 348 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha himself, and falls within the broader category of avadāna literature found in that collection. The text was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian preceptor Jinamitra together with the great-revision translator, the monk Devacandra.

title: The Noble Sūtra of Prince Siddhārtha
explainer: The Noble Sūtra of Prince Siddhārtha, known in Sanskrit as the Arthasiddhi Sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa rgyal bu don grub kyi mdo, is a canonical Buddhist sūtra recounting events centered on the Buddha and his attendant Ānanda. The text opens at Śrāvastī, where the Buddha's sudden smile prompts Ānanda to inquire into its cause, setting the stage for a narrative likely connected to the life and spiritual significance of Prince Siddhārtha. It is Toh 351 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general category of sūtra literature, and appears to have been preceded in the same manuscript volume by a related work called "The Prior Connection of the Golden Hue," suggesting it forms part of a sequence of narratively linked texts. As a sūtra of the Kangyur, it preserves teachings and stories attributed to the historical Buddha, presented within the traditional framework of an account heard and transmitted by Ānanda.

title: The Sūtra of Brahma's Net
explainer: The Brahmajāla Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Tsangpé Drawé Do (Tshang pa'i dra ba'i mdo), or "The Sūtra of Brahma's Net," is a discourse in which the Buddha, traveling through Magadha with a large assembly of monks, laypeople, and wandering mendicants, sets out an extensive analysis of the views held by various religious teachers of his day. The text takes its evocative title from the image of Brahmā's celestial net, whose countless jeweled nodes serve as a metaphor for the interconnected web of speculative doctrines — concerning the self, the world, and ultimate existence — that the Buddha systematically examines and transcends. It belongs to a class of early sūtra literature concerned with distinguishing the Buddha's teaching from the philosophical and ascetic movements of ancient India, and it is particularly notable for its detailed enumeration of sixty-two wrong views. This work is Toh 352 in the Kangyur, where it is preserved among the sūtra collections.

title: The sutra of repaying the kindness of the buddha who has great skill in means
Teaching the causes and results of good and ill
The sutra that teaches the ripening of virtuous and nonvirtuous actions
From the Sūtra Requested by the Noble Candragarbha: A Prophecy on How the Buddha's Teaching Abides and Declines
explainer: Toh 356 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in English as "A Prophecy on How the Buddha's Teaching Abides and Declines," drawn from the larger Sūtra Requested by the Noble Candragarbha, which is known in Sanskrit as the Candragarbhaparipṛcchā and in Tibetan as Zla ba'i snying pos zhus pa'i mdo. It belongs to the class of Mahāyāna sūtras and concerns itself with the duration and eventual decline of the Buddhist teaching, presenting a prophetic account spoken by the Buddha Śākyamuni while dwelling on Mount Ṛkṣavat in the presence of an extraordinary assembly of bodhisattvas, arhats, gods, nāgas, and other beings. The text opens dramatically with rays of light blazing from between the Buddha's brows and illuminating the four continents, signaling the importance of the revelation that follows. As part of the Kangyur, it sits among the canonical scriptures regarded as the word of the Buddha, and its subject matter — the fate and longevity of the Dharma — places it within a prominent tradition of prophetic sūtra literature concerned with the preservation of the teaching across time.

title: The Sūtra Called the Twelve Eyes
explainer: The Sūtra Called the Twelve Eyes, known in Sanskrit as the Dvādaśalocana-nāma-sūtra and in Tibetan as Mig bcu gnyis pa zhes bya ba'i mdo, is a Buddhist sūtra concerned with the interpretation of celestial omens and the divinatory science traditionally known as the Twelve Eyes. The text is set in Rājagṛha, where King Rūpahṛdaya, troubled by alarming signs in the sky — lightning, falling stars, and meteoric iron — is directed by his brahmin astrologers toward this body of knowledge, prompting him to seek clarification from the Buddha himself. It belongs to the sūtra literature of the Kangyur and was translated into Tibetan by the Indian abbot Ajitaśrībhadra together with the great translator Śākyaod. It is catalogued as Toh 359 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the general sūtras.

title: The sutra of the fourty two sections
The True Names of Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Being, in Their Ultimate Sense — a Song of Praise
explainer: Toh 360 in the Kangyur is the Mañjuśrī-jñānasattvasya-paramārthanāma-saṃgīti, known in Tibetan as the Jampal Yeshe Sempe Döndam Tshen Yangdakpar Jöpa, and rendered in English as "The True Names of Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Being, in Their Ultimate Sense — a Song of Praise." It is a celebrated tantric praise-hymn, or nāmasaṃgīti, devoted to the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in his aspect as the embodiment of non-dual wisdom, and it recounts his names and attributes in verse as a means of conveying the deepest nature of awakened mind. The text opens with the great Vajrapāṇi, lord of secret mantra, addressing the Buddha and requesting the teaching, establishing the work firmly within the Vajrayāna liturgical and doctrinal tradition. Widely regarded as one of the most important texts in Indo-Tibetan tantric Buddhism, it sits within the tantra section of the Kangyur and has generated an exceptionally rich commentarial literature across multiple schools of Tibetan Buddhism.

title: The Glorious Kālacakra Subsequent Tantra: Heart of the Subsequent Tantra
sanskrit: Śrī Kālacakra Tantrōttara Tantra Hṛdaya Nāma
explainer: Toh 363 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Kālacakra Tantrōttara Tantra Hṛdaya, and in Tibetan as the Dpal Dus Kyi 'Khor Lo'i Rgyud Phyi Ma Rgyud Kyi Snying Po, rendered in English as "The Heart of the Subsequent Tantra of the Glorious Kālacakra." It belongs to the Kālacakra cycle, one of the most elaborate and celebrated systems within the Vajrayāna tradition, and serves as a condensed or essential extraction drawn from the Subsequent Tantra of the Kālacakra. The text is set within the legendary kingdom of Śambhala, where, in the palace of Kalāpa, the teachings on the king of tantras are proclaimed to assembled sages, weaving together cosmological, astrological, and soteriological themes that are characteristic of the Kālacakra system. As part of the Kangyur, it is classified among the tantric scriptures and opens with a homage to Mañjuśrī, situating it within a tradition that regards this wisdom deity as a presiding presence over the revelation of these profound teachings.

title: The Heart of the Tantra Called the Glorious Wheel of Time
explainer: Toh 364 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Kālacakra Garbha Nāma Tantra and in Tibetan as the Dpal Dus Kyi 'Khor Lo Zhes Bya Ba'i Rgyud Kyi Snying Po, rendered in English as The Heart of the Tantra Called the Glorious Wheel of Time. It belongs to the Kālacakra cycle, one of the most elaborate and celebrated traditions within Vajrayāna Buddhism, dealing with cosmology, time, the subtle body, and the path to liberation through tantric practice. The text is cast in the form of a tantra, opening with a homage to Mañjuśrī and a request by King Candrabhadra, and it presents in condensed verse the essential teachings of the Wheel of Time system, including meditative absorption, vital energies, and the means of liberation particularly suited to an age of strife. As the "heart" or essence of the broader Kālacakra Tantra, it distills key doctrinal and practical elements of that tradition and is preserved among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur.

title: The Rite of Empowerment
explainer: Toh 365 in the Kangyur is a tantric ritual text known in Sanskrit as the Śekaprakriyā and in Tibetan as the Rite of Empowerment, or Dbang gi rab tu byed pa. It is a liturgical and instructional work concerned with the conferral of empowerments, describing in detail the ceremonies by which disciples are introduced into a maṇḍala, consecrated through vase and other empowerments, and bound by the appropriate vows and precepts. The text invokes the compassionate bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and proceeds through the stages of ripening initiates into particular tantric families, outlining the ritual actions, symbolic adornments, and ethical commitments — including the five precepts against killing, false speech, taking another's consort, theft, and intoxicants — that govern those who enter the path. As a work belonging to the tantric or Vajrayāna portion of the Kangyur, it represents the kind of practical ceremonial manual that would guide a qualified master in conducting empowerment rites within the context of Buddhist tantric tradition.

title: Subsequent Tantra of the Glorious Union with All Buddhas, the Illusory Net of the Ḍākinī, the Supreme Bliss
sanskrit: Śrī Sarvabuddha Samayoga Ḍākinījāla Saṃvara Nāma Uttara Tantra
explainer: Toh 366 in the Kangyur is a Vajrayāna tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Sarvabuddha Samayoga Ḍākinījāla Saṃvara Uttara Tantra and in Tibetan as the Dpal sangs rgyas thams cad dang mnyam par sbyor ba mkha' 'gro ma sgyu ma bde ba'i mchog, rendered in English as the Subsequent Tantra of the Glorious Union with All Buddhas, the Illusory Net of the Ḍākinī, the Supreme Bliss. It belongs to the class of Highest Yoga Tantras and is presented as a "subsequent" or continuation tantra, meaning it elaborates on and supplements a root tantra of the same cycle devoted to the union of all buddhas. The text centers on Vajrasattva as the embodiment of all buddhas, on the figure of the ḍākinī as the supreme illusory expression of non-dual bliss, and on the esoteric principle that the illusory net of feminine energy is the highest vehicle transcending both attachment and renunciation. As a canonical Vajrayāna tantra, it is placed among the Anuttarayoga tantric scriptures of the Kangyur, the collection of translated words of the Buddha in the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: Compendium of All Conceptuality: The Uttara-Uttara Tantra of the Ḍākinī-Net Union with All Buddhas Called the Compendium of All Conceptuality
explainer: Toh 367 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Sarvakalpasamuccaya-nāma-sarvabuddhasamayoga-ḍākinījāla-saṃvara-uttarottara-tantra, rendered in Tibetan as the Uttara-Uttara Tantra of the Illusory Bliss-Supreme Ḍākinī-Net Union with All Buddhas, Called the Compendium of All Conceptuality. It belongs to the class of highest yoga tantras and concerns the union of all buddhas through the ḍākinī-net, centering on Vajrasattva as the embodiment of great bliss and the essence of all awakened beings. The text opens with homage to Vajrasattva and proceeds in verse, celebrating the non-conceptual mind in which suchness abides, the supreme secret of great attachment and great bliss, and the all-encompassing nature of tantric realization. As the closing colophon of the preceding chapter makes clear, this scripture is organized around the metaphor of the great wheel-turning of all conceptuality, and it sits within the tantra section of the Kangyur as a scripture of the ḍākinī-net or Saṃvara cycle.

title: The Glorious Concise Saṃvara, King of Tantras
explainer: The Glorious Concise Saṃvara, King of Tantras — known in Sanskrit as the Tantra-rāja-śrī-laghu-saṃvara and in Tibetan as the Rgyud kyi rgyal po dpal bde mchog nyung ngu — is a tantric scripture belonging to the tradition of the Cakrasaṃvara or Heruka cycle, one of the most important systems of Yoginī or Mother Tantra in Vajrayāna Buddhism. The text presents itself as a condensed or "concise" version of the Saṃvara teachings, opening with a homage to Vajrasattva and proceeding in verse to expound the secret doctrine of supreme bliss, the nature of the ḍākinīs, and the samaya vows that bind practitioners within this tradition. Its poetry moves through themes of non-duality, self-arisen awareness, and the inseparability of all phenomena within the nature of great bliss, characteristic concerns of the highest tantric literature. It is Toh 368 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the tantric texts, and represents a key scriptural authority within the broader Saṃvara tantric corpus.

title: The Subsequent Tantra Called the Vajra Ḍākinī
explainer: Toh 371 in the Kangyur is a Vajrayāna tantric scripture known in English as the Subsequent Tantra Called the Vajra Ḍākinī, in Sanskrit as the Vajraḍāka-nāma-uttaratantra, and in Tibetan as the Rdo rje mkha' 'gro zhes bya ba'i rgyud phyi ma. As its Sanskrit title indicates, it is a "subsequent" or continuation tantra, functioning as a companion or supplementary text to a root tantra of the same cycle centered on Vajraḍākinī, a wrathful and enlightened feminine deity closely associated with secret wisdom, bliss, and the nature of reality. The text belongs to the class of Highest Yoga Tantra and opens with verses extolling Vajraḍākinī as a self-arisen, non-dual primordial wisdom embodied in all women and identified with the supreme bliss that transcends attachment, freedom, and conventional philosophical categories. It sits within the Kangyur's tantric section, where such texts transmitting esoteric teachings on deity yoga, ḍākinī practice, and the realization of awakening through tantric means are collected.

title: The tantra of the arising of samvara
The Glorious Manifest Arising of the Blood-Drinker
explainer: Toh 374 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in English as "The Glorious Manifest Arising of the Blood-Drinker," given in Sanskrit as the Śrī Herukābhyudaya and in Tibetan as the Dpal khrag 'thung mngon par 'byung ba. It belongs to the class of Yoganiruttara or Highest Yoga Tantra texts centered on the deity Heruka, a wrathful blood-drinking form associated with advanced Vajrayāna practice. The text opens with verses proclaiming an esoteric teaching of supreme wonder, emphasizing that accomplishment is attained through practice unconstrained by conventional ritual observances such as auspicious dates, purification rites, fasting, or the social customs of ordinary householders. As Toh 374 in the Kangyur, it is preserved among the canonical tantric scriptures of the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and reflects the antinomian spirit characteristic of the Heruka cycle of teachings.

title: The Conduct of the Yoginī
explainer: Toh 375 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist tantric text known in English as The Conduct of the Yoginī, in Sanskrit as the Yoginīsañcārya, and in Tibetan as the Rnal 'byor ma'i kun tu spyod pa. It belongs to the class of Yoginī tantras within the Kangyur's collection of tantric scriptures, and it concerns the esoteric rites and modes of conduct associated with advanced Vajrayāna practice, including the sequential and reversed orders of arising, the reading of signs, and the cultivation of great bliss through the path of yoga. The text opens with a homage to the glorious Vajrasattva and a verse salutation to the guru as vajra-holder, through whose grace the state of great bliss is said to be attained in a single instant. Its content is presented as an explication of teachings that remain concealed within the broader tantric corpus, laid out as a practical guide for the accomplished yogic practitioner.

title: The Tantra Called the Union of the Four Yoginīs
explainer: The Union of the Four Yoginīs, known in Sanskrit as the Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭatantra and in Tibetan as Naljorma Zhiyi Khasbyorgy Gyud, is a tantric scripture belonging to the class of Yoginī or Mother Tantras within Tibetan Buddhist esotericism. The text concerns the symbolic and meditative union of four yoginīs associated with the four directional faces, the five elements, and the interplay of vowels and consonants, presenting these as keys concealed throughout the tantras and here set forth in systematic exposition. It opens with homage to the glorious Vajrapāṇi and proceeds in verse, unfolding doctrinal content related to subtle-body geography, including the navel center, the principles of moon and sun, and sensory and elemental correspondences. This text is Toh 376 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the tantric scriptures of that collection.

title: The Awakening Named Vajravārāhī: From the Subsequent Tantra of the Explicit Explanation
sanskrit: Ākhyāta Tantrottara Vajravāhyābhidhānāda Vārāhya Vibodhanam Nāma
explainer: Toh 377 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Ākhyāta Tantrottara Vajra Vāhya Abhidhānāda Vārāhya Vibodhanam, and in Tibetan as a chapter on the manifest awakening of Vajravārāhī drawn from the Subsequent Tantra of the Explicit Explanation of Vajravārāhī. It belongs to the class of yoginī tantras within the Vajrayāna tradition, centering on the deity Vajravārāhī and presenting a condensed yoga practice said to fulfill all desired aims, illuminating the guru lineage for the benefit of practitioners. The text takes the form of a tantric chapter in verse, describing esoteric teachings associated with the ḍākinīs and the attainment of siddhi for yogins. It was translated into Tibetan by Chingwa Yönten Bar and subsequently reviewed and finalized in consultation with two paṇḍitas of that period.

title: The King of Tantras Called the Manifest Arising of Vajravārāhī, the Inconceivable Vajra Wisdom of the Non-Dual Mind of All Ḍākinīs
sanskrit: Ḍākinī Sarva Citta Advaya Acitta Jñāna Vajra Vārāhī Abhibhava Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: Toh 378 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in English as The King of Tantras Called the Manifest Arising of Vajravārāhī, the Inconceivable Vajra Wisdom of the Non-Dual Mind of All Ḍākinīs, with the Sanskrit title Ḍākinī Sarva Citta Advaya Acitta Jñāna Vajra Vārāhī Abhibhava Tantra Rāja and the Tibetan title Mkha' 'gro ma thams cad kyi thugs gnyis su med pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i ye shes rdo rje phag mo mngon par 'byung ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po. It belongs to the class of Anuttarayoga or highest yoga tantras and centers on the fierce female deity Vajravārāhī, presenting her as the embodiment of inconceivable co-emergent wisdom and the non-dual mind of all ḍākinīs. The text opens in the classic sūtra-style setting of the Buddha — here identified with the wrathful Heruka — dwelling at a great charnel ground together with his five consorts, establishing the revelatory context for the tantra's teachings. As a tantra of the Vajrayāna tradition preserved in the Kangyur, it belongs to the tantric section of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: Toh 379 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Tibetan as "Dur khrod bda
explainer: Toh 379 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Tibetan as "Dur khrod bdag mo'i gsol pa" and associated with the deity Vārāhī, the sow-headed vajrayāna goddess also known in Sanskrit as Vārāhī. It belongs to the class of Highest Yoga Tantra texts and takes the form of a dialogue in which the Mistress of the Charnel Ground petitions the hero Heruka with questions concerning the body colors of the assembled goddesses, the meaning of the name Vārāhī, the significance of the seed syllables, and the nature of the generation and completion stages. Heruka's responses unfold as a teaching on the five wisdoms, the qualities of pacification, and liberation within the unchanging basic space of one's own mind, placing the text firmly within the Cakrasaṃvara or Heruka cycle of tantric literature. As Toh 379 in the Kangyur, it sits among the tantra section of the canonical collection of Buddha's translated word preserved in the Tibetan tradition.

title: The Sādhana of Vajrayoginī the Wisdom-Holder
explainer: Toh 380 in the Kangyur is a sādhana known in Sanskrit as the Vidyādhariṇī Vajrayoginī Sādhana Nāma and in Tibetan as the Sādhana of Vajrayoginī the Wisdom-Holder. It is a ritual and contemplative practice text belonging to the Vajrayāna tradition, presenting a structured method of visualization and meditation focused on Vajrayoginī, a prominent female tantric deity associated with wisdom and liberation. The text draws on the Great Net of Illusion tantra, grounding its instructions in the non-dual, dream-like nature of appearances arising from the heart center, and guides the practitioner through the generation of the deity from a seed syllable. It was translated into Tibetan from Sanskrit by the translator Gyi Jodawa Dawé Özer working from the oral teaching of the paṇḍita Gayadhara, and sits among the tantric sādhana literature of the Kangyur.

title: Toh 382 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture belonging to the class of highest
explainer: Toh 382 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture belonging to the class of highest yoga tantra, known in Tibetan as a section treating the profound esoteric doctrine of bindus — subtle drops or essential points — within the context of the self-arisen deity and the great elements. The text opens with the bodhisattva Vajragarbha and other great beings making offerings and prostrating before the Blessed One, then posing questions in verse about the nature of the self-arisen, its relation to the supreme deity, and the inner meaning of union with all buddhas, situating it within the genre of dialogic tantric revelation. While a distinct Sanskrit title is not clearly determinable from the available material, the scripture is framed as a teaching on the deepest secret of nondual bliss and the central element understood through inference. The colophon notes that the translation was written after Kongba examined and made revisions, indicating it passed through a phase of editorial refinement characteristic of later canonical transmission in Tibet.

title: The Glorious Secret Vajra, King of Tantras
explainer: Toh 383 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist tantra known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Guhyavajra Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal Gsang Ba Rdo Rje Rgyud Kyi Rgyal Po, rendered in English as the Glorious Secret Vajra, King of Tantras. It is a tantric scripture belonging to the class of esoteric teachings, structured as a dialogue between the Blessed One and a goddess identified as the Goddess of the Beautiful Long Eyes, in which she requests instruction on the profound and secret wheel — a teaching said to surpass what is disclosed in other tantras. The text opens with a series of questions about the nature of the secret, the wheel, the vajra, and the lotus, inviting systematic exposition of tantric doctrine centered on binding vows and hidden knowledge. As its title suggests, it belongs among the highest register of tantric literature in the Kangyur, presenting itself as a king among tantras and engaging themes of secrecy, initiation, and esoteric realization.

title: Glorious king tantra resolves all secrets
The Glorious Cakrasaṃvara, King of Tantras, the Secret and Inconceivable
explainer: Toh 385 in the Kangyur is known in English as The Glorious Cakrasaṃvara, King of Tantras, the Secret and Inconceivable, in Sanskrit as the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Guhyācintya Tantrarāja, and in Tibetan as Dpal 'khor lo sdom pa gsang ba bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po. It is a tantra of the Highest Yoga class belonging to the Mother Tantra tradition, centered on the deity Cakrasaṃvara, also known as Heruka, and concerned with the secret and inconceivable nature of saṃsāric phenomena, the union of great bliss and emptiness, and the esoteric teachings imparted by the Blessed One to Vajrapāṇi and an assembled retinue. The text opens in the classic sūtra-style frame of "thus did I hear," situating the Buddha in meditative union with a vajra-queen as the embodiment of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, before moving into verse dialogue on the ultimate nature of conventional appearances. As Toh 385 in the Kangyur, it belongs to the tantric section of that great Tibetan canonical collection and stands as one of the important scriptural sources for the Cakrasaṃvara cycle, which occupies a central place in the Vajrayāna traditions of Tibet.

title: The tantra Equal to the Sky
The Glorious King of Tantras of the Great Sky
explainer: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Great Sky, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Mahākha Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as Dpal Nam mkha' chen po'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, is a Buddhist tantric scripture belonging to the Kangyur, where it is catalogued as Toh 387. It is a tantra of the highest class, set within the visionary framework of the Blessed One dwelling in union with a vajra lady amid an assembly of heroes and ḍākinīs, a setting characteristic of Anuttarayoga or similar advanced tantric literature. The text opens with the bodhisattva Vajrahṛdaya posing a series of profound questions to the Buddha regarding what is subdued, what is possessed, and what constitutes the great fear, inviting a doctrinal exposition that unfolds in verse and prose. As its title suggests, the scripture is centrally concerned with the symbolism and realization of the great sky — an expression pointing to the vast, unobstructed nature of mind and reality as understood in Vajrayāna Buddhism.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of Body, Speech, and Mind
sanskrit: Śrī Kāya Vāk Citta Tantra Rāja
explainer: The Glorious King of Tantras of Body, Speech, and Mind, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Kāya Vāk Citta Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Palden Ku Sung Tuk Gi Gyud Kyi Gyalpo, is a Buddhist tantric scripture centering on the inseparable nature of body, speech, and mind as understood within Vajrayana practice. The text opens with a dialogue between a supplicant and Vajradhara, who expounds on the symbolic identities of body, speech, and mind with the vase, the secret, and primordial wisdom respectively, situating these teachings within a broader mandala of buddha figures including Māmakī, Samayatārā, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī. It is classified as a tantra and belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur, where it is catalogued as Toh 388. The text was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Gayādhara together with the monk-translator Śākyaśes, a well-known collaborative pair responsible for transmitting several important tantric works into Tibet.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras: The Precious Garland
explainer: The Glorious King of Tantras, the Precious Garland, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Ratnamālā Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal Rin Chen Phreng Ba'i Rgyud Kyi Rgyal Po, is a Buddhist tantric text belonging to the class of Highest Yoga Tantra associated with the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. It takes the form of a dialogue in which a goddess petitions Vajradhara to explain the meaning of the "precious garland" — a threefold teaching concerning the jewel of the vessel-world, the jewel of sentient beings, and a third jewel transcending both — as it relates to the practice of Cakrasaṃvara. The text is Toh 389 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the tantras, and its opening homage to Glorious Mahāsukha situates it firmly within the bliss-centered soteriology characteristic of the Cakrasaṃvara tantric tradition.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Great Commitment
explainer: Toh 390 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in English as The Glorious King of Tantras of the Great Commitment, corresponding to the Sanskrit Śrī Mahāsamaya Tantra Rāja and the Tibetan Dpal dam pa chen po'i rgyud kyi rgyal po. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric texts and concerns the samaya, or sacred commitments and vows, that practitioners undertake within the tantric path, presented through the voice of the bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressing an assembly of yoginīs. The text opens in the characteristic manner of a buddha-word scripture, with the Blessed One abiding in meditative absorption within a tantric setting, framing the ensuing teachings on commitment and conduct as a direct revelation. Translated into Tibetan by the Indian abbot Ratnavajra together with the translator-monk Śākya Yeshe and later revised against a subsequent manuscript, it is preserved among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious Tantra King of Great Power
explainer: Toh 391 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Mahābala Tantra Rāja, in Tibetan as Dpal stobs po che'i rgyud kyi rgyal po (The Glorious Tantra King of Great Power), and in English as The Glorious King of Tantras of Great Power. It belongs to the class of Vajrayāna tantric texts and opens in the manner of a buddha-word sūtra, describing the Blessed One dwelling in meditative equipoise surrounded by an assembly of bodhisattvas, ḍākinīs, yoginīs, and māmos, pointing to its character as an esoteric teaching concerned with vows, the conquest of the six great enemies, and practices associated with wrathful and feminine tantric figures. The text proceeds in a mixture of verse and prose, situating it within the broader tradition of yoginī or mother tantras. It was translated into Tibetan by the monk-translator Śākya Ye shes and is preserved as Toh 391 in the Kangyur, among the tantric scriptures of that collection.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of Secret Wisdom
explainer: Toh 392 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñānaguhyatantrarāja and in Tibetan as the Glorious King of Tantras of Secret Wisdom, rendered into English as The Glorious King of Tantras of Secret Wisdom. It belongs to the class of Vajrayāna tantras and is concerned with the esoteric teachings of the generation stage, including the nature of deities, the sixty-four excellent marks, the thirty-seven factors of awakening, the five wisdoms, and the four empowerments as expressions of the body's channel-wheels. The text is presented in a condensed instructional style, with short declarative lines addressed to a practitioner in the manner characteristic of higher tantric literature. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Gayādhara together with the Tibetan monk-translator Śākya Yeshe, a renowned collaboration responsible for several important tantric transmissions in the canon.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras, the Garland of Primordial Wisdom
explainer: Toh 393 in the Kangyur, this text is known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñāna Mālā Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal ye shes phreng ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras, the Garland of Primordial Wisdom. It is a tantric scripture belonging to the class of Buddhist tantras, structured as a dialogue in which a questioner addresses Vajrasattva — the Holder of the Vajra and Master of Secrets — asking about the view and conduct of the unsurpassed secret teaching. The text's opening response identifies the view with the Perfection of Wisdom, described as primordially free of conceptual elaboration, luminous within self-aware primordial wisdom, and beyond adoption or rejection, placing this tantra within a doctrinal register that emphasizes the non-dual nature of awareness. As Toh 393 in the Kangyur, it is preserved among the tantric texts of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras, Blazing Wisdom
explainer: Toh 394 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñāna Jvāla Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal ye shes 'bar ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras, Blazing Wisdom. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric literature and concerns the nature of non-dual wisdom, great bliss, and self-awareness, framed as a dialogue in which a questioner addresses the Buddha and receives teachings from a figure identified as the Great Terrifier. The text opens with verses of wonder and inquiry about the tantra itself, before unfolding its esoteric content around themes of maṇḍala, self-consecration, and the direct realization of reality. As a tantra associated with Samantabhadra and situated among the highest teachings of the Kangyur, it represents the kind of condensed, symbolically rich scripture characteristic of the tantric collections of that canon.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras, the Garland of the Moon
explainer: Toh 395 in the Kangyur is a Vajrayāna tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Candramālatantrārāja and in Tibetan as Dpal Zla ba'i phreng ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras, the Garland of the Moon. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric texts and takes the form of a dialogue in which a disciple addresses Vajrasattva, the vajra-bearing lord, with questions concerning the nature and measure of the twenty-four lamps and the abiding of what is established by intrinsic nature. The Blessed One's response unfolds as instruction on tantric practice, including contemplation of the guru's grace and the examination of practice in charnel grounds and similar conducive settings. The text was translated into Tibetan by Ma Tsamdamala and the monk Śākya Yeshe, and it is preserved among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious Blazing Jewel, King of Tantras
explainer: Toh 396 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Ratna Jvala Tantra Rāja, in Tibetan as Dpal Rin chen 'bar ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, and in English as the King of Tantras called the Glorious Blazing Jewel. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric literature and concerns the interplay of skillful means, wisdom, and non-duality, expressed through esoteric syllables and their associations with body, speech, and mind, the twenty-four sacred sites, and the practices of sky-going beings. The text opens with invocations characteristic of the Vajrayāna tradition, addressing vajra-essence and ḍākinīs and expounding the arising of tantras of skillful means, wisdom, and non-duality from seed syllables. It was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian abbot Gayādhara together with the monk-translator Śākyayeśe, a renowned collaborative team active during the later period of translation in Tibet.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras Called the Wheel of the Sun
sanskrit: Śrī Sūrya Cakra Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: The Glorious King of Tantras Called the Wheel of the Sun, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Sūrya Cakra Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal Nyi Ma'i 'Khor Lo'i Rgyud Kyi Rgyal Po, is a tantric scripture belonging to the Vajrayāna tradition. It is Toh 397 in the Kangyur, classified among the tantric texts, and takes the form of a teaching delivered by the Blessed One on the profound practices of the generation and completion stages. The text concerns the non-relinquishment of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources as bases for generation stage practice, alongside the role of symbolic implements, solar and lunar principles, syllables, and the guru's oral instructions as conditions for realization. With its opening invocation to the glorious Great Bliss and its address to heroes or tantric practitioners, the work is clearly oriented toward advanced Vajrayāna practitioners seeking instruction on the arising of the two buddha bodies as the fruit of sealed and unified body and speech.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras: The Tantra of the Glorious King of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 398 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñānarāja Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal ye shes rgyal po'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras, the Tantra of the Glorious King of Wisdom. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and concerns the nature of self-awareness beyond duality, the primordially unborn character of reality, and the profound equivalence of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, themes conveyed through verse teachings addressed to the Buddha and oriented toward the role of the guru in guiding practitioners to liberation. The text opens with homage to the Glorious Great Bliss, signaling its orientation toward the Mahāyoga or higher tantric traditions in which bliss and non-dual awareness are central soteriological categories. As Toh 398, it is preserved among the tantric works of the Kangyur, the Tibetan collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha himself.

title: The Glorious Secret Tantra of the Vajra Ḍākinī, the King of Tantras
explainer: Toh 399 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in English as The Glorious Secret Tantra of the Vajra Ḍākinī, King of Tantras, corresponding to the Sanskrit Śrī Vajraḍākinī Guhyatantrarāja and the Tibetan Dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro gsang ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po. It belongs to the class of Anuttarayoga or higher yoga tantras and centers on teachings associated with the Heruka cycle, addressing esoteric subjects such as empowerment, the nature of samayas and their confession, and the non-dual relationship between sentient beings and buddhas. The text is cast as a dialogue in which a questioner poses profound doctrinal questions and the Blessed One responds by expounding the illusory yet certain nature of empowerment and the dissolution of conceptual duality into primordial wisdom. It was translated into Tibetan by the monk Śākyayeśe and is preserved among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Secret Blazing Fire
explainer: Toh 400 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jvālāgni Guhya Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal gsang ba me 'bar ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras of the Secret Blazing Fire. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric texts and is presented in the classic sūtra style, opening with the Buddha dwelling in meditative absorption, after which the bodhisattva Vajravārāhī poses a series of questions concerning yoga, transference, death, and related esoteric themes involving fire, ash, and ritual substances. The text's concerns with subtle yogic processes, death and the body, and the symbolism of fire suggest it belongs to the corpus of highest yoga tantra or a closely related tradition within the Kangyur's tantric section. As with many tantras of this type, its teachings unfold as a dialogue between an enlightened presence and a requesting deity, situating it firmly within the Vajrayāna ceremonial and contemplative literature preserved in the Tibetan canon.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Secret Nectar
explainer: Toh 401 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist tantra known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Amṛta Guhya Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal gsang ba bdud rtsi'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras of the Secret Nectar. It belongs to the class of esoteric tantric literature and concerns the practices of maṇḍala construction, mantra recitation, torma offerings, fire offerings, and related ritual worship, presented through a dialogue between the bodhisattva Vajrahṛdaya and the Blessed One. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling in a characteristic tantric setting described in terms of the vajra union of all Tathāgatas, situating it firmly within the Vajrayāna tradition. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Gayadhara together with the monk and translator Śākya Yeshe.

title: Tantra of the Ornament of the Glorious Charnel Ground
explainer: Toh 402 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in English as the Glorious Ornament of the Charnel Ground, corresponding to the Sanskrit title Śrī Śmaśāna Alaṃkāra Tantra and preserved in Tibetan as དཔལ་དུར་ཁྲོད་ཀྱི་རྒྱན་གྱི་རྒྱུད or similar. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and concerns the symbolic and ritual significance of the charnel ground, describing its general and specific features, its directional divisions, and its ornaments within the context of a tantric dialogue between the Blessed One and a vajra-hearted interlocutor. The text is framed as a question-and-answer exchange exploring the nature of the charnel ground as a sacred and terrifying abode associated with great bliss and wrathful practice, situating it within the cosmology of the measureless palace and vajra fence. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian master Gayābhara together with the monk-translator Śākya Yeshé, and it appears in the Kangyur immediately following the completion of the related Glorious Secret Nectar Tantra, suggesting a close association between these two works in the tantric corpus.

title: The Glorious Great Tantra of the Vajra King
explainer: The Glorious Tantra of the Great Vajra King, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajrarāja Mahātantra and in Tibetan as Dpal rdo rje rgyal po'i rgyud chen po, is a Buddhist tantric scripture belonging to the class of Vajrayāna canonical texts. Set within a celestial assembly of heroes and ḍākinīs, the tantra opens with Vajrahṛdaya and other attendants posing questions to the Blessed One about the nature of the vajra, the tantra, and the king, framing the text as a revelation of esoteric doctrine concerning the inseparability of body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. The work is associated with charnel ground symbolism and the ornamental or transformative dimensions of tantric practice. It is Toh 403 in the Kangyur, where it is classed among the tantric texts, and was translated into Tibetan by the paṇḍita Gayadhara and the monk-translator Śākya Yeshe.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras on the Intention of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 404 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñānāśaya Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as Dpal ye shes bsam pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras on the Intention of Wisdom. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric texts and concerns the nature, varieties, and sovereign power of wisdom, explored through a dialogue in which the Hero Wisdom-Ḍākinī petitions the Blessed One — identified with the glorious Vajrasattva — to explain the intrinsic character of wisdom and those who embody or are tamed by it. The teaching unfolds in verse within an assembly of innumerable heroes and ḍākinīs gathered at a secret place of wisdom, placing this text firmly within the esoteric Vajrayāna tradition of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras, the King of Passion
explainer: The Glorious King of Tantras, the King of Glorious Passion — known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Rāgarāja Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as Dpal chags pa'i rgyal po'i rgyud kyi rgyal po — is a Buddhist tantric scripture belonging to the Kangyur, where it is catalogued as Toh 405. It is a tantra text in which the Blessed One, dwelling in union with the Vajra Queen, responds to the bodhisattva Vajragarbha's questions concerning the buddha-nature of sentient beings, their major and minor marks, and the various modes of birth and liberation. The text opens with homage to the Glorious Vajra Ḍākinī, immediately signaling its orientation within the Vajrayāna tradition and its concern with esoteric teachings on enlightened body, speech, and mind shared by all tathāgatas. As a tantra of this character — combining devotional, cosmological, and soteriological themes framed within a dialogue between teacher and bodhisattva — it belongs to the broader class of tantric works preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Vows of the Ḍākinī
sanskrit: Śrī Ḍākinī Saṃvara Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: Toh 406 in the Kangyur is a Vajrayāna tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Ḍākinī Saṃvara Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal mkha' 'gro ma'i sdom pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, meaning "The Glorious King of Tantras of the Vows of the Ḍākinī." It belongs to the class of yoginī tantras and concerns the sacred vows and pledges associated with the ḍākinī, exploring the nature of those commitments, their root and branch transgressions, and the proper guarding of tantric samaya. The text is structured as a dialogue, with Vajradhara being questioned about the ḍākinī's nature and vows, and Vajravārāhī responding with instruction. It was translated into Tibetan by the yoginī Candramālā together with the monk-translator Śākya Yeshe.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Garland of Fire
explainer: Toh 407 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Agni Māla Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal me'i phreng ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, meaning in English the Glorious King of Tantras of the Garland of Fire. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and opens with a homage to Vajrasattva, after which a questioner poses a series of symbolic inquiries about the syllables and epithets constituting the name Heruka, to which the Blessed One responds by unfolding their esoteric meanings in terms of non-dual wisdom, freedom from accumulation, and the four empowerments. The text is thus concerned with the nature and practice of Heruka, presenting his identity and the stages of empowerment through a dialogue that interweaves doctrinal explanation with tantric symbolism. As a king of tantras, it represents an authoritative revelation within the Vajrayāna tradition preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras, the Secret Blaze of the Ḍākinī
explainer: The Glorious King of Tantras, the Secret Blaze of the Ḍākinī, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Ḍākinī Guhyajvala Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as Dpal Mkha' 'gro ma gsang ba 'bar ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, is a tantric scripture belonging to the class of highest yoga tantra and centering on the ḍākinīs — enlightened female wisdom figures who play a central role in Vajrayāna practice. The text is structured as a dialogue in which the nature and classifications of the ḍākinīs, mothers, secrets, and tantras are systematically enumerated, with particular attention to the empowerments, channels, winds, and other elements of tantric contemplative practice associated with the path to great bliss. It opens with the characteristic invocatory exclamation "Kye — alalaho!" and proceeds to outline four ḍākinīs, three mothers, six secrets, eight tantras, and nineteen kings of tantra, framing these within a graduated system of empowerments designed to uproot increasingly subtle forms of conceptual grasping. This text is Toh 408 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the tantric scriptures of that collection.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras, the Tantra of the King of Wisdom of Great Power
explainer: Toh 410 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist tantric scripture known in English as The Glorious King of Tantras, the Tantra of the King of Wisdom of Great Power, in Sanskrit as the Śrī Mahābala Jñānarāja Tantra Rāja, and in Tibetan as Dpal stobs chen po ye shes kyi rgyal po'i rgyud. It belongs to the class of tantric texts and opens in the characteristic style of a discourse delivered by the Buddha, here depicted as dwelling in a sacred tantric setting surrounded by hero-vajras, ḍākinīs, and māmakīs, with the hero-vajra posing a question after offering homage. The text concerns the profound wisdom teachings associated with Vajrasattva and the tantric pantheon of enlightened beings. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Gayādhara together with the Tibetan monk-translator Śākya Yeshe, a celebrated partnership responsible for transmitting a number of important tantric works into the Tibetan canon.

title: Glorious King of Tantras of the Vow of the Net of Vajra Accomplishment
sanskrit: Śrī Vajrasiddha Jāla Saṃvara Tantra Rāja
explainer: Toh 411 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajrasiddha Jāla Saṃvara Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal Rdo rje grub pa dra ba'i sdom pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras of the Vow of the Net of Vajra Accomplishment. It belongs to the class of Highest Yoga Tantras associated with the Cakrasaṃvara or Saṃvara cycle, concerning the sacred vows, esoteric practices, and the assembly of heroes and yoginīs within a tantric maṇḍala framework. The text opens with the Buddha residing in the Tuṣita heaven alongside the bodhisattva Maitreya and a vast retinue, and proceeds to expound teachings on the illusory lineage and the outer, inner, and secret offerings of unsurpassed worship. It was translated into Tibetan by the scholar Śākya Yeshé and is preserved among the tantric texts of the Kangyur.

title: Tantra of the Essential Meaning of the Mind of All the Tathāgatas
explainer: Toh 412 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in Sanskrit as the Sarvatathāgatacittagarbhārthatantra and in Tibetan as the Tantra of the Essential Meaning of the Mind of All the Tathāgatas. It belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur and is a text concerned with the nature of the mind of all buddhas, centering on Vajrasattva as the embodiment of the gnosis body of the tathāgatas and exploring themes of enlightened mind, emptiness, and the relationship between existence and liberation. The text opens with verse exchanges involving Vajrasattva and the Blessed One, situating its teachings within a tantric dialogic framework characteristic of this class of scripture. It was translated into Tibetan from Sanskrit by the Indian master Gayādhara together with the Tibetan monk-translator Śākya Yeshé.

title: The Glorious Cakrasaṃvara, King of Tantras: The Wondrous Charnel Ground Ornament
sanskrit: Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Tantra Rāja Adbhuta Śmaśāna Alaṃkāra Nāma
explainer: Toh 413 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Tantra Raja Adbhuta Śmaśāna Alaṃkāra, in Tibetan as the Dpal 'khor lo sdom pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po dur khrod kyi rgyan rmad du byung ba, and in English as The Glorious Cakrasaṃvara, King of Tantras: The Wondrous Charnel Ground Ornament. It belongs to the Anuttarayoga class of tantric literature and centers on the deity Cakrasaṃvara, also called Heruka, presenting teachings on the nature of nondual wisdom, vows, and the symbolism of the tantric cycle in the form of a dialogue between the Blessed One Vajradhara and an assembly of heroes and heroines. The text opens in the traditional sūtra style — "Thus did I hear at one time" — before unfolding as a royal tantra concerned with the profound doctrines of body, speech, and mind as embodied by all Tathāgatas. As a canonical tantra preserved in the Kangyur, it represents one of the most important scriptural sources for the Cakrasaṃvara cycle, which became central to many Tibetan Buddhist lineages.

title: Toh 414 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Anābhila
explainer: Toh 414 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Anābhila Tantra and in Tibetan as the Dpal 'khor lo sdom pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po dur khrod kyi rgyan rmad du byung ba, which may be rendered in English as something like the Wondrous Charnel Ground Ornament, a King of Tantras of Glorious Chakrasaṃvara. It belongs to the class of Highest Yoga Tantras associated with the Chakrasaṃvara cycle, a tradition of great importance in Vajrayāna Buddhism centered on the deity Chakrasaṃvara and his consort. The text opens with an invocation to the vajra ḍākinī and proceeds to expound the ultimate nature of awakening — described as beyond marks, analogies, and conceptual elaboration — in a manner characteristic of advanced tantric instruction aimed at guiding practitioners toward direct realization. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Gayadhara together with the monk-translator Śākya Yeshe, placing it within the broader corpus of Indian tantric literature transmitted to Tibet during the great translation period.

title: Toh 415 in the Kangyur is a Vajrayāna tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī
explainer: Toh 415 in the Kangyur is a Vajrayāna tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Saṃvara Khasama Tantra Rāja, in Tibetan as the Dpal Khor Lo bDe mChog Nam mKha' dang mNyam pa'i rGyud kyi rGyal po, and in English as The Glorious Cakrasaṃvara — the King of Tantras Equal to Space. It belongs to the class of highest yoga tantras (Anuttarayogatantra) associated with the Cakrasaṃvara cycle, a major stream of Indo-Tibetan tantric practice centered on the deity Cakrasaṃvara and the ḍākinī Vajravārāhī, and it concerns the esoteric instructions on the net-vow of the ḍākinīs, the sequential blessing of the tantra, and the profound secret teachings requested by Vajrasattva in the presence of the Blessed One. The text opens in the classic sūtra-style framing of the Vajrayāna canon, with the Buddha dwelling in union with the Vajra Lady and responding to Vajrasattva's request for the most secret of teachings. It was translated into Tibetan by the Indian paṇḍita Gayādhara together with the Tibetan lotsāwa, the fully ordained monk Śākya Yeshé.

title: The tantra of the protector the arising of secret accomplishments
Hevajra Tantra, the King of Tantras
explainer: The Hevajra Tantra, known in Sanskrit as the Hevajra Tantra Raja and in Tibetan as Kyé Dorjé (ཀྱེའི་རྡོ་རྗེ་), is one of the most celebrated and influential texts in the Vajrayāna Buddhist tradition, belonging to the class of Yoginī or Highest Yoga Tantras. It is a royal tantra — "king of tantras" as its own title declares — centered on the deity Hevajra, a wrathful, enlightened form whose practice encompasses profound teachings on the nature of reality, the nonduality of compassion and emptiness, and the transformation of experience through esoteric ritual and meditation. The text unfolds as a dialogue prompted by the bodhisattva Vajrahṛdaya questioning the Blessed One, who speaks from a state identified as the very essence of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. This text is Toh 417 in the Kangyur, preserved within the collection of Tantric scriptures, and its importance is reflected in the extensive commentarial literature it generated across the major schools of Tibetan Buddhism.

title: The Manifest Awakening of Vajra-Essence: A King of Tantras Drawn from the Vows of the Web of Ḍākinīs of Hevajra
explainer: Toh 418 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Tibetan as Dorje Nyingpo Ngönpar Jangchubpa (རྡོ་རྗེ་སྙིང་པོ་མངོན་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་), rendered in English as "The Manifest Awakening of Vajra-Essence," and associated in Sanskrit with the Hevajra tantric cycle. It belongs to the class of Yoganiruttara or Highest Yoga Tantras and forms part of the broader Hevajra (Kye Dorje) corpus, being drawn from the vows of the web of ḍākinīs of Hevajra. The text concerns ritual procedures including fire offerings, the construction and consecration of sacred maṇḍalas, the purification and animation of images through the summoning of buddhas from space, and the enumeration of mantra recitation counts for different classes of beings such as gods, asuras, and mantra practitioners. As Toh 418 in the Kangyur, it sits within the collection of Buddha's word preserved in the Tibetan canon, specifically among the tantric scriptures, and takes the form of a dialogue between the Blessed One and the bodhisattva Vajra-Essence, who petitions the Buddha to explain these esoteric teachings in their proper sequence.

title: The Examination of the Noble Ḍākinī Vajra Tent, the Great King of Tantras
explainer: Toh 419 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in English as the Noble Ḍākinī Vajra Tent, the Great King of Tantras, in Sanskrit as the Āryaḍākinīvajrapañjaramahātantrarājakalpa, and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Khandro Dorje Gur. It belongs to the class of Anuttarayoga tantras and is one of the most important mother tantras in the Vajrayana tradition, closely associated with the Hevajra cycle and concerned with ḍākinīs, vajra wisdom, and the esoteric geography of enlightened reality. The text unfolds as a vast kalpa or auxiliary tantra, presenting teachings on pure and impure realms, the nature of sentient beings, and the grounds of tantric practice through a densely symbolic and enumerative style characteristic of the highest yoga tantras. As a foundational scriptural authority for numerous Tibetan lineages, particularly the Sakya school, it holds a prominent place among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious Bindu of Mahāmudrā, Sovereign Lord of the King of Tantras of the Great Yoginī
sanskrit: Śrī Mahāmudrātilaka Nāma Mahāyoginī Tantra Rāja Adhipati
explainer: Toh 420 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Mahāmudrātilaka and in Tibetan as Dpal Phyag rgya chen po'i thig le, which may be rendered into English as the Glorious Bindu of Mahāmudrā. It belongs to the class of Yoginī tantras — among the highest yoga tantras — and takes the form of a dialogue in which a ḍākinī questions Hevajra on the ultimate nature of reality, focusing especially on the esoteric doctrine of the bindu, or sacred drop, and its relationship to mahāmudrā, the great seal of awakening. The text presents itself as a sovereign among tantric scriptures, situating its teachings on the six yogic unions and the nature of suchness within the framework of the Hevajra cycle. As Toh 420 in the Kangyur, it is preserved among the Tibetan Buddhist canonical scriptures transmitted from the Indian tantric tradition.

title: The Glorious Essence of Wisdom, King of Kings among the Great Tantras of the Yoginī
explainer: The Glorious Essence of Wisdom, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñānagarbha Yoginī Mahātantra Rāja Yati Rāja and in Tibetan as Dpal Ye shes snying po, is a yoginī tantra belonging to the highest class of esoteric Buddhist literature. It takes the form of a dialogue set at the summit of Mount Meru, where the Buddha, surrounded by vast assemblies of ḍākas and ḍākinīs, reveals tantric teachings in the context of sacred union with the goddess Lekgyé Wangmo. As its full title proclaims, it presents itself as the King of Kings among the Great Tantras of the Yoginī, indicating its exalted status within the Vajrayāna textual tradition. It is catalogued as Toh 421 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the tantric scriptures.

title: Glorious Wisdom Drop: The Supreme and Wondrous King of the Yoginī Tantra
sanskrit: Śrī Jñānatilaka Yoginītantra Rāja Parama Mahādbhuta Nāma
explainer: Toh 422 in the Kangyur is a yoginī tantra known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñānatilaka Yoginītantra and in Tibetan as the Glorious Great King of the Tantra of the Yoginī of Wisdom Drop, Supremely Wondrous. It belongs to the class of highest yoga tantras centered on yoginī practice, presenting teachings that unfold in the context of the Blessed One dwelling in the bhaga of the vajra queen, surrounded by heroes and heroines — a setting characteristic of advanced tantric instruction. The text is specifically identified as the latter part of the latter section of a larger tantric cycle concerning the Great Seal Drop Yoginī, indicating it forms the concluding portion of an extended scriptural collection. It was translated from the Indian master Śrī Prajñāguhya and sits among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha himself.

title: The Glorious Lamp of Suchness, the King of the Great Yoginī Tantras
sanskrit: Śrī Tattva Pradīpaṃ Nāma Mahāyoginī Tantra Rāja
explainer: Toh 423 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Tattva Pradīpa and in Tibetan as the Dpal de kho na nyid kyi sgron ma, rendered in English as the Glorious Lamp of Suchness. It belongs to the class of Yoginī tantras, the highest division of the Anuttarayoga tantras, and is designated a "King of the Great Yoginī Tantras," signaling its authoritative standing within that tradition. The text opens in the characteristic sūtra style — "Thus did I hear at one time" — before establishing its tantric setting: the Blessed One abiding within the bhaga of wisdom together with Vajradhātvīśvarī and a vast assembly of yoginīs, framing the ensuing teachings within the ritual and contemplative world of Vajrasattva and the female buddha-consorts. As a Yoginī tantra, its concerns center on the nondual union of method and wisdom, the nature of reality (tattva), and the practices of great bliss associated with the maṇḍala of heroines.

title: The Glorious Buddha Skull, King of the Yoginī Tantras
sanskrit: Śrī Buddhakāpāla Nāma Yoginī Tantra Rāja
explainer: Toh 424 in the Kangyur is the Glorious Buddha Skull, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Buddha Kapāla Nāma Yoginī Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal sangs rgyas thod pa zhes bya ba rnal 'byor ma'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, meaning "The Glorious Buddha Skull, the King of the Yoginī Tantras." It belongs to the class of Yoginī or Mother Tantras within the Highest Yoga Tantra tradition, texts centered on fierce feminine deity practices and the transformation of subtle energies through advanced tantric yoga. The text takes the form of a canonical tantra, opening with the traditional "Thus did I hear" setting in which the Buddha expounds esoteric teachings on mantras, maṇḍalas, and the union of wisdom and method to an assembly of Tathāgatas, yoginīs, and bodhisattvas gathered within a great vajra maṇḍala. As one of the important Yoginī tantras preserved in the Kangyur, it centers on the deity Buddhkapāla, a wrathful tantric Buddha whose practice involves skull imagery and ritual elements characteristic of this genre.

title: The Great King of Tantras Called Vajra Āralī
explainer: Toh 426 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in Sanskrit as the Vajra Āralī Mahātantra Rāja and in Tibetan as Dorje Arali zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chenpo, which may be rendered into English as "The Great King of Tantras Called Vajra Āralī." It belongs to the class of highest yoga tantras associated with the Hevajra cycle, as indicated by its opening homage to Hevajra and its characteristic setting in which the Blessed One dwells in the bhaga of the Perfection of Wisdom of all Tathāgatas. The text proceeds to offer instructions on ritual practice and visualization, including meditating on the syllable RE PHA at the heart and the arising of a vajra sun, all framed within the traditional tantra structure of questions posed by bodhisattvas and responses given by the Buddha to Vajrapāṇi. As a tantric scripture concerned with the generation-stage practices of Heruka and related deity yoga, it represents an important esoteric work within the Kangyur's collection of Vajrayāna teachings.

title: The King of Tantras Called the Rigi Āralī
explainer: Toh 427 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Rigi Ārali Tantra Rāja, in Tibetan as the Rigi Āralī Gyü Gyelpo, and in English as The King of Tantras Called the Rigi Āralī. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric texts and takes the form of a dialogue set in a visionary sacred context, in which the female deity Ārali poses questions to Rigi, a supreme lord of yoga, concerning the nature of abodes, fields, and related esoteric categories of tantric practice. The text opens in the classic sūtra-style with the Buddha dwelling in a non-dual meditative state, framing what follows as a revealed teaching within the tantric tradition. Translated into Tibetan from the Indian original by the monk Śākyayeśes working with the Indian master Kāyasthapagayadhara, it is preserved in the Kangyur as Toh 427 among the tantric scriptures.

title: The Great Royal Tantra of the Yoginī Called the Glorious Four Seats
sanskrit: Śrī Caturpīṭha Mahāyoginī Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: Toh 428 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in English as The Glorious Four Seats: The Great Royal Tantra of the Yoginī, corresponding to the Sanskrit Śrī Caturpīṭha Mahāyoginī Tantra Rāja and the Tibetan Dpal gdan bzhi pa zhes bya ba. It belongs to the class of Yoginī tantras, an advanced category of highest yoga tantra focused on practices associated with enlightened female principles and the realization of wisdom inseparable from emptiness. The text opens with the Blessed One, situated in a pure abode and described as dwelling within the net of the yoginī, turning to address Vajrapāṇi amid an assembly of tens of millions of lords of yoga, establishing the dramatic and visionary setting characteristic of this genre. As one of the major tantric cycles in the Kangyur, the Caturpīṭha is an important scripture within the Yoginī tantra tradition and has been the subject of extensive commentary in Indian and Tibetan Buddhist scholarship.

title: The Glorious Tantra King of Exposition of the Four Seats, Called 'The Mantra Section'
explainer: Toh 429 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śicatuḥpīṭhākhyāta Tantra Rāja Mantrāṃśa Nāma and in Tibetan as the Dpal gdan bzhi pa'i bshad pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po sngags kyi cha, rendered in English as "The Glorious Tantra King of Exposition of the Four Seats, Called 'The Mantra Section.'" It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric literature, specifically presenting itself as a mantra section — the third part of the first tantra — associated with the tradition of the Four Seats, a cluster of sacred sites and related esoteric teachings connected with the Yoginī or Highest Yoga Tantra corpus. The text opens with homage to the Blessed One as the Glorious Yoga of Space and to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, along with the vajra ḍākinīs, before proceeding in verse to expound on the secret and supremely condensed suchness of mantra practice. As Toh 429 in the Kangyur, it is preserved among the canonical tantric scriptures of the Tibetan Buddhist tradition.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras Called the Explanation of the Four Seats
explainer: Toh 430 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in English as The Glorious King of Tantras Called the Explanation of the Four Seats, in Sanskrit as the Śrī Caturvīṭhābhikhyā Tantra Rāja, and in Tibetan as the Dpal gdan bzhi pa'i rnam par bshad pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po. It belongs to the class of Yoginī or Highest Yoga Tantras and centers on teachings delivered by an omniscient buddha figure — identified with the Yogi of Space and associated with Vajrayoga and the Vajrayoginīs — in response to questions posed by Vajrapāṇi among a vast assembly of yoga lords. The text opens with homages to key figures of the Vajrayāna pantheon, including Avalokiteśvara and Vajrasattva, before presenting the tantra's doctrinal and ritual content concerning the "four seats," a framework of sacred bodily or geographical locations that plays an important role in certain tantric systems. As Toh 430 in the Kangyur, it is preserved among the canonical scriptures of Tibetan Buddhism and represents the type of esoteric tantra concerned with advanced yogic practice, subtle-body teachings, and the transformative methods associated with the Vajrayoginī cycle.

title: The Noble King of Tantras of the Ritual of the Immovable One
explainer: Toh 432 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Āryācala-kalpa-tantra-rāja and in Tibetan as the Phags pa mi g.yo ba'i rtog pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as "The Noble King of Tantras of the Ritual of the Immovable One." It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and centers on the deity Acala, the Immovable One, a wrathful protector figure closely associated with the power of mantra and the subjugation of obstructive forces. The text opens in the familiar sūtra style, with the Buddha entering a profound meditative absorption and emanating the foundational mantra Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, whereupon a vast assembly of Indian gods, planetary deities, and spirit beings — including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla, and many others — are summoned into the scene, reflecting the text's ritual and cosmological scope. As a king of tantras devoted to Acala and his associated rites and mantras, it represents an important specimen of tantric literature within the Kangyur's collection of esoteric teachings.

title: The Tantra Called the Wrathful King, the Secret of All Secret Mantras
explainer: Toh 433 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in English as "The Wrathful King, the Secret of All Secret Mantras," corresponding to the Sanskrit Krodharāja Sarvamantra Guhyatantra and the Tibetan Khro bo'i rgyal po thams cad gsang sngags gsang ba'i rgyud. It belongs to the class of tantric scriptures in the Kangyur and centers on the wrathful deity Acala — the Immovable Protector — presenting teachings on mantra, mudrā, and meditative absorption associated with this powerful protective figure. The text opens with a verse narrative in which the Great Vajradhara, moved by compassion for beings of the three realms afflicted by aversion, pays homage in a blazing charnel ground and entreats the wrathful king to teach, establishing the devotional and soteriological framing characteristic of this class of tantra.

title: The Noble Great Secret Tantra of Acala (the Immovable One)
