explainer: The Noble Great Secret Tantra of Acala, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Acala Mahāguhya Tantra and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Mi Yowa'i Sang Gyü Chenpo, is a Vajrayāna tantric scripture centered on Acala (the Immovable One), a wrathful deity closely associated with Mañjuśrī and the purification of obstacles. The text belongs to the class of tantric literature and takes the form of a tantra spoken by the great Vairocana, presenting teachings on maṇḍala arrangement and esoteric practice within an assembly of bodhisattvas and vajra-holders dwelling in the realm of Akaniṣṭha. It is Toh 434 in the Kangyur, classified among the tantric texts of that collection.

title: Tantra of the Vajra Nectar
explainer: Toh 435 in the Kangyur is the Vajra Amṛta Tantra, known in Tibetan as the Rdo rje bdud rtsi'i rgyud, or the Tantra of the Vajra Nectar. It is a Buddhist tantric text belonging to the class of esoteric scriptures, and its opening situates it within a visionary setting in which the Blessed One dwells in the secret lotus of the Vajra Nectar and sports together with the goddess Māmakī in a stacked palace of immeasurable dimensions. The text takes the form of a dialogue in which the goddess petitions the deity to reveal methods of accomplishment associated with the nectar of the vajra, a subject connected to purification, transformation, and the esoteric powers of enlightened body, speech, and mind. Notably, the translation opens with what is presented as the fourth and final chapter of a separate but related work, the Great Secret of the Immovable, before the Vajra Amṛta Tantra itself begins, suggesting a close editorial relationship between these two tantric cycles within the Kangyur collection.

title: The Fifty Verses on Kulalokanātha
explainer: Toh 436 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Kulalokanātha Pañcadaśaka and in Tibetan as Rigs kyi 'jig rten mgon po lnga bcu pa, rendered in English as "The Fifty Verses on the Protector of the World of the Noble Clan." It belongs to the class of tantric literature and concerns the esoteric teachings surrounding Kulalokanātha, a deity associated with the noble clan, presenting instruction on sacred commitments, mantra, and the nature of the genuine deity through verse. The text opens with a homage to the Protector of the World of the Noble Clan and proceeds to expound non-dual mantra teachings framed as supremely secret doctrine. It was translated into Tibetan by the translator Gyico Dawé Özer and sits within the tantric section of the Kangyur.

title: The praise of tara in twentyone homages
A Fragment of the Root Tantra of the Vajra Kīla
explainer: The Fragment of the Root Tantra of the Vajra Kīla, known in Sanskrit as the Vajrakīlaya Mūlatantra Khaṇḍa and in Tibetan as Dorje Phurpa Tsawé Gyü Kyi Dumbu, is a tantric text belonging to the Vajrakīlaya cycle, one of the most important traditions of wrathful deity practice in Tibetan Buddhism. It concerns the fierce deity Vajrakumāra, the Vajra Youth, and presents teachings on the transformation of negative forces — particularly aversion — through the ritual and meditative power of the kīla, or ritual dagger, understood as an emanation of vajra wrath and compassion. The text weaves together verse, mantra, and doctrinal instruction, treating the kīla not as an instrument of mere destruction but as a means of liberating beings by transmuting the aggregates of existence into vajra. It is Toh 439 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the tantric scriptures, and survives as a fragment, suggesting it represents a portion of a larger root tantra rather than a complete and self-contained work.

title: The Tantra Called 'Obtained As It Is, Equal to Space'
explainer: The Tantra Called "Obtained As It Is, Equal to Space," known in Sanskrit as the Yathālabdha-kha-samatantra and in Tibetan as Ji Zhin Nyepa Namkha Dang Nyampa, is a tantric text belonging to the Kangyur as Toh 441. It is a Buddhist tantra centered on the nature of mind and ultimate reality, framed around the figure of Vajrasattva and invoking the five buddhas, Vajradhara, and other primordial buddha forms. The text explores the theme that the intrinsic nature of awakened mind is like space — beginningless, unproduced, and beyond conceptual elaboration — and that genuine meditation on the ultimate cannot be reduced to mere mental purification. It opens with a verse homage to Vajrasattva and proceeds in a doctrinal and poetic register characteristic of the higher tantric literature of the Kangyur.

title: Toh 443 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Tibetan as the Gyud Chima
explainer: Toh 443 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Tibetan as the Gyud Chima, meaning "The Subsequent Tantra," and it belongs to the broader corpus of the Guhyasamāja cycle, functioning as a continuation or sequel tantra within that tradition. The text opens with an assembly of great bodhisattvas, led by Maitreya, who address all the Tathāgatas after having fully comprehended the empowerment and the secret teachings of the body, speech, and mind of all buddhas. It is a tantra of the Highest Yoga class concerned with the nature of vajra body, speech, and mind, the empowerments conferred by all Tathāgatas, and the essential purity of all sentient beings across the three times as expressed in verses of praise to Samantabhadra. The text was carefully edited and established as a definitive version by Dharma Lord Dpal, indicating a history of scholarly redaction within the Tibetan transmission. As Toh 443 in the Kangyur, it is classified among the tantras and represents an important companion text to one of the most influential cycles in Tibetan Vajrayāna literature.

title: The Tantra Called 'The Explanation of the Intent'
explainer: Toh 444 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in Sanskrit as the Sandhivyākaraṇa-nāma-tantra and in Tibetan as the Dgongs pa lung bstan pa zhes bya ba'i rgyud, which may be rendered into English as "The Tantra Called 'The Explanation of the Intent.'" It belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur and opens with homage to Vajrasattva, the presiding deity whose gnosis and inconceivable qualities are celebrated throughout the text. The tantra is concerned with the nature of mind and reality as understood through Vajrayāna teaching, weaving together themes of dependent origination — the twelve links from ignorance through aging and death — with the luminous, space-like awareness identified as the pure heart of all beings. As its title suggests, it takes the form of an authoritative revelation that discloses or "explains" a profound inner intent, situating it within the broader tradition of tantric scriptures that communicate awakened wisdom through the voice of Vajrasattva as the Lord of Secrets.

title: The Enquiry of the Four Goddesses
explainer: Toh 446 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Caturdevīparipṛcchā and in Tibetan as Lhamo Zhis Yongsu Zhüpa, rendered in English as The Enquiry of the Four Goddesses. It belongs to the class of Vajrayāna canonical texts and takes the form of a dialogue in which the goddess Locanā and her three divine companions pose questions to the Blessed One Vajrasattva, who abides in the great union of supreme bliss, making its subject the esoteric teachings on the awakening mind and the nature of the dharmadhātu. The text opens with a series of evocative verses establishing the luminous, bliss-suffused setting from which these teachings arise, situating it firmly within the tantric literary tradition. It was translated into Tibetan by the great translator and divine king of Tibet, the monk Śāntiprabha, whose careful revision and definitive establishment of the text are noted at the outset.

title: The Tantra Called the Compendium of Vajra Wisdom
explainer: The Compendium of Vajra Wisdom, known in Sanskrit as the Vajrajñānasamuccaya-nāma-tantra and in Tibetan as Yeshe Dorje Künle Tupa (ye shes rdo rje kun las btus pa), is a Buddhist tantra concerned with the nature of wisdom, mind, and ignorance as understood through the framework of the three vajras — the vajra body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas. The text takes the form of a dialogue in which the bodhisattva Maitreya and a great assembly of bodhisattvas question the Blessed One, who responds by revealing the intrinsic nature of wisdom arising from these three vajras. It belongs to the class of tantric literature within the Kangyur and is catalogued as Toh 447.

title: The King of Yoginī Tantras called 'The Ultimate Assembly of Tārā, Accomplishing All Activities'
explainer: Toh 448 in the Kangyur is a yoginī tantra known in Sanskrit as the Samāja-parasārtha-sarva-karmodyāna-nāma-hārāloginī-tantra-rāja and in Tibetan as the Phrin las thams cad 'byung ba'i sgrol ma 'dus pa don dam pa, rendered in English as "The King of Yoginī Tantras called 'The Ultimate Assembly of Tārā, Accomplishing All Activities.'" It is a tantric scripture centered on the goddess Tārā, presenting her as a supreme deity whose power encompasses the full range of enlightened activities, including the attainment of siddhis, the subjugation of gods, demons, and humans, and the command of nāgas and other non-human beings. The text belongs to the class of yoginī tantras, a category of highest yoga tantra literature associated with feminine deity cycles, and sits within the tantra section of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious Compendium of All Wisdom-Vajra
explainer: Toh 450 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Jñāna Vajra Samuccaya and in Tibetan as the Dpal ye shes rdo rje kun las bsdus pa, rendered in English as "The Glorious Compendium of All Wisdom-Vajra." The text takes the form of a buddha's discourse addressed to an assembly of great bodhisattvas, including Maitreya, who pose questions about fundamental topics such as ignorance, mental factors, and the nature of mind. The Blessed One, described as the very embodiment of wisdom dwelling in the secret expanse of all Tathāgatas, responds from within a profound meditative absorption that unifies the body, speech, and mind of all buddhas. The text belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur and opens with homage to the Glorious Mañjuvajra, indicating its association with the Mañjuśrī or Vajradhātu cycle of tantric teachings.

title: The Tantra Called the Glorious Vajra-Heart Ornament
explainer: The Glorious Vajra-Heart Ornament Tantra, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajrahṛdayālaṃkāra Tantra and in Tibetan as the Dpal Rdo rje snying po rgyan gyi rgyud, is a tantric text belonging to the Buddhist Vajrayāna tradition. It centers on Vajrasattva, a buddha embodying the essence of body, speech, and mind of all tathāgatas, and unfolds in the classical sūtra style of a teaching witnessed by an assembly that here consists notably of vajra ḍākinīs gathered in a context of tantric union. The text is principally concerned with samaya vows, primordial wisdom, and the activities of these ḍākinī figures, themes characteristic of the inner or higher tantras. It is catalogued as Toh 451 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the class of tantric texts.

title: The Noble Great King of Tantras Victorious in the Equality of Non-Duality
explainer: Toh 452 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-dvaya-samatā-vijaya-kṣubhikalpa-mahārāja and in Tibetan as Phakpa Nyisu Mepa Nyamnyi Nampar Gyalwa Zheybyai Tokpai Gyalpo Chenpo, rendered into English as "The Noble One Victorious in the Equality of Non-Duality: A Great King of Tantras." It belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur and is presented as a teaching delivered by the Buddha while residing in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, surrounded by an vast assembly of bodhisattvas who had each attained the stage of Vajrasattva. The text concerns the profound theme of non-duality and equality, framed within a Vajrayāna context and introduced with homage to the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, who also figures among the principal figures in the surrounding assembly alongside Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and other great beings.

title: The beginning chapter of the supremely great vajra
The Tantra Called 'The Noble Blue-Clad Vajrapāṇi Taming the Three Fierce Ones'
explainer: Toh 454 in the Kangyur is a tantra known in English as "The Noble Blue-Clad Vajrapāṇi Taming the Three Fierce Ones," corresponding to the Sanskrit Ārya-Nīlāmbara-dhara-Vajrapāṇi-Rudra-vitri-vinata-tantra and the Tibetan Phakpa Lakna Dorjé Gö Ngönpo Chen Drakpo Sum. It belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur and concerns the wrathful bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi in his blue-clad form, who is empowered by countless buddhas to subdue three fierce or wrathful beings. The text opens in a classic sūtra-like frame, with the Buddha residing in the celestial Akaniṣṭha palace of Other-Wielding Emanations, from which he commissions Vajrapāṇi as the great commander of the yakṣas to take up and transmit this teaching. As a tantra centered on a powerful, wrathful emanation of Vajrapāṇi, it reflects the broader tradition of deity-focused tantric literature concerned with protection, subjugation, and the esoteric transmission of buddha-authorized teachings.

title: The Analysis of the Secret Tantras, Called the Taming of the Three Fierce Ones
explainer: The Analysis of the Secret Tantras, Called the Taming of the Three Fierce Ones, known in Sanskrit as the Vibhaṅgaguhyatantrānāṃ Trirudradamanaṃ and in Tibetan as Gsang ba'i rgyud rnams kyi rnam par 'byed pa drag po gsum 'dul, is a tantric text belonging to the Kangyur, where it is catalogued as Toh 455. The text concerns the analysis and classification of secret tantras, framed around the taming of three fierce or wrathful beings, and opens with Vajrapāṇi inquiring into the secret meaning of practice, abode, and characteristics as declared by the awakened buddha. Its verses describe a fearsome, multi-faced and multi-armed deity set amid dramatic landscapes including iron-peak mountains, dense forests, and stūpas, situating the work firmly within the tradition of wrathful tantric practice. The text was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by an Indian master together with the monk-translator Dharma Sangpo.

title: The Ritual of Vajrapāṇi of the Blue Garment: the Tantra of the Vajra Staff
explainer: The Ritual of Vajrapāṇi of the Blue Garment: the Tantra of the Vajra Staff, known in Sanskrit as the Vajrapāṇi-nīlāmbara-vidhi-vajradaṇḍa-tantra and in Tibetan as Lag na rdo rje gos sngon po can gyi cho ga rdo rje be con gyi rgyud, is a tantric text centered on the wrathful deity Vajrapāṇi in his form as the Blue-Garmented one, designated as the wrathful emanation of karmic activity of all the Tathāgatas of the three times. The text opens with a vivid description of this fearsome deity — fierce-fanged, fire-breathing, and adorned with nāgas — situating him in a secluded and pure realm inhabited by yakṣas, and proceeds to present the ritual and tantric teachings associated with his cult. As a tantra, it belongs to the class of esoteric Buddhist scriptures concerned with wrathful protective deities, ritual procedures, and the transformation of karmic forces. It is Toh 456 in the Kangyur, preserved among the tantric texts of that collection.

title: Vajrapāṇi Clad in Blue, the Tantra of the Vajra Resounding, Victor over the Three Realms
explainer: Toh 457 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in English as "Vajrapāṇi Clad in Blue, the Tantra of the Vajra Resounding, Victor over the Three Realms," with a Sanskrit title reconstructed as Nīlāmbaradhara Vajrapāṇi Vajrabhāṇaka Tantra Trailokya Vijaya, and a Tibetan title of Lag na rdo rje gos sngon po can rdo rje gdengs pa'i rgyud khams gsum las rnam par rgyal ba. The text belongs to the tantra section of the Kangyur and centers on Vajrapāṇi, the powerful bodhisattva Lord of Secrets, here depicted in his wrathful blue-robed form as a deity who conquers and subdues all three realms of existence. The opening describes Vajrapāṇi entering a profound samādhi that causes the three realms to tremble, after which he emanates a mantra of tremendous power that strikes terror into nāgas and compels homage from all beings. As a tantric scripture, it belongs to the broader class of esoteric Buddhist literature concerned with ritual, mantra, and the wrathful enlightened activity associated with this important protector deity.

title: Glorious Tantra of the Secret Mind of the Wrathful Vajra
sanskrit: Śrī Vajra Caṇḍa Citta Guhya Tantra
explainer: Toh 458 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajra Caṇḍa Citta Guhya Tantra and in Tibetan as the Dpal rdo rje gtum po thugs gsang ba'i rgyud, rendered in English as the Glorious Tantra of the Secret Mind of the Glorious Wrathful Vajra. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and centers on Vajrapāṇi in his wrathful form, presenting esoteric teachings on the enlightened body, speech, and mind of the Sugatas as experienced from the pure realm of Akaniṣṭha. The text opens in the classical sūtra style with the phrase "Thus did I hear," situating its revelations within a celestial assembly where the Buddhas work for the benefit of beings through the sambhogakāya, nirmāṇakāya, and other emanation bodies arising from the dharmakāya. As a tantra devoted to a wrathful emanation of Vajrapāṇi, it is placed among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur, reflecting the tradition's deep engagement with the transformative power of wrathful enlightened activity.

title: The Glorious Subsequent Secret Mind Tantra of Vajra Caṇḍa
sanskrit: Śrī Vajra Caṇḍa Citta Guhya Tantra Uttara
explainer: Toh 459 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajra Caṇḍa Citta Guhya Tantra Uttara and in Tibetan as the Dpal rdo rje gtum po thugs gsang ba'i rgyud phyi ma, rendered in English as the Glorious Subsequent Secret Mind Tantra of Vajra Caṇḍa. It belongs to the class of tantric texts and takes the form of a revelation unfolding in response to a request by Śakra, lord of the gods, who asks the Buddha to disclose the supreme secret of body, speech, and mind. The text centers on the fierce deity Vajra Caṇḍa, a wrathful tantric figure depicted as a vast, dark-blue goddess of terrifying aspect, and it unfolds teachings on empowerment and the hidden dimensions of awakened mind. As a "subsequent" or "uttara" tantra, it is understood to be a continuation of an earlier tantra associated with the same deity, situating it within a broader cycle of Vajra Caṇḍa practice literature preserved among the tantric texts of the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious Tantra of the Secret Mind of the Wrathful Vajra, the Latter of the Latter
explainer: Toh 460 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajra Caṇḍacitta Guhyatantra Uttarottara and in Tibetan as the Dpal rdo rje gtum po thugs gsang ba'i rgyud phyi ma'i phyi ma, meaning in English "The Glorious Tantra of the Secret Mind of the Wrathful Vajra, the Latter of the Latter." It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and concerns the wrathful deity Vajra Caṇḍacitta, a fierce manifestation associated with the yakṣa Wrathful Vajra-in-Hand, addressing themes of malicious forces, poisons, and the harm caused by hostile beings in a degenerate future age. The text unfolds as a dialogue set before the Blessed One, in which Wrathful Vajra-in-Hand rises from the assembly to describe beings who torment others through the poisons of touch and breath. As the "Latter of the Latter," it presents itself as a concluding or supplementary tantra within a sequence of related texts in this cycle of the Kangyur.

title: Toh 460 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in English as the Dhāraṇī C
explainer: Toh 460 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in English as the Dhāraṇī Called Seeing Dreams, with Vajrapāṇi — the fierce great lord of the yakṣa hosts — as its presiding deity. The text consists primarily of a series of sacred mantra syllables accompanied by a brief ritual instruction directing the practitioner to recite the dhāraṇī over a vessel of water, drink it, and lie down with a composed mind in order to receive dream visions from Vajrapāṇi. It belongs to the dhāraṇī class of canonical literature, a genre dedicated to the preservation and transmission of potent ritual formulas believed to confer specific spiritual and practical benefits. As a compact, self-contained ritual text, it sits within the broader collection of dhāraṇī and mantra works found in the Kangyur.

title: The Tantra Called the Vajra Flame Tongue of Vajrapāṇi, the Blue-Robed, the Fierce Great Yakṣa
sanskrit: Nīlāmbaradhara Vajrapāṇi Yakṣa Mahārudra Vajrānala Jihvātantra nāma
explainer: Toh 461 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Nīlāmbaradhara Vajrapāṇi Yakṣa Mahārudra Vajrānala Jihvātantra and in Tibetan as the Vajra Flame Tongue of Vajrapāṇi, the Blue-Robed, the Fierce Great Yakṣa. It belongs to the class of action or ritual tantras and centers on Vajrapāṇi in his fierce, blue-robed form as a great yakṣa overlord, depicting him as a wrathful emanation of the Buddha presiding over vast assemblies of yakṣas and other fierce beings throughout the cosmos. The text opens with the Blessed One adopting a wrathful posture and surveying the ten directions, framing what follows as a revelation of fierce protective and ritual power associated with this form of Vajrapāṇi. As Toh 461 in the Kangyur, it is preserved among the tantric scriptures of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: Dhāraṇī Called Vajra Heart, Descending Vajra Tongue
explainer: The Dhāraṇī Called "Vajra Heart, Descending Vajra Tongue," known in Sanskrit as the Vajrahṛdaya Vajrajihvānala Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Dorjé Nyingpo Dorjé Ché Babpa Shyejawé Zung, is a dhāraṇī text centered on a powerful mantra-incantation revealed by the Buddha while dwelling in the charnel ground of the Cool Grove. The text belongs to the dhāraṇī genre of Buddhist literature, which preserves sacred formulas believed to carry great protective and liberating power, and its narrative frame describes the Buddha entering a meditative absorption called Vajra Heart, from which radiant light emanates to relieve the suffering of all sentient beings throughout the cosmos. It is Toh 462 in the Kangyur, the collection of canonical texts attributed to the Buddha, and sits within the general class of dhāraṇī literature found in that collection.

title: The Glorious Tantra of the Secret Teaching of Vajrapāṇi
explainer: The Glorious Tantra of the Secret Teaching of Vajrapāṇi, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Guhyavajrapāṇi Abhideśa Tantra and in Tibetan as Dpal Phyag na rdo rje gsang ba bstan pa'i rgyud, is a tantric scripture centered on the deity Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, and the qualities and practices required of a yogin who seeks to accomplish him. Set in the celestial palace of Akaniṣṭha and framed as a dialogue between a ḍākinī and the Blessed One, the text belongs to the genre of Buddhist tantra and addresses themes of empowerment, compassion, wisdom, and the three trainings as foundations for tantric accomplishment. It is Toh 463 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the tantric texts, and its translation into Tibetan is attributed to Māgragdra.

title: The Tantra King Called the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi's Manifest Revelation of Secrets
sanskrit: Bhagavān Vajrapāṇi Guhyābhideśa Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: Toh 464 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Bhagavān Vajrapāṇi Guhyābhideśa Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Bcom ldan 'das phyag na rdo rje gsang ba mngon par bstan pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Tantra King Called the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi's Manifest Revelation of Secrets. It belongs to the class of tantric texts in the Kangyur and takes as its central subject the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, whose esoteric teachings and wrathful power are here revealed in the form of a royal tantra. The text opens in the familiar sūtric style, with the Buddha residing in the Willow Palace surrounded by an immense assembly of buddhas, bodhisattvas, vidyā wrathful ones, asuras, and yakṣas, before entering a meditative absorption called Subduing All Māras and setting the stage for Vajrapāṇi's revelation of secret doctrine. As a tantra king, it occupies a prominent place among the esoteric scriptures of the Kangyur, reflecting the tradition's emphasis on Vajrapāṇi as a supreme guardian and revealer of tantric teachings.

title: The King of Tantras of Vajra Bliss and Wrath
explainer: Toh 465 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist tantra known in Sanskrit as the Vajrasukha-krodha-tantra-rāja and in Tibetan as the Dorje Dekhro Gyü kyi Gyalpo, meaning in English "The King of Tantras of Vajra-Bliss-and-Wrath." It belongs to the class of tantric scriptures and takes the form of a teaching given by the Blessed One, described as Thoroughly Victorious over Māra, while dwelling in the celestial palace of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations in Akaniṣṭha. The text opens with a great bodhisattva, moved by compassion, appealing to Maitreya on behalf of sentient beings trapped in suffering across the various realms of existence, suggesting that the tantra's central concerns include liberation from cyclic suffering through esoteric means. It was established in its canonical form in accordance with a Kashmiri source tradition, situating it within the broader corpus of Vajrayāna literature preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Great King of Tantras Called the Net of Magical Illusion
explainer: The Net of Magical Illusion, known in Sanskrit as the Māyājālamahātantrarāja and in Tibetan as Gyutrul Drawa (rGyud kyi rgyal po chen po sgyu 'phrul dra ba), is a major Mahāyoga tantra belonging to the Nyingma class of the Vajrayāna tradition. It takes the form of a discourse delivered by the Blessed One in a transcendent jeweled palace and centers on the elaborate maṇḍala of Vairocana and the emanational display of the Tathāgatas, unfolding teachings on the nature of magical illusion as a key to understanding reality and enlightened activity. As a "great king of tantras," it holds a position of particular doctrinal importance within the tantric literature associated with the Mahāyoga vehicle. This text is Toh 466 in the Kangyur, classified among the tantric scriptures of the collection.

title: The Tantra Called the Glorious Great Vajrabhairava
explainer: Toh 468 in the Kangyur is the tantra known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajra Mahābhairava Nāma Tantra and in Tibetan as Dpal Rdo rje 'jigs byed chen po'i rgyud, rendered into English as the Tantra Called the Glorious Great Vajrabhairava. It belongs to the class of Anuttarayoga tantras and centers on Vajrabhairava, a wrathful deity described as the King of Wrath who inspires terror in all the gods, presenting instructions for his ritual accomplishment. The text sets out the practical context for this practice, specifying a range of suitable locations — from charnel grounds and river banks to crossroads and mountain peaks — in which the mantra practitioner should work toward the fulfillment of various purposes. As a tantra devoted to one of the most important wrathful meditational deities of the Vajrayana tradition, it holds a significant place among the tantric scriptures preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious Black Yamāri Tantra, King of Tantras, the Third Kalpa
sanskrit: Śrī Kṛṣṇa Yamāri Tantra Rāja Trikalpanāma
explainer: Toh 469 in the Kangyur is known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Yamāri Tantra Rāja Trikalpanāma and in Tibetan as the Glorious Black Yamāri Tantra, King of Tantras, the Third Kalpa. It is a tantric text belonging to the class of Highest Yoga Tantra, focused on the wrathful deity Yamāri — the Black Yamāri — who is celebrated as the conqueror of Yama, the lord of death, and is understood in ultimate terms as an emanation of the dharmakāya. The text concerns ritual instructions for practitioners who have completed the approach practice, guiding them in the construction of a maṇḍala in a charnel ground or other secluded place and the performance of associated rites connected with Yamāri's wheel of activity. It was translated into Tibetan by the monk Vajragrapha in collaboration with the accomplished Indian paṇḍita Bāro Phyagdum, and it forms part of the broader cycle of Yamāri tantras preserved within the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious King of Investigative Tantras of Vajrabhairava
explainer: Toh 470 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Vajrabhairava Kalpa Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal rdo rje 'jigs byed kyi rtog pa'i rgyud, rendered in English as the Glorious King of Investigative Tantras of Vajrabhairava. It belongs to the class of Highest Yoga Tantras centered on Vajrabhairava, the wrathful deity who is a fierce manifestation of Mañjuśrī and whose practice is concerned with the subjugation of Yama, the lord of death, and the liberation of beings from suffering through secret mantra accomplishment. The text is structured as a series of investigations, or kalpa sections, and the portion preserved here constitutes what is labeled the third such investigation, suggesting it forms part of a larger tantric cycle related to the Black Yamāntaka tradition. As a canonical tantra of the Vajrayāna, it sits within the Kangyur alongside other Vajrabhairava and Yamāntaka scriptures, presenting ritual and meditational instructions involving wrathful deity yoga, mantra, and the esoteric deployment of protective and liberating forces.

title: Praise of the Glorious Vajrabhairava
explainer: Toh 471 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Tibetan as Dpal Dorje Jikjé, and in Sanskrit as Śrī Vajrabhairava, belonging to the cycle of teachings associated with the wrathful deity Vajrabhairava, the great destroyer of death. The text is a ritual or narrative scripture in which Vajrabhairava, arising from the vajra body, speech, and mind of the Buddha, storms the southern realm of Yama, the Lord of Death, shattering iron fortresses and compelling the terrified demonic and infernal forces to submit and pledge their obedience. It belongs to the class of tantric literature within the Kangyur and is connected to the Vajrabhairava cycle, one of the most important Highest Yoga Tantra traditions preserved especially in the Geluk school of Tibetan Buddhism. The translation into Tibetan was made by Nyima Gyaltsen, and the text's vivid, hymnic opening sets the scene of Vajrabhairava's cosmic victory over the forces of death and obstruction.

title: The Ritual Called the Chuchuṇḍhara (Ritual of Teu-lopa)
explainer: Toh 472 in the Kangyur is a tantric ritual text known in Sanskrit as the Chuchundharakalpa and in Tibetan as Teulo pa'i cho ga, meaning roughly the Ritual of Teu-lopa or the Chuchuṇḍhara Ritual. The text belongs to the class of tantric manuals concerned with the practical application of a specific vidyā-mantra associated with Chuchuṇḍhara, a figure invoked alongside Yamāntaka, the wrathful slayer-deity. It prescribes a sequence of ritual activities including offerings of fragrance, flowers, and incense, prolonged mantra recitation, and the use of powdered remains of the chuchuṇḍhara creature to achieve various forms of tantric accomplishment. As a sādhana-style compendium of ritual procedures oriented toward worldly and supramundane goals, it sits within the broader category of Tantric texts in the Kangyur.

title: The Tantra King Called 'The Black Karma of Yamāri, the Enemy of the Lord of Death, Which Accomplishes All Through the Wheel'
sanskrit: Yamāri Kṛṣṇakarma Sarva Cakra Siddha Kara Nāma Tantra Rāja
explainer: Toh 473 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Yamāri Kṛṣṇakarma Sarva Cakra Siddha Kara Nāma Tantra Rāja, and in Tibetan as the tantra king called "The Black Karma of Yamāri, the Enemy of the Lord of Death, Which Accomplishes All Through the Wheel." It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantric literature and centers on Yamāri, a wrathful deity who conquers Yama, the lord of death, with the text presenting teachings on ritual accomplishment through the mandala or wheel associated with this deity's dark, or black, activity. The text opens in the characteristic sutra-style framing of tantric scriptures, with the Buddha figure identified as the Blessed One surrounded by a vast assembly of vajra deities and mothers, suggesting an elaborate tantric setting concerned with the transformation of the five poisons and the elements into awakened qualities. As a tantra king, it represents a prestige category within the Kangyur's collection of tantric scriptures, relating to the Yamāri cycle of practice that was influential in Indian and Tibetan Buddhism.

title: The Glorious Tantra King Called the Red Yamāri
explainer: Toh 474 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Raktayamāritantrarāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal gshin rje'i gshed dmar po zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, meaning in English "The Glorious Tantra King Called the Red Yamāri." It belongs to the class of highest yoga tantras and centers on Raktayamāri, the Red Yamāri, a wrathful deity understood as the slayer or destroyer of Yama, the lord of death, who serves as a central focus of esoteric practice and ritual. The text opens in the classic canonical style with the declaration "Thus did I hear," locating the teaching in a visionary setting where the Blessed One abides within the secret essence of all the Tathāgatas, and the great bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi poses questions about the nature and number of those who destroy Yama. As a tantra king, this scripture holds a position of particular authority within its cycle, presenting doctrine, meditation, and the qualities of Yamāri practice in a revealed, dialogic form characteristic of the Vajrayāna tantric literature preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Glorious King of Tantras of the Red Yamāri
sanskrit: Śrī Māṃrakta Yamāri Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: Toh 475 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Māṃrakta Yamāri Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal ldan gshin rje gshed dmar po'i rgyud kyi rgyal po, rendered in English as The Glorious King of Tantras of the Red Yamāri. It belongs to the class of highest yoga tantras and is dedicated to Raktayamāri, the red wrathful deity who embodies the destruction of death and is a fierce manifestation central to the Yamāri cycle of practice. The text opens in the classical sūtra-style framing of a teaching given by the Blessed One, but quickly establishes its tantric character by invoking figures such as Hevajra and referencing related tantras like the Saṃpuṭa, situating it within a broader network of Vajrayāna scriptural traditions. As a king of tantras concerned with ritual methods ranging from the attainment of sovereign power to healing and the full range of worldly and liberating aims, it stands as an important canonical example of the Yamāri tantric literature preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Great King of Tantras Called the Glorious Blessed One Ekajaṭā's Great Kalpa Tantra
sanskrit: Śrī Bhagavatī Ekajaṭā Mahākalpa Tantra Rāja Nāma
explainer: Toh 476 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Bhagavatī Ekajaṭā Mahākalpa Tantra Rāja and in Tibetan as the Dpal bcom ldan 'das ral pa gcig pa'i brtag pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po, rendered in English as The Great King of Tantras Called the Glorious Blessed One Ekajaṭā's Tantra. It belongs to the tantric section of the Kangyur and is devoted to the fierce protective deity Ekajaṭā, a prominent figure in the Vajrayāna tradition associated with the safeguarding of the Dharma and wrathful enlightened activity. The text opens in classical sūtra style, with the Buddha residing at the summit of Vajra Mountain at Caṇḍālā in the company of an assembly of great bodhisattvas accomplished in the profoundly secret teachings, suggesting a scripture that expounds ritual, maṇḍala, and tantric practice centered on Ekajaṭā. As a Mahākalpa tantra — a "great tantra of ritual procedures" — it provides an extensive doctrinal and ceremonial framework within the broader corpus of Vajrayāna canonical literature preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The tantra of the secret ornament of the moon
The great secret yogatantra the tip of the vajra
The King of Tantras Called 'The All-Secret'
explainer: Toh 481 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in English as "The King of Tantras Called 'The All-Secret,'" in Sanskrit as the Sarva-rahasya-nāma-tantra-rāja, and in Tibetan as Thamché Sangwa Zhejawa Gyüdkyi Gyalpo. It belongs to the class of Buddhist tantras and is addressed to the Wisdom Bodhisattva, opening with verses on the nature of mind, the five elements as expressions of essential reality, and the non-dual wisdom of the buddhas as the supreme secret underlying all phenomena. The text presents itself as a "king of tantras," suggesting a text of particular authority within the tantric corpus, and its themes of self-knowing awareness, the unborn nature of mind, and the path to buddhahood through meditative cultivation place it within the broader tradition of highest yoga tantra literature preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Great King of Ritual Procedures, Victorious over the Three Worlds
explainer: Toh 482 in the Kangyur is a text known in Sanskrit as the Trailokya-vijaya-mahākalpa-rāja and in Tibetan as Kham gsum rnam par rgyal ba'i rgyal po chen po, meaning "The Great King of Ritual Procedures, Victorious over the Three Worlds." It is a mahākalpa, or great tantra of ritual procedures, belonging to the class of tantric scriptures and concerned with Vajrasattva and the practices associated with conquest over the three realms of existence. The text opens in the classic sūtra style with the phrase "Thus did I hear," situating the teaching on the summit of Mount Meru before an assembly of bodhisattvas and a vast retinue of divine and semi-divine beings. It was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian preceptor Padmākara and the celebrated great-revision translator, the monk Rinchen Zangpo, and belongs among the tantric collections of the Kangyur.

title: The Tantra Called the Examination of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened Buddha, King of Radiant Splendor, Purifier of All Lower Destinies
explainer: Toh 483 in the Kangyur is a tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Sarva-durgati-pariśodhana-tejorāja-tathāgatārhat-samyaksambuddhasya-kalpa and in Tibetan as the Dé zhin shekpa dra chompa yangdakpar dzokpé sangyé ngenso tamché yongsu jongwa zibrijé kyi... — rendered in English as "The Tantra Called the Examination of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened Buddha, King of Radiant Splendor, Purifier of All Lower Destinies." It is a ritual tantra concerned with the purification of beings from the lower realms of rebirth, drawing on the power and radiance of a specific transcendent buddha figure to cleanse negative karma and free sentient beings from unfortunate destinies. The text opens in the manner of a sūtra, with the Buddha residing in a celestial grove of great magnificence surrounded by divine assemblies, suggesting a blending of sūtra-style framing with tantric content and practice. As Toh 483 in the Kangyur, it belongs to the tantric section of the canon and is associated with the broader Sarva-durgati-pariśodhana cycle, a well-known corpus of kriyā or caryā tantra literature devoted to funerary rites, purification, and the liberation of beings from lower existences.

title: Single-Portion Examination of the King of Glorious Purification
explainer: Toh 484 in the Kangyur is a tantric ritual text known in Tibetan as Yongsu Jongwa Ziji Kyi Gyalpo, which translates into English as the Examination of the King of Glorious Purification. It belongs to the class of tantric literature and concerns the performance of fierce or wrathful ritual action, known in Sanskrit as abhicāra, prescribing detailed instructions for constructing fire-pits and ritual platforms in liminal spaces such as charnel grounds and the dwellings of butchers and demons. The text as preserved in the Kangyur represents a single-portion examination, suggesting it formed part of a larger tantra or cycle of related teachings. It was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian abbot Śāntaṃgarbha together with the Tibetan translator monk Jayarakṣita, and subsequently edited and finalized by the ācārya Rinchen Chok according to the later standardized Tibetan terminology.

title: A One-Sided Examination of the King of Radiance, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened Buddha Who Thoroughly Purifies All the Lower Realms
explainer: "A One-Sided Examination of the King of Radiance, the Tathāgata Who Thoroughly Purifies All the Lower Realms" is a canonical Buddhist sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Sarvaduṛgatipariśodhana Tejorarāja and in Tibetan as Dེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ངན་སོང་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་སྦྱོང་བ་གཟི་བརྗིད་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོའི་བརྟག་པ་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པ. The text belongs to the tradition of purification literature, centering on the luminous buddha figure known as the King of Radiance, whose enlightened qualities are celebrated for their power to cleanse beings of the sufferings associated with lower rebirths. Presented in the classical sūtra format — opening with the Buddha dwelling in a resplendent celestial grove filled with jeweled trees and many varieties of sacred flowers — the text unfolds as a discourse attributed directly to Śākyamuni Buddha. It is Toh 485 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general class of dhāraṇī-related or ritual purification sūtras within the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: Tantra That is a Condensed Summary of the Rite of Consecration
explainer: The Tantra That is a Condensed Summary of the Rite of Consecration, known in Sanskrit as the Supratiṣṭhātantrasaṃgraha and in Tibetan as Rab tu gnas pa mdor bsdus pa'i rgyud, is a tantric text concerned with the proper performance of consecration rites for sacred images, whether cast, painted, or sculpted in relief. It opens in the manner of a Buddha-word teaching, with the Blessed One entering a specific meditative absorption before expounding the requirements for both the officiant and the sacred object — covering the master's qualifications, the correct proportions and marks of images, and the associated mudrās, mantras, and ritual procedures. The text is presented in a mixture of prose and verse, giving it a character typical of condensed liturgical or ritual manuals within the tantric tradition. It is Toh 486 in the Kangyur, where it belongs among the tantric scriptures, and its homage to Vajrasattva situates it within the broader Vajrayāna ritual literature concerned with the empowerment and activation of devotional supports.

title: The Glorious Primordial: The King of Conceptual Elaboration of the Great Vehicle
explainer: Toh 487 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna tantric text known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Paramādi Nāma Mahāyāna Kalārāja and in Tibetan as Dpal Mchog Dang Po, rendered in English as The Glorious Primordial, with the fuller title The King of Conceptual Elaboration of the Great Vehicle. It belongs to the tantric division of the Kangyur and is associated with the Perfection of Wisdom, as indicated by its opening homage to the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā. The text unfolds in the classic sūtra style of "Thus did I hear," presenting the Buddha as a supremely empowered figure endowed with the vajra blessing of all the Tathāgatas, sovereign over the three realms, and master of all mudrās and wisdoms. As a tantra concerned with the gnosis, samayas, and yogic realization connected to Prajñāpāramitā, it represents a distinctive meeting point between the Perfection of Wisdom literature and Mahāyāna tantric practice.

The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra Called 'The Twenty-Five Gates of the Perfection of Wisdom'
explainer: "The Twenty-Five Gates of the Perfection of Wisdom," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-pañcaviṃśatika-prajñāpāramitā-mukha and in Tibetan as Shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i sgo nyi shu rtsa lnga pa, is a Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom family of texts. It presents the Buddha's teaching on prajñāpāramitā — the transcendent wisdom that lies at the heart of the bodhisattva path — organized around twenty-five distinctive "gates" or approaches to that wisdom. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling on the peak of Mount Meru amid an immense assembly of bodhisattvas and a vast array of divine and non-human beings, establishing a suitably cosmic setting for the discourse that follows. It is Toh 491 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras of that collection.

title: The Tantra King Called the Ornamental Array of Secrets of Body, Speech, and Mind of All the Tathāgatas
explainer: Toh 492 in the Kangyur is a tantric scripture known in English as The Tantra King Called the Ornamental Array of Secrets of Body, Speech, and Mind of All the Tathāgatas, and in Sanskrit as the Sarva-tathāgata-kāya-vāk-citta-guhyālaṃkāra-vyūha-tantra-rāja, with its Tibetan title rendered as De bzhin gshegs pa thams cad kyi sku dang gsung dang thugs kyi gsang ba rgyan gyi bkod pa zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po. It belongs to the class of tantra texts within the Kangyur and is concerned with the esoteric dimensions of the body, speech, and mind of all the buddhas, expounded through the rich symbolic language of vajra-wisdom, great mudrās, empowerments, and meditative absorptions. The text opens in the classic sūtra-style frame of "thus did I hear," situating the teaching with the Blessed One at its center, surrounded by an elaborate assembly invoked through the intertwined themes of vajra-wisdom and the three secrets common to Vajrayāna discourse. Its translator's homage to both the guru and Mañjuśrī at the outset reflects the standard Tibetan transmission conventions for tantric works of this kind.

title: The Noble Sūtra Called the Secret Jewel-Dot
explainer: Toh 493 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryaguhyamaṇitilakā and in Tibetan as the Phags pa gsang ba nor bu thig le, rendered in English as the Noble Sūtra Called the Secret Jewel-Dot. It belongs to the tantric-inflected sūtra literature of the Kangyur, situated among texts with a strongly Vajrayāna character, and opens with an elaborate description of the Buddha Vairocana enthroned in his role as the Dharma King of the three realms, invested with the samaya-wisdom and mudrās of all Tathāgatas. The text's imagery of vajra consecration, crown empowerment, and the boundless compassion of the All-Illuminating one places it squarely within the esoteric doctrinal world shared by Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna traditions. As Toh 493 in the Kangyur, it is preserved as part of the canonical scriptural heritage transmitted into Tibetan Buddhism.

The Dhāraṇī of the Eight Noble Goddesses
explainer: The Dhāraṇī of the Eight Noble Goddesses, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Aṣṭa Devī Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phakpa Lhamo Gyé kyi Zung, is a short dhāraṇī text belonging to the broader category of dhāraṇī and mantra literature within the Kangyur. The text centers on a powerful dhāraṇī presented as the speech of Vajrapāṇi, who proclaims it as the supreme mantra of the Mother of the Tathāgatas — a figure praised for her capacity to purify misdeeds, pacify illness, destroy obstacles, and bestow all forms of excellence. The dhāraṇī itself takes the form of a ritual mantra invocation addressed to the eight noble goddesses associated with these protective and purifying functions. It is Toh 497 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the dhāraṇī collections of that canon.

title: The Noble Vajrapāṇi, Wearer of the Dark Blue Garment, Vajrapātāla Tantra
explainer: Toh 499 in the Kangyur is a Buddhist tantra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Vajrapāṇi-nīlāmbara-dhara-vajrapātāla-nāma-tantra and in Tibetan as "The Tantra Called 'The Noble Vajrapāṇi, Wearer of the Dark Blue Garment, Vajrapātāla.'" It is a Vajrayāna tantric text centered on the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the powerful wielder of the thunderbolt who serves as a protector of the Buddhist teachings, and its narrative unfolds in the underground realm of the nāga kings, where the Buddha transmits esoteric instructions. The text belongs to the tantra section of the Kangyur and was translated into Tibetan by the Kashmiri paṇḍita Tselu together with the Tibetan translator known as the noble Śerab. The opening of the surviving Tibetan text begins at what is labeled the thirteenth chapter, suggesting this may be a partial or later portion of a larger tantric cycle.

title: The King of Ritual Manuals Called 'Traversing the Three by Vajra'
explainer: Toh 500 in the Kangyur is a tantric ritual text known in English as "The King of Ritual Manuals Called 'Traversing the Three by Vajra,'" corresponding to the Sanskrit Vajrabhūmitricaraṇarājakalpa and the Tibetan Rdo rjes gsum du rgyu ba zhes bya ba'i rtog pa'i rgyal po. It belongs to the class of kalpa or ritual manual literature associated with Vajrayāna practice, concerning the use of deity, mantra, and meditative practice as a path in which conceptuality is overcome through conceptuality itself, ultimately leading to the peace of the wrathful deity realization. The text is presented as a teaching proclaimed by the Lord of Secrets in connection with Śākyamuni of the wrathful family, and it includes detailed instructions on the formation of seed syllables and their embellishments, situating it firmly within the esoteric tantric corpus of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Tantra Called 'Vajrapāṇi Wearing the Blue Garment: Taming the Three Worlds'
explainer: The Noble Tantra Called "Vajrapāṇi Wearing the Blue Garment: Taming the Three Worlds" is a Buddhist tantric scripture known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Vajrapāṇi-nīlāmbara-dhara-triloka-vinaya-nāma-tantra and in Tibetan as the Pakpa Chakna Dorje Gö Ngönpo Chen Zhéja Jigtén Sum Dulwé Gyü. It belongs to the class of tantric texts and concerns the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the powerful wielder of the thunderbolt, who here appears in his blue-garmented form as a master capable of taming the three worlds of gods, humans, and other beings. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling in a celestial palace to the north of Mount Meru, where he enters a samādhi called "Taming the Three Worlds" and emanates rays of three-colored light from the maṇḍala at his heart, addressing an immeasurable assembly with words of reassurance. This text is Toh 501 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the tantric scriptures of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: The sovereign tantra orderly arrangement of the three vows
The sutra describing in full the specific previous vows of the seven tathagatas
