The Noble Great Vehicle Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Casket of the Secret Relics, the Heart of the Blessing of All the Tathāgatas
explainer: Toh 507 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī sūtra known in English as "The Great Vehicle Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Noble Casket of the Secret Relics, the Heart of the Blessing of All the Tathāgatas," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-sarva-tathāgata-adhiṣṭhāna-hṛdaya-guhya-dhātu-karaṇḍa-nāma-dhāraṇī-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa de bzhin gshegs pa thams cad kyi byin gyi rlabs kyi snying po gsang ba'i ring bsrel za ma tog ces bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo. The text belongs to the dhāraṇī sūtra genre, presenting sacred syllables and ritual instructions centered on the power of the relics and blessings of all the tathāgatas — a subject with strong connections to stūpa veneration and the consecration of reliquary objects. The sūtra opens with the Buddha residing in Magadha, surrounded by a vast assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and an array of divine and semi-divine beings, establishing the classic setting for the revelation of a teaching of far-reaching spiritual efficacy.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called 'The Hundred Thousand Ornaments of the Seat of Awakening'
explainer: Toh 508 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Bodhimaṇḍasya Yakṣālāṅgāra Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the dhāraṇī called "The Hundred Thousand Ornaments of the Seat of Awakening." As its title suggests, the text belongs to the dhāraṇī literature of the Kangyur, a genre devoted to sacred ritual formulas believed to confer protection and spiritual benefit, and its content centers on a dhāraṇī associated with the seat or place of enlightenment. The text is set in the familiar sūtra frame of the Buddha teaching at Vārāṇasī in the presence of a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, lending it the authority of a direct discourse of the Blessed One. It was translated into Tibetan by the translator Tsang Devendrarakṣita and is preserved among the dhāraṇī collections of the Kangyur.

title: Dhāraṇī of a Hundred Thousand Ornaments of the Essence of Enlightenment
explainer: Toh 509 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Bodhigarbhālaṃkāralakṣadhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Byaṅ chub kyi snyiṅ po'i rgyan 'bum gyi gzuṅs, rendered in English as the Dhāraṇī of the Ornament of a Hundred Thousand Essences of Awakening. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and consists primarily of a ritual dhāraṇī formula — a string of sacred syllables and invocations addressed to the buddhas and bodhisattvas, including Śākyamuni — intended to concentrate and transmit the spiritual essence of awakening. According to a note preserved in the text itself, this collection appears to have been extracted from a larger source and was written out separately only because the earlier portions of that source were temporarily unavailable. As a dhāraṇī text, it exemplifies the class of canonical works that distill vast stores of merit and wisdom into consecrated verbal formulas for recitation and practice.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'The Radiance of the Pure, Stainless Ray of Light'
explainer: Toh 510 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-raśmi-vimala-viśuddha-prabhā-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Özer Drima Mepa Nampar Dakpé Ö, meaning "The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'The Radiance of the Pure, Stainless Ray of Light.'" It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and presents a sacred incantation concerned with the power of pure, radiant light, framed within a discourse delivered by the Buddha at the great city of Kapilavastu before an assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and a host of divine and semi-divine beings. The text opens by noting that it was extracted from a larger work, the Bodhyagryābharaṇaśatasāhasra, suggesting it originally formed part of a much more extensive collection. The gathering of prominent bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Vajrapāṇi, and Maitreya points to the Mahāyāna character of the text, situating it within the broader tradition of dhāraṇī literature aimed at invoking protective and purifying spiritual power.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called 'The Twelve Buddhas'
explainer: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called "The Twelve Buddhas," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-dvādaśabuddha-nāma-mahāyānasūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangye Chunyipa Zhejawa Tekpa Chenpo'i Do, is a Mahāyāna sūtra in which the Buddha, dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, addresses the bodhisattva Maitreya and reveals the existence of twelve buddhas presiding over distant buddha-fields in the eastern direction. The text belongs to the genre of buddhānusmṛti, or recollection of the buddhas, presenting the names and qualities of these awakened beings as objects of devotion and aspiration. It is Toh 511 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the general sūtra collections of the Mahāyāna section of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle called The Seven Buddhas
sanskrit: Ārya Sapta Buddhaka nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra
explainer: The Seven Buddhas, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sapta Buddhaka Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa sangs rgyas bdun pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, is a Mahāyāna sūtra that recounts a teaching delivered by the Blessed One at the summit of Mount Tise, in the presence of a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas including Maitreya, Ākāśagarbha, and Samantabhadra. As its title indicates, the text concerns the seven buddhas, a traditional grouping of awakened beings that spans the distant past to the historical Buddha Śākyamuni, and it belongs to the devotional and narrative dimension of Mahāyāna literature. It is Toh 512 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the general sūtra collections of that canon.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'Endowed with the Limbs of All Buddhas'
explainer: Toh 513 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-sarvabuddhāṅgavatī-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Sangye Tamché Kyi Yenlak Dangdenpa Zhejawa'i Zung, rendered in English as "The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Endowed with the Limbs of All Buddhas." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts centered on sacred ritual formulas believed to confer protection and spiritual benefit. The text opens with the Buddha addressing the four guardian kings on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, teaching that human beings face four great fears — old age, sickness, decline, and death — with the fear of death being the most fearsome and inescapable of all. Against these terrors, the dhāraṇī is presented as a powerful means of protection and liberation, embodying the qualities of all buddhas.

title: The Dharma Categories of the Dhāraṇī Called 'The Noble Heart of the Buddha'
explainer: Toh 514 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-buddha-hṛdaya-nāma-dhāraṇī-dharma-viparyāya and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Sangyé kyi Nyingpo zhé byawé Zung kyi Chö kyi Namgrang, rendered into English as "The Dharma Categories of the Dhāraṇī Called 'The Noble Heart of the Buddha.'" As its title indicates, the text belongs to the dhāraṇī literature of the Kangyur, presenting a classification or enumeration of Dharma teachings organized around a sacred dhāraṇī associated with the heart or essence of the Buddha. The work opens in the familiar sūtra style, with the Buddha present in a wondrous assembly of vast numbers of bodhisattvas at an extraordinary sacred site, suggesting that the dhāraṇī and its accompanying doctrinal categories are revealed within a visionary and ceremonially elevated setting. Sitting among the dhāraṇī collections of the Kangyur, this text reflects the broader tradition of canonical works that combine liturgical or mantra-based practice with systematic Dharma exposition.

title: The Noble Heart of the Buddha: A Named Dhāraṇī
explainer: Toh 515 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-buddha-hṛdaya-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Sangyé Kyi Nyingpo Shéja Wé Zung, meaning "The Noble Heart of the Buddha." As its name suggests, it belongs to the dhāraṇī class of canonical literature, presenting a sacred formula and its associated teaching within a narrative frame in which the Buddha addresses an assembly of gods of the Pure Abodes. The text opens with the Buddha prophesying a future Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma, situating the dhāraṇī within a broader vision of ongoing Buddhist transmission across time. It is preserved in the Kangyur in a version that was revised and definitively established through the correction of newly emerged terminology, indicating a careful editorial history in the Tibetan transmission.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called 'The Noble Heap of Flowers'
explainer: The dhāraṇī known in Sanskrit as the Āryapuṣpakūṭa nāma dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as "The Noble Heap of Flowers" is a dhāraṇī scripture belonging to the Kangyur, catalogued as Toh 516. As a dhāraṇī text, it presents a sacred formula of spiritual power set within a narrative frame in which the Buddha teaches at the great lake Anavatapta, in the palace of the nāga king Anavatapta, before a vast assembly of monks and highly advanced bodhisattvas. The text belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of works that transmit mantra-based practices associated with protection, purification, and spiritual attainment. It was translated into Tibetan by the monk and great editor-translator Yeshé Dé in collaboration with the Indian scholar Dānaśīla, and was subsequently revised and finalized in accordance with the standardized Tibetan terminology established during the imperial period of translation.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'The Stainless One'
explainer: Toh 517 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Vimala nāma dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as "The Stainless One" (Phags pa dri ma med pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs), belonging to the broader collection of noble dhāraṇīs. The text records a teaching delivered by the Buddha at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, addressed to the bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, and concerns the complete purity of the Tathāgata as expressed through moral discipline, meditative absorption, patience, and related virtues. As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it combines doctrinal exposition on the qualities of buddhahood with the sacred formulaic character typical of this genre of canonical literature. It is preserved in the Kangyur alongside a preceding dhāraṇī text known as the "Stack of Flowers," with which it shares a colophon, situating it within the dhāraṇī section of the collection.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'Sandalwood Limb'
explainer: Toh 518 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in English as "The Noble Sandalwood Limb," in Sanskrit as the Ārya-candanāṅgā-nāma-dhāraṇī, and in Tibetan as Pakpa Tsendan Yangkyi Zhukpa Shyejawa'i Zungwa. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts centered on the preservation and recitation of sacred ritual formulas believed to confer protection and spiritual benefit. The text opens with a standard sūtra framing, presenting the Buddha dwelling at Rājagṛha amid a vast assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and gods, before addressing the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, suggesting the dhāraṇī is closely associated with this bodhisattva's compassionate activity. The text was translated into Tibetan by the monk Yeshé Dé and subsequently revised in accordance with the standardized imperial terminology established during Tibet's early translation period.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī of the Rite of the Heart of Dependent Origination
explainer: Toh 519 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Āryapratītyasamutpādahṛdayavidhidhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Noble Dhāraṇī of the Rite of the Heart of Dependent Origination. It belongs to the dhāraṇī class of canonical literature and centers on a sacred formula rooted in the doctrine of dependent origination, accompanied by the ritual instructions for its recitation and application for the benefit of sentient beings. The text opens with the celebrated verse summarizing the Buddha's teaching on causally arisen phenomena, situating the dhāraṇī firmly within the framework of this foundational Buddhist teaching. It was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian preceptors Jinamitra and Dānaśīla together with the great editor-translator, the monk Ye shes sde, and was subsequently revised in accordance with the standardized new terminology of the imperial translation period.

title: The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called Dependent Origination
explainer: Toh 520 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryapratītyasamutpāda nāma mahāyānasūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo, rendered in English as The Noble Sūtra of the Great Vehicle Called Dependent Origination. The text belongs to the sūtra section of the Kangyur and takes as its central subject the doctrine of dependent origination, one of the most foundational teachings in Buddhist thought, which describes how all phenomena arise in dependence upon causes and conditions. The sūtra opens with the Buddha dwelling in the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods in the company of a vast assembly of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and divine beings including Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Brahmā, and Śakra, suggesting a setting of great cosmic significance befitting its profound doctrinal content. As a Mahāyāna sūtra, it frames the teaching on dependent origination within the broader perspective of the bodhisattva path and the liberation of all beings.

title: The Heart of Noble Dependent Origination
explainer: The Heart of Noble Dependent Origination, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Pratītyasamutpāda Hṛdaya and in Tibetan as Phags pa rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba'i snying po, is a brief Mahāyāna sūtra centered on the doctrine of dependent origination, one of the Buddha's most fundamental teachings. The text presents the celebrated verse — "Those phenomena that arise from causes, their causes, and the cessation of those causes: thus has the Tathāgata declared" — which encapsulates the entire teaching of conditioned arising and is traditionally considered a potent distillation of the Dharma. Alongside the verse in both translation and original Sanskrit, the text attributes great purificatory and protective power to its recitation, positioning it as a kind of dhāraṇī-like heart essence. It is Toh 521 in the Kangyur, classified among the Mahāyāna sūtras.

title: Toh 522 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Jñānolkā-
explainer: Toh 522 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Jñānolkā-nāma-dhāraṇī-sarvagati-pariśodhanī and in Tibetan as the Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Torch of Wisdom, which Thoroughly Purifies All Destinies of Beings. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and presents a sacred formula of great ritual and soteriological power, focused on the luminous wisdom of the tathāgata Jñānolkā and associated with the purification of all states of rebirth. The text opens with a series of homages to several named tathāgatas — including Satyavākya, Suvarṇaprabhasaṃcayabhāsa, and Bhayaśabdarāja — and unfolds through the voice of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, situating it within the broad Mahāyāna tradition of protective and purificatory scripture. A colophon note preceding the text indicates that reciting or focusing upon this dhāraṇī as an object of offering is said to be equivalent to making offerings that fill an entire world-system, underscoring the immense merit attributed to its recitation.

title: The Noble Great Lord of the Earth
explainer: Toh 523 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Āryamahāmahāindra-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as "The Noble Great Lord of the Earth" (འཕགས་པ་སའི་དབང་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་གཟུངས). It belongs to the dhāraṇī class of canonical literature, presenting a sacred incantation framed within a discourse involving the buddha Sarvaprabha and a brahmin figure called Great Lord of the Earth. The text is concerned with the purification of all beings, as reflected in the closing colophon of the preceding work, which describes the dhāraṇī's power to completely purify all sentient beings. It sits within the Kangyur's collection of dhāraṇī scriptures, a broad grouping of texts that preserve mantric and ritual formulas regarded as the speech of enlightened beings.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'The Indestructible'
explainer: Toh 524 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "The Indestructible" and bearing the related title "The Great Lord" (Sanskrit: Mahāpati or similar), belonging to the broad category of dhāraṇī and ritual scripture. The text recounts a scene in which Śakra, lord of the gods, approaches the Buddha at Vaiśālī near the Monkey Pond and requests a teaching to protect him from the ongoing attacks of the asuras, providing the narrative occasion for the Buddha to impart a powerful dhāraṇī. As is typical of this genre, the text combines a framing story with a protective formula intended to confer spiritual and worldly benefit on those who receive and recite it. It was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian preceptors Jinamitra and Dānaśīla together with the renowned Tibetan editor-translator Ye shes sde, and was later revised to conform to standardized orthographic conventions, placing it among the carefully edited canonical dhāraṇī collections of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'Accomplishing by Means of Limitless Doors'
explainer: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Accomplishing by Means of Limitless Doors," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Anantamukhāsādhaka-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phags pa sgo mtha' yas pa sgrub pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs, is a dhāraṇī sūtra set against the poignant backdrop of the Buddha's final months before his parinirvāṇa. The text opens with the Blessed One dwelling in Vaiśālī, where he announces to the assembled monks and bodhisattvas that he will pass into nirvāṇa after three months, providing the dramatic occasion for the teaching and transmission of this dhāraṇī. As a dhāraṇī text, it belongs to a class of scripture concerned with the preservation and empowerment conveyed through sacred formulas, here framed within a narrative of the Buddha's imminent passing. It is catalogued as Toh 525 in the Kangyur, situated among the dhāraṇī collections of that canon.

title: Toh 526 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "Phags pa sgo mtha'
explainer: Toh 526 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "Phags pa sgo mtha' yas pas bsgrub pa" and in Sanskrit as the "Ārya Anantamukhasādhaka," rendered into English as "The Noble Accomplishment Through Boundless Gates." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts centered on sacred verbal formulas believed to confer protection and spiritual benefit. The text presents the Buddha teaching a dhāraṇī called "The Six Gates" to an assembly of bodhisattvas gathered in a jewel-adorned space above a monastery courtyard, framing the practice as a means of alleviating suffering for all beings wandering through saṃsāra. As is characteristic of dhāraṇī scriptures, it combines a narrative setting drawn from sūtra convention with the transmission of a potent ritual formula intended for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

title: The King Who Arrays the Qualities of All Phenomena
sanskrit: Ārya Sarva Dharma Guṇa Vyūha Rāja Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra
explainer: Toh 527 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The King Who Arrays the Qualities of All Phenomena," in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarva Dharma Guṇa Vyūha Rāja Nāma Mahāyāna Sūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa chos thams cad kyi yon tan bkod pa'i rgyal po. It belongs to the sūtra class of canonical texts and presents a discourse of the Buddha delivered at the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka in Rājagṛha before a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, the latter distinguished by their attainment of dhāraṇī and their mastery of skillful means. The text concerns the spiritual qualities and profound wisdom associated with the Dharma, set within the devotional and doctrinal framework characteristic of Mahāyāna scripture. It appears in the Kangyur immediately following the dhāraṇī text known as "The Six Gates," with which it shares a manuscript gathering.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī, King of Wisdom-Mantras, Supreme Lamp
explainer: Toh 528 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-agrapradīpa-dhāraṇī-vidyārāja and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Rik Ngak Kyi Gyalpo Drönma Chok Gi Zung, rendered in English as "The Noble Dhāraṇī, King of Wisdom-Mantras, Supreme Lamp." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and presents a sacred dhāraṇī — a ritual formula of protective and spiritual power — framed within a classic sūtra setting in which the Buddha teaches at Śrāvastī surrounded by monks, gods, and bodhisattvas. The text introduces a distant buddha-field called Boundless Flowers, where another buddha currently dwells and teaches, situating the dhāraṇī within a vast, cosmologically expansive vision of multiple awakened beings active throughout the universe. As a vidyārāja, or "king of wisdom-mantras," the dhāraṇī is presented as possessing supreme efficacy, placing this work among the canonical collections that blend Mahāyāna doctrinal vision with the practical transmission of powerful mantric formulas.

title: The Noble Great Dhāraṇī
explainer: The Noble Great Dhāraṇī, known in Sanskrit as the Āryamahādhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Zungchenpo, is a dhāraṇī text presenting a powerful ritual formula taught by the Buddha to his disciple Ānanda. Set in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, the text opens with Ānanda visiting the Buddha after completing a rains retreat, establishing a narrative frame for the transmission of this sacred dhāraṇī. As a dhāraṇī scripture, it belongs to a class of texts concerned with the recitation and protective efficacy of condensed, mantra-like formulas regarded as embodiments of the Buddha's teaching. It is catalogued as Toh 529 in the Kangyur, the Tibetan canon of translated Buddhist scriptures.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables
explainer: Toh 530 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryasvalpākṣaraprajñāpāramitā and in Tibetan as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables. As its name suggests, it belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom, family of texts — scriptures concerned with the nature of emptiness and transcendent wisdom — and takes the compact form of a dhāraṇī, a condensed sacred formula embodying that wisdom. The text is set at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and gods, a classic framing shared with many sūtras of this genre. It was translated from Sanskrit into Tibetan by the Indian preceptors Jinamitra and Dānaśīla together with the renowned Tibetan editor-translator Yeshé Dé, and was subsequently revised in accordance with the standardized later translation conventions.

title: The Heart of the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 531 in the Kangyur is the Heart Sūtra, known in Sanskrit as the Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya and in Tibetan as the Bcom ldan 'das ma shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i snying po, meaning "The Heart of the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom." It is one of the most celebrated and widely recited texts in the entire Buddhist canon, belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras, and it distills the vast Prajñāpāramitā literature into a concise teaching on emptiness and the nature of the five aggregates. Set on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, the text unfolds as an exchange involving the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the monk Śāriputra, arising through the Buddha's meditative power, and culminates in the famous proclamation that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. As Toh 531 in the Kangyur, it is classed among the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras and represents one of the shortest yet most doctrinally concentrated expressions of Mahāyāna Buddhist insight.

title: The Dhāraṇī Together with Mantras of the One Hundred and Eight Names of the Buddha, the Blessed One
explainer: Toh 532 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Buddha Bhagavān Aṣṭaśatanāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das kyi mtshan brgya rtsa brgyad pa gzungs sngags dang bcas pa, rendered in English as "The Dhāraṇī Together with Mantras of the One Hundred and Eight Names of the Buddha, the Blessed One." As its title indicates, the text belongs to the dhāraṇī genre and is devoted to enumerating one hundred and eight names and epithets of the Buddha, each reflecting an aspect of his enlightened qualities — his compassion, his physical majesty, his freedom from wrongdoing, and his perfection of wisdom — embedded within a framework of dhāraṇī and mantra recitation. Such name-dhāraṇī texts were widely used in Indian and Tibetan Buddhist practice as a means of generating merit, invoking the Buddha's blessings, and internalizing his qualities through liturgical recitation. It is classified among the dhāraṇī and mantra collections of the Kangyur, the Tibetan canon of translated Buddhist scriptures.

title: The One Hundred and Eight Names of the Blessed One, Together with the Dhāraṇī Mantra
explainer: Toh 533 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in English as "The One Hundred and Eight Names of the Blessed One, Together with the Dhāraṇī Mantra," dedicated to the Buddha Śākyamuni, whose name in Sanskrit is Śākyamuni and in Tibetan is ཤཱཀྱ་ཐུབ་པ. The text belongs to the dhāraṇī class of canonical literature, presenting a collection of one hundred and eight epithets of the Buddha alongside a concluding mantra — the well-known formula "muṇi muṇi mahāmunaye svāhā" — together with assurances of the vast merit to be gained through its recitation. Texts of this type serve both devotional and ritual purposes, offering practitioners a structured means of venerating the Buddha through his names while invoking the protective and purifying power of the accompanying dhāraṇī. It sits within the Kangyur, the Tibetan canon of translated Buddha-word, as Toh 533, in the broader category of dhāraṇī and mantra literature.

title: Toh 534 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as the Essence o
explainer: Toh 534 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as the Essence of the Noble Śākyamuni, corresponding to the Sanskrit designation Āryaśākyamunidhāraṇī, and it belongs to the broader category of dhāraṇī literature within the canon. The text presents a concentrated ritual formula invoking the purifying power of the Buddha Śākyamuni alongside homages to the Tathāgata Vairocana and the bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, promising that recitation of its mantra will cleanse even grave accumulations of non-virtuous deeds. It further assures practitioners of protection from physical dangers — weapons, fire, water, and poison — as well as from human adversaries such as kings and thieves. As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it exemplifies the genre of compact, apotropaic scripture found throughout the Kangyur's collection of protective and purificatory texts.

title: The Essence of the Noble Vairocana
explainer: Toh 535 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "Zla ba'i 'od" and in Sanskrit as something approximating the Candraprabha, meaning "Moonlight" in English. It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī literature, short ritual and protective scripture collections that form part of the broader dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, and it concerns the recitation of a sacred mantra formula invoking the Tathāgata Moonlight alongside blessings of the Three Jewels. The text promises that those who recite this dhāraṇī — particularly sons and daughters of good family who do so at dawn or by moonlight — will be protected from epidemic diseases, harmful influences, and contagious illnesses, and will attain the meditative absorption known as Stainless Light. It appears immediately following the closely related Essence of the Noble Vairocana dhāraṇī, suggesting these short protective texts were transmitted and preserved together as a cluster within the canon.

title: Toh 536 in the Kangyur is a brief canonical text known in English as "The Recoll
explainer: Toh 536 in the Kangyur is a brief canonical text known in English as "The Recollection of the Name Candraprabha," with Candraprabha being the Sanskrit name meaning "Moonlight" and corresponding to the Tibetan Zla ba'i 'od. It belongs to the genre of name-recollection texts, a form of devotional and merit-generating scripture that extols the spiritual benefits of calling to mind the name of a particular buddha or bodhisattva. The text teaches that by recollecting the name Candraprabha one will remember past lives across forty thousand aeons and be protected from rebirth in the lower realms. As it stands in the Kangyur, it is a very short, self-contained piece that preserves only the concluding statement of its teaching, suggesting it may be a brief extract or condensed liturgical passage drawn from a larger scriptural context.

title: Recollection of the Heart of All the Tathāgatas
explainer: Toh 537 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī or mantra text known in Sanskrit as the Tathāgata-hṛdaya, meaning "The Heart of the Tathāgata," and in Tibetan as De bzhin gshegs pa spyi'i snying po. It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī literature and presents a series of sacred mantras associated with the Tathāgatas and specific buddhas, most notably the Buddha Ratnasikhin (the Jewel-Crested One), together with the spiritual benefits conferred by their recitation, such as the purification of vast karmic obscurations and liberation from rebirth in lower realms. The text is compact in form, consisting primarily of mantra formulas accompanied by brief prose statements extolling their efficacy, a structure typical of canonical dhāraṇī collections. It is found in the Kangyur, the Tibetan canon of buddhavacana, or words of the Buddha, and represents the kind of practical devotional material that circulated widely in Indian and Tibetan Buddhist communities.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called 'Cloud of Offerings'
explainer: Toh 538 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Pūjāmegha dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Mchod pa'i sprin zhes bya ba'i gzungs, meaning "The Dhāraṇī Called Cloud of Offerings." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and presents a sacred mantra formula together with a brief account of its extraordinary merit, according to which the mere act of recollecting it is said to be equivalent to making vast offerings and prostrations to all the buddhas of the ten directions. The text opens with homage to the Three Jewels and to the tathāgata Vajrasārapramardanī, followed by the dhāraṇī itself in Sanskrit transliteration, before describing the immense spiritual benefits that arise from its recitation and remembrance.

title: Toh 539 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as མཆོད་པའི་སྤྲིན (Chö
explainer: Toh 539 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as མཆོད་པའི་སྤྲིན (Chödpé Trin) and in Sanskrit as Pūjāmegha, meaning "Cloud of Offerings." It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī literature and presents a sequence of ritual dhāraṇī formulas for protection, homage, praise, and the consecration of offerings, with the promise that even a single recollection of the dhāraṇī suffices to obtain its benefits and ensure rebirth in the pure realm of Sukhāvatī. The text is a compact liturgical work, structured around successive mantra recitations each accompanied by a brief indication of their purpose, reflecting the practical devotional use typical of dhāraṇī collections within the Kangyur.

title: Toh 539 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as Rinpoche Darwé Zung
explainer: Toh 539 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as Rinpoche Darwé Zung, which can be rendered into English as the Dhāraṇī of Rubbing with Jewels. It belongs to the general class of dhāraṇī literature within the Kangyur, a category of texts centered on sacred ritual formulas believed to carry protective and purifying power. The text presents a mantra invocation accompanied by homages to a tathāgata called Lotus-Eye and a bodhisattva known as Remover of All Obscurations, and it opens with a visualization in which rubbing jewels generates an immeasurable offering of parasols and victory banners that fills all of space. Following the dhāraṇī formula itself, the text goes on to provide practical instructions for its recitation, including guidance on the auspicious timing and frequency of practice.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called Surūpa
explainer: The Dhāraṇī Called Surūpa, known in Sanskrit as the Surūpa-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Su rū pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs, is a short ritual dhāraṇī text concerned with the benefits conferred by reciting a sacred mantra formula, including the beautification of the body and the gladdening of the mind. The text centers on a dhāraṇī addressed to the tathāgata Surūpa and provides practical instructions for its use, particularly the recitation of the mantra seven times over food mixed with water as an offering to hungry ghosts, suggesting a compassionate aim of relieving the suffering of beings in lower states of existence. It is Toh 540 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general class of dhāraṇī literature, and it appears alongside the preceding dhāraṇī of the Lotus Eyes of the Noble One, indicating it forms part of a broader collection of such ritual and apotropaic texts within the canon.

title: The Noble One Who Liberates from the Eight Great Fears: A Dhāraṇī
explainer: Toh 541 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-aṣṭa-mahābhaya-tāriṇī-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Jikpa Chenpo Gyé Lé Drolwa Zhejawa'i Zung, meaning "The Noble Dhāraṇī Called the One Who Liberates from the Eight Great Fears." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and centers on the bodhisattva Tārā in her aspect as a protector who delivers beings from eight categories of great fear. The text opens with homages to a series of tathāgatas and to the great compassionate bodhisattva who grants fearlessness, before presenting the dhāraṇī formula itself, which practitioners would recite for protection and liberation from danger. As a dhāraṇī, it is a relatively concise ritual and devotional text, representing the widespread Buddhist tradition of invoking Tārā's saving power through sacred speech.

title: The Noble and Distinguished Dhāraṇī
explainer: Toh 542 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-viśeṣavatī-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Phags pa khyad par can zhes bya ba'i gzungs, which may be rendered into English as "The Noble and Distinguished One." As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it belongs to the broad class of canonical texts that transmit sacred formulae endowed with protective and liberating power, and its opening narrative situates the teaching within a specific time and place, recounting how a monk named Tshebrjod encountered an extraordinary vision during a journey. The text appears immediately following the dhāraṇī called "The Noble One Who Liberates from the Eight Great Fears," suggesting it was transmitted and compiled as part of a related cluster of protective dhāraṇī literature. It is preserved among the dhāraṇī collections of the Kangyur, the Tibetan canon of scriptures regarded as the word of the Buddha.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called 'Spoken from the Mouth of Noble Mañjuśrī'
explainer: The Dhāraṇī Called "Spoken from the Mouth of Noble Mañjuśrī," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Mañjuśrī-svākhyāto-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Jampelyang gi zhalnyi su sung shé jawa zhé ja wa'i zungwa (འཕགས་པ་འཇམ་དཔལ་གྱི་གསུང་གི་གཞལ་), is a dhāraṇī text dedicated to the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, consisting primarily of a sacred mantra formula invoking his wisdom and blessings for the benefit of all beings. As a dhāraṇī, it belongs to a genre of canonical texts that preserve potent syllabic formulas believed to embody the enlightened qualities of buddhas and bodhisattvas, here specifically channeling the insight and protective power of Mañjuśrī, the embodiment of wisdom. The text opens with homages to the Three Jewels and to Mañjuśrī himself before presenting an extended Sanskrit mantra invocation that calls upon tathāgatas, bodhisattvas, and a host of divine beings including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas. It is Toh 545 in the Kangyur, belonging to the dhāraṇī class of texts, and was translated into Tibetan by the renowned Indian abbot Dīpaṃkara Śrījñāna (Atiśa) together with the monk-translator Géwé Lodrö, and subsequently finalized by the monk Tsultrim Gyalwa.

title: Mañjuśrī's Questions
explainer: Toh 546 in the Kangyur is a short esoteric scripture centered on the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, known in Sanskrit as Mañjuśrī and in Tibetan as Jampal Zhönnu (འཇམ་དཔལ་གཞོན་ནུར་གྱུར་པ), the youthful emanation of wisdom. The text belongs to the class of vidyā or dhāraṇī literature, presenting a sacred mantra-formula that Mañjuśrī rises to proclaim before the Buddha and the assembled retinue, who greet his intention with enthusiastic approval. As a dhāraṇī text, it combines narrative framing — in which Mañjuśrī performs devotional prostrations and addresses the Blessed One — with the transmission of a potent vidyā said to be a source of wonder when proclaimed. It is preserved among the dhāraṇī collections of the Kangyur, reflecting the canonical importance of Mañjuśrī as a focal deity for wisdom-oriented ritual and recitation practice.

explainer: Toh 548 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text dedicated to Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva of wisdom, known in Sanskrit as Mañjuśrī and in Tibetan as འཇམ་དཔལ (Jampal). The text belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and consists of a series of sacred mantra formulas along with enumerated benefits for their recitation, including the retention of teachings heard, the purification of even the most severe karmic obscurations, and the direct beholding of Mañjuśrī's form. It presents itself as a pledge made by Mañjuśrī himself, lending the dhāraṇī a quality of direct spiritual guarantee. As a compact liturgical and protective text, it is representative of the genre of bodhisattva-associated dhāraṇīs found throughout the Kangyur's collections of such material.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called 'The Growth of Wisdom and Intelligence through the Noble Venerable Mañjuśrī'
explainer: Toh 549 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Āryamañjuśrībhaṭṭārakasya Prajñābuddhivarddhanā Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the dhāraṇī of "The Growth of Wisdom and Intelligence through the Noble Venerable Mañjuśrī." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and centers on a short but potent mantra invocation dedicated to Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva of wisdom. The text promises a remarkable range of benefits to those who hold, carry, or recite the dhāraṇī, including the swift arising of intelligence and eloquence, the recall of past lives, great learning, and the accumulation of vast merit across countless eons. As a dhāraṇī scripture, it exemplifies the genre of compact ritual and contemplative texts that pair a sacred formula with descriptions of its spiritual efficacy.

title: The Ritual of the Single-Syllable Mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī
explainer: Toh 550 in the Kangyur is a short ritual text known in Tibetan as "Phags pa 'Jam dpal gyi sngags yi ge 'bru gcig pa'i cho ga" and in Sanskrit as the "Ekākṣaramantravidhi of Noble Mañjuśrī," concerning the single-syllable secret mantra "Oṃ Kṣmīṃ" associated with the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. The text belongs to the class of dhāraṇī and mantra literature found in the Kangyur and follows directly after a related dhāraṇī concerned with the growth of wisdom and intelligence through Mañjuśrī. It is a practical ritual manual describing the mantra's supreme efficacy as the heart-essence of all the Tathāgatas and providing specific instructions for its application in healing ailments such as toothache, eye disease, and wounds caused by weapons. As such, it sits among the collections of dhāraṇī and tantric ritual texts in the Kangyur, reflecting the broader tradition of using sacred syllables and mantra recitation for both spiritual and worldly benefit.

It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts within the Kangyur and takes the form of a hymn or praise text enumerating one hundred and eight epithets of the Perfection of Wisdom personified as a blessed female deity, regarded as the mother of all buddhas of past, present, and future. The text opens with a verse prologue proclaiming its intention to recite these names for the benefit of those who wish to prosper, before proceeding through the enumerated epithets in sequence. As a praise text centered on the Perfection of Wisdom, it sits at the intersection of the prajñāpāramitā literary tradition and devotional practice directed toward wisdom as a sacred feminine principle.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom Called Kauśika
explainer: Toh 554 in the Kangyur is a Perfection of Wisdom sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Kauśika Prajñāpāramitā and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa kau shi ka, meaning "The Noble Perfection of Wisdom Called Kauśika." It belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā class of texts and takes the form of a teaching delivered by the Buddha at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, addressed specifically to Śakra, the lord of the gods, whose epithet Kauśika gives the text its name. The discourse expounds the nature of the Perfection of Wisdom through a series of paradoxical formulations — neither two nor not-two, neither marked nor without marks — pointing beyond conceptual elaboration to the non-dual character of wisdom itself. As one of the shorter Prajñāpāramitā sūtras preserved in the Kangyur, it distills the essential insight of the broader Perfection of Wisdom literature into a concise and direct exchange.

It belongs to the genre of protective dhāraṇī literature, presenting a series of invocations and sacred formulas intended to guard practitioners against a wide range of dangers — including fear of enemies, wild beasts, poison, fire, and water — as well as illnesses arising from imbalances of wind, bile, and phlegm. The Peacock (Mayūra) is a figure of ancient Indian religious tradition associated with the neutralization of poison and the warding off of harm, and this text draws on that symbolism to offer comprehensive spiritual and physical protection. Sitting within the Kangyur's collection of dhāraṇī and mantra literature, it represents an important example of the ritual-protective scriptures that formed a significant part of Buddhist practice across South and Central Asia.

It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and centers on Mārīcī, a goddess associated with the rays of light that precede the sun and moon, who is described as utterly invincible, invisible, and immune to all harm and obstruction. The text is set in Śrāvastī, where the Buddha addresses a large assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, presenting this dhāraṇī as a means by which practitioners may invoke Mārīcī's protective and wish-fulfilling powers. As a dhāraṇī scripture, it belongs to the broader class of canonical texts that transmit sacred formulas believed to confer blessings, protection, and spiritual benefit upon those who recite or uphold them.

The text presents itself as extracted from a larger twelve-thousand-section tantra called The Arising of Radiant Rays, of which it constitutes the supremely essential seven-hundred-section heart. Set within the classic sūtra frame of the Buddha teaching on Vulture Peak Mountain, it is classified among the tantric scriptures of the Kangyur and exemplifies the genre of protective ritual literature centered on powerful knowledge-mantra queens.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'She Who Possesses Victory'
explainer: Toh 568 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Jayavatī Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Gyalwa Chen Zhejawa'i Zung, meaning "The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'She Who Possesses Victory.'" It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī and vidyā mantra literature, presenting a sacred incantation taught by the Buddha for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings and for the protection of worldly rulers. The text is set on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, where Vajrapāṇi, the great lord of the yakṣa host, approaches the Buddha and requests the teaching of this vidyā mantra queen known as Jayavatī. As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it sits within the broader collection of such protective and meritorious scripture texts preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called Empowerment
explainer: Toh 569 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-abhiṣecanī-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phags pa dbang bskur ba zhes bya ba'i gzungs, meaning "The Noble Empowerment." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and presents a sacred incantation along with its framing discourse, in which the Buddha, dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, addresses the venerable Śāriputra on the qualities and path of the bodhisattva, including the bodhisattva's mother, former conduct, aspiration of truth, and the taking up of the grounds. The text follows the familiar sūtra opening of a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, situating the dhāraṇī within a Mahāyāna context that emphasizes the empowerment and spiritual development of those on the bodhisattva path.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'Possessed of Riches'
explainer: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called "Possessed of Riches," known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-Hiraṇyavatī-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Phags pa dbyig dang ldan pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs, is a dhāraṇī text in which the Buddha, dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven among a vast assembly of bodhisattvas, exhorts the bodhisattva Supratiṣṭhita to receive and uphold this sacred dhāraṇī, emphasizing that any bodhisattva who fails to do so has never truly encountered the Tathāgatas of the three times. The text belongs to the genre of dhāraṇī literature, presenting a condensed sacred formula framed within a brief narrative setting that underscores the incalculable spiritual merit and protection the dhāraṇī confers. It is catalogued as Toh 570 in the Kangyur, where it belongs to the broader collection of dhāraṇī and mantra texts preserved within the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: The Noble Wisdom-Mantra Called 'Poison Remover'
explainer: Toh 571 in the Kangyur is a short canonical sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Jiguli Nāma Vidyā and in Tibetan as Pakpa Duksel Zhejawa Rikpa (འཕགས་པ་དུག་སེལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་རིག་པ་), meaning "The Noble Wisdom-Mantra Called 'Poison Remover.'" It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī or vidyā texts — scripture centered on a protective mantra — and its content concerns the Buddha recounting, in the form of a past-life narrative, the origin and virtues of a powerful mantra capable of removing poison. The text is set in the familiar sūtra frame of the Buddha addressing his monks at Śrāvastī, lending it the authority of direct Buddhavacana. It was translated into Tibetan from Sanskrit by the Indian masters Jinamitra and Dānaśīla together with the great Tibetan editor-translator Yeshé Dé, and was subsequently revised in accordance with the standardized new terminology of the imperial translation period.

title: The Queen of Mantras Called the Noble Blessed Lady Aṅgulī, Accomplished by Reading
explainer: Toh 572 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in English as "The Queen of Mantras Called the Noble Blessed Lady Aṅgulī, Accomplished by Reading," corresponding to the Sanskrit Siddhapaṭita Bhagavatī Āryāṅguli-nāma-vidyārājñī and the Tibetan Bklag pas grub pa bcom ldan 'das ma 'phags ma sor mo can zhes bya ba rig pa'i rgyal mo. It belongs to the vidyārājñī genre — a class of powerful mantra texts associated with a female sovereign of spells — and is concerned with the recitation of protective mantras capable of eliminating the venom of nāgas, serpents, and a wide range of malevolent spirits and dangerous creatures. The text is presented as a teaching delivered by the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to an assembly dwelling on Gandhamādana mountain, framing its mantras as both spiritually authoritative and practically efficacious for protection and healing. As a dhāraṇī scripture, it sits within the broader collection of ritual and incantation texts preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Mother of All Phenomena
explainer: Toh 573 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Āryā Sarvadharmamātṛkā Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Pakma Chö Tamché Kyi Yum Shyé Jawé Zung, meaning in English the Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Mother of All Phenomena. As a dhāraṇī scripture, it belongs to the broader category of tantra-adjacent ritual texts and takes the form of a discourse delivered by the Buddha to his attendant Ānanda at Śrāvastī, in which the Buddha transmits a sacred spell said to pacify all illness and to have been proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas. The text includes the dhāraṇī mantra itself along with testimony from the gods of the Pure Abodes, situating it within a celestial and devotional frame characteristic of such works. It appears in the Kangyur as a self-contained dhāraṇī sūtra and is immediately preceded in the same manuscript by a distinct text called the Queen of Knowledge-Spells Known as She of the Finger-bones, indicating it was transmitted as part of a collection of related dhāraṇī works.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called 'The Jewel at the Crown'
explainer: Toh 574 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-cūḍāmaṇi-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Tsuk gi Norbu Zhejawa'i Zung, rendered in English as "The Noble Dhāraṇī Called The Jewel at the Crown." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts centered on sacred ritual syllables and formulas understood to concentrate and transmit the power of enlightened beings. The text opens with reverential homage to the buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions, and gives particular prominence to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, praised for his great compassion and his power to protect beings from fear, poverty, epidemic, and other terrors. As a dhāraṇī literature it serves both devotional and practical purposes, offering practitioners a means of invoking protective and liberating blessings through recitation.

title: The Noble Six-Syllable Wisdom Mantra
explainer: Toh 575 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī scripture known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-ṣaḍakṣara-vidyā and in Tibetan as Phags pa yi ge drug pa'i rig sngags, meaning in English the Noble Six-Syllable Wisdom Mantra. It belongs to the class of canonical dhāraṇī texts and concerns a powerful six-syllable mantra said to have been proclaimed by six fully awakened buddhas, the four world-guardian kings, and twenty-eight great yakṣa commanders, and which the Buddha instructs his disciple Ānanda to hold, recite, master, and perfect. The text is framed as a discourse delivered by the Blessed One at Śrāvastī and follows the conventional sūtra opening, presenting the mantra together with its lineage of transmission and implicit merit. Translated into Tibetan by the Śes-sde translation team, it forms part of the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur.

title: The noble dhāraṇī known in Tibetan as Shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa stong phr
explainer: The noble dhāraṇī known in Tibetan as Shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa stong phrag brgya pa'i gzungs and in Sanskrit as the Śatasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitādhāraṇī — the Dhāraṇī of the Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Verses — is a short dhāraṇī text belonging to the broader Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom, tradition. It presents a series of mantra formulas whose recitation or retention is said to confer upon the practitioner the merit and wisdom equivalent to holding the vast one-hundred-thousand-verse Perfection of Wisdom scripture in its entirety. The text appears immediately after the conclusion of the Six Syllables vidyā-mantra, suggesting it formed part of a cluster of related dhāraṇī and mantra texts within the collection. It is Toh 576 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the dhāraṇī class of texts.

title: The Dhāraṇī of the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Verses
explainer: Toh 577 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in English as the Dhāraṇī of the Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Verses, with its Tibetan title rendered as Shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa stong phrag nyi shu lnga pa'i gzungs, and its Sanskrit as Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Dhāraṇī. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts within the Kangyur and takes the form of a concentrated dhāraṇī — a sacred formulaic incantation — that distills and invokes the power of the vast Perfection of Wisdom scripture in twenty-five thousand verses. The text opens with homage to the Blessed Lady, the Mother, the Perfection of Wisdom, and presents a dhāraṇī in Sanskrit syllables calling upon her qualities of wisdom, illumination, and knowledge, promising spiritual attainment to those who hold it. As a dhāraṇī associated with one of the great Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, it sits at the intersection of the wisdom and tantric ritual traditions preserved within the Kangyur.

title: The Dhāraṇī of the Noble Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 578 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa brgyad stong pa'i gzungs," which can be rendered in English as the Dhāraṇī of the Noble Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom, with a Sanskrit title reconstructable as something like Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitādhāraṇī. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts within the Kangyur and takes the form of a condensed dhāraṇī, or sacred incantation, associated with the celebrated Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom sūtra. The text presents a short mantra formula whose recitation and memorization are said to confer the merit of holding the full Perfection of Wisdom scripture, while also purifying karmic obscurations and averting misfortune. As the opening lines make clear, this dhāraṇī follows directly upon a companion dhāraṇī linked to the Twenty-Five Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom, suggesting it belongs to a series of such condensed protective formulas associated with the major Prajñāpāramitā scriptures.

title: Toh 579 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as Pha rol tu phyin pa
explainer: Toh 579 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as Pha rol tu phyin pa drug gi snying po'i gzungs, which may be rendered in English as the Dhāraṇī of the Essence of the Six Perfections, with a likely Sanskrit title along the lines of Ṣaṭpāramitāhṛdayadhāraṇī. It belongs to the broader Perfection of Wisdom class of canonical literature and follows directly upon a dhāraṇī associated with the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, distilling the essence of all six perfections — generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom — into a compact ritual formula. The text instructs that holding and continuously reciting this dhāraṇī enables the practitioner to grasp the meaning of all six perfections, realize the emptiness of all phenomena, and purify grave misdeeds including the five actions of immediate karmic retribution. As a dhāraṇī sūtra situated within the Kangyur's Perfection of Wisdom section, it represents a concise, mantrically oriented expression of prajñāpāramitā teaching intended for devotional and purificatory practice.

explainer: Toh 580 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as something close to "The Essences of the Perfections," presenting a series of sacred mantra formulas — one for each of the six perfections, including generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, and the rest — paired with the assurance that merely hearing each formula once will cause one to attain that quality. The text belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a broad category that gathers spells, incantations, and condensed ritual formulas drawn from the broader Mahāyāna tradition. Its structure is liturgical and mnemonic rather than discursive, making it representative of the practical, practice-oriented scriptural material preserved alongside the major sūtras and tantras. No distinct Sanskrit title is recoverable with certainty from the available source lines, though the mantras embedded in the text are clearly transliterated from Sanskrit originals.

title: The Essence of the Ten Perfections
explainer: Toh 581 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "Pha rol tu phyin pa bcu'i snying po," which may be rendered in English as "The Essence of the Ten Perfections," with its Sanskrit title reconstructable as something close to Daśapāramitāhṛdaya. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts preserving sacred mantra formulas and their associated spiritual benefits. The text concludes a preceding dhāraṇī said to bring about the taking up of the six perfections, then opens a brief teaching on the essence of the ten perfections, promising remarkable merit to anyone who hears it even once. As is characteristic of this genre, the content blends Sanskrit dhāraṇī syllables with short doctrinal framing, situating the power of the formula within the Mahāyāna framework of the perfections.

title: Dhāraṇī for Attaining the Ten Perfections
explainer: Toh 582 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Daśapāramitāpāripūrakā, or "Dhāraṇī for Attaining the Ten Perfections," with a corresponding Tibetan title that can be rendered as Pha rol tu phyin pa bcu thob par 'gyur ba'i gzungs. It belongs to the broad class of dhāraṇī and mantra literature found within the Kangyur, presenting a series of short sacred formulas, each to be recited once in order to attain a specific spiritual quality. The text moves systematically through virtues such as loving-kindness, compassion, and joy, linking each to an invocation of all the tathāgatas, reflecting the Mahāyāna ideal of the ten perfections that a bodhisattva cultivates on the path to awakening. Though brief, it exemplifies the practical and devotional character of dhāraṇī collections, in which the recitation of consecrated syllables is understood to produce direct spiritual benefits for the practitioner.

explainer: Toh 583 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text associated with the Perfection of Wisdom, known in Tibetan as the Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā tradition. It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī or mantra literature within the Kangyur, presenting a series of sacred syllables and formulaic phrases intended to confer specific spiritual attainments upon the practitioner. The text opens with dhāraṇī formulations oriented toward the cultivation of the four immeasurables — loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity — and proceeds with homage to the Blessed Lady, the noble Perfection of Wisdom, situating it within the broader Prajñāpāramitā scriptural tradition. While precise Sanskrit and Tibetan title lines are not fully determinable from the available material, the text's content and framing place it firmly within the esoteric or dhāraṇī-bearing dimensions of Prajñāpāramitā literature preserved in the Kangyur.

title: Dhāraṇī for Holding the Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Verses
explainer: Toh 584 in the Kangyur is a collection of dhāraṇī texts — short, potent ritual formulas — each associated with a major canonical scripture, promising the practitioner that by holding or reciting the formula they gain the full merit and blessings of engaging with the root text itself. In Sanskrit the genre is known as dhāraṇī, and in Tibetan as gzungs. The collection includes formulas linked to celebrated works such as the Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Verses and the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, among others, making it a kind of condensed gateway to several foundational Mahāyāna scriptures. Sitting within the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, the text belongs to the broad class of canonical dhāraṇī literature that was gathered and preserved alongside the sūtras and tantras of the Tibetan Buddhist canon.

title: Dhāraṇī of the Array of Stalks Sūtra
explainer: Toh 585 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text associated with the Gaṇḍavyūha, known in Sanskrit as the Gaṇḍavyūhadhāraṇī and in Tibetan in connection with the sūtra called Sdong po bkod pa, meaning the Array of Stalks. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts preserving sacred syllables and mantra formulas held to carry concentrated spiritual power. This particular text consists of a brief mantra invocation addressed to the buddhas whose teaching is unobstructed, and it carries the remarkable claim that reciting or holding this dhāraṇī is equivalent to having perfectly read the entirety of the vast and celebrated Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra, one of the great Mahāyāna scriptures describing the spiritual journey of the youth Sudhana. Its inclusion in the Kangyur reflects the tradition of condensing the merit of extensive canonical works into a single potent dhāraṇī formula.

explainer: Toh 586 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as the heart essence of the Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra, corresponding to the Sanskrit title Gaṇḍavyūhahṛdaya, meaning "The Heart of the Gaṇḍavyūha." It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and distills the spiritual power of the celebrated Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra — the magnificent concluding chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra describing the bodhisattva Sudhana's pilgrimage — into a concentrated series of mantric formulas and sacred pledges. The text promises that one who holds this dhāraṇī will thereby come to hold the essence of great sūtras such as the Sūtra of the King of Meditative Absorption, and will gain knowledge of the maṇḍalas, samaya, and mudrās of both worldly and transcendent realms. As a dhāraṇī belonging to the broader Vajrayāna liturgical tradition, it exemplifies the canonical tendency to crystallize vast sūtra teachings into brief, potent formulas intended for recitation and ritual practice.

title: The Essence of the Noble Great Peacock
explainer: Toh 587 in the Kangyur is a brief dhāraṇī text known in Tibetan as "Phags pa rma bya chen mo'i snying po," which translates into English as "The Essence of the Noble Great Peacock," corresponding to the Sanskrit Mahāmāyūrī-hṛdaya. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a class of texts preserving short, potent ritual formulae held to confer protection and spiritual benefit on those who memorize or recite them. This particular text presents the seed-essence or heart dhāraṇī of the Great Peacock, a celebrated protective deity associated with the longer Mahāmāyūrī dhāraṇī cycle, and its transmission here is immediately followed by the opening of a related text devoted to the great queen of wisdom Mahāpratisarā. The text is thus a concise liturgical formula rather than a discursive scripture, and its placement in the canon reflects the Kangyur's extensive collection of dhāraṇī and mantra literature.

title: Mantra Syllables of the Noble Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
explainer: Toh 589 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text associated with the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, known in Tibetan as Phags pa lang kar gshegs pa'i gzungs, and belonging to the broader class of dhāraṇī and mantra literature within the canon. The text presents a series of mantra syllables addressed to the bodhisattva Mahāmati, the principal interlocutor of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, and promises powerful protection to any man or woman of noble lineage who holds, recites, or masters these syllables. It asserts that no deity, nāga, yakṣa, asura, garuḍa, or any other supernatural being will be able to find an opening or occasion to harm such a practitioner. Functioning as a protective spell closely linked to one of the great Mahāyāna sūtras, this brief text illustrates the important role that dhāraṇī formulas played in extending the spiritual and apotropaic power of canonical scripture into daily religious life.

title: The Noble Great Queen of Mantra-Vidyā Who Emerged from the Uṣṇīṣa of All the Tathāgatas, Bearing the White Parasol, Unconquerable, the Averter of All
explainer: Toh 590 in the Kangyur is the Noble Great Queen of Mantra-Vidyā Who Emerged from the Uṣṇīṣa of All the Tathāgatas, Bearing the White Parasol, Unconquerable, the Averter of All, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-sarva-tathāgatoṣṇīṣa-sitātapatrā-aparājitā-pratyaṅgirā-mahāvidyārājñī, and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Dezhin Shekpa Thamché kyi Tsuktor né jungwa Dukkar Pochen zhéjawa Zhengyi mi tubma Chirzokpé Riksngakma Chenmo. It is a dhāraṇī sūtra belonging to the Tantra section of the Kangyur, centering on the powerful and protective spell that radiates from the uṣṇīṣa — the crown protrusion — of all the buddhas, personified as a goddess bearing a white parasol and renowned for her capacity to avert all harm and liberate beings from lower rebirths. The text takes the form of a canonical discourse delivered by the Buddha while dwelling among the Gods of the Thirty-Three, where he enters a special meditative absorption and from his uṣṇīṣa emanates the great mantra-vidyā at the heart of the teaching. The Sitātapatrā tradition became one of the most widely venerated dhāraṇī cycles across the Buddhist world, prized for its purificatory and protective power.

This version was finalized by the paṇḍita Parahitabhadra and the Tibetan translator Gzu Dga' Rdor, who collated their work against an old manuscript preserved at the temple of Amṛtabhava in Kashmir, attesting to the care taken in establishing an authoritative text.

It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and centers on the powerful mantra of Uṣṇīṣavijayā, one of the most celebrated dhāraṇīs in the Buddhist tradition, renowned for its capacity to purify negative karma and liberate beings from lower rebirths. The text opens with a narrative frame set among the gods of the Thirty-Three, where a deity named Supratiṣṭhita receives a prophetic warning about his impending death and unfavorable rebirths, prompting the intervention of the Buddha, who reveals this dhāraṇī as a means of purification and protection. The inclusion of a detailed explanation alongside the dhāraṇī itself reflects the text's character as both a ritual and a doctrinal work, combining practical instruction with the soteriological promise of liberation from the lower realms.

explainer: Toh 599 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Samantamukhapraveśaraśmivimalośṇīṣaprabhāsasarvatathāgatahṛdayasamayavilokitanāmadhāraṇī, rendered in Tibetan as "The Dhāraṇī Entitled Gazing upon the Heart-Essence and Sacred Pledge of All the Tathāgatas by means of the Radiance of the Uṣṇīṣa's Stainless Light that Enters through Every Gateway." It belongs to the dhāraṇī class of canonical literature, a genre concerned with sacred formulas and their associated teachings and ritual power. The text opens with the Blessed One residing in the divine abode of Tuṣita, teaching the Dharma of the six perfections to an vast assembly that includes bodhisattvas, gods of the Long-Life Heaven, and great divine beings such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. title: Blazing Crown Protrusion
explainer: Toh 600 in the Kangyur is a short dhāraṇī text known in English as the Blazing Crown Protrusion, corresponding to the Sanskrit Uṣṇīṣavirocana and the Tibetan Gtsug tor 'bar ba. It belongs to the broader category of dhāraṇī and mantra literature, presenting a powerful incantation attributed to the assembly of all buddhas whose teaching cannot be obstructed, and which is said to accomplish a vast range of karmic purifications, auspicious aims, and the pacification of ill-omened dreams. The text opens with a homage to the Blazing Crown Protrusion and proceeds in verse to enumerate the mantra's extraordinary efficacy across thousands of actions and circumstances. It is classified among the dhāraṇī collections of the Kangyur, representing the widespread Indian tradition of condensing buddhadharma into potent ritual formulas for protection and benefit.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called 'The Stūpa Accomplished by the Perfection of All Wisdom'
explainer: Toh 601 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Sarva-prajñānta-pāramitā-siddha-caitya-nāma-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Dhāraṇī Called "The Stūpa Accomplished by the Perfection of All Wisdom." As its titles suggest, it is a ritual and devotional text centered on a sacred dhāraṇī formula associated with the perfection of wisdom and the consecration or empowerment of a stūpa, promising to dispel evil and ill omens through its recitation. The text opens with homages to Vajrapāṇi, the buddhas of the three times, and key bodhisattvas including Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Avalokiteśvara, situating it within a rich Vajrayāna devotional context. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur, a broad category of texts preserving powerful sacred formulas accompanied by their ritual and narrative frameworks.

title: Dhāraṇī of the Vimalā Uṣṇīṣa
explainer: The Dhāraṇī of the Vimalā Uṣṇīṣa, known in Sanskrit as the Vimalā Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Bimalā Uṣṇīṣa'i gzungs, is a dhāraṇī text belonging to the broader category of incantation literature focused on the ritual construction and consecration of stūpas. It presents sacred mantras and accompanying ritual procedures for the planting of stūpas, explaining how even a single stūpa, when properly consecrated through the recitation of these dhāraṇīs over materials such as clay, can accrue merit equivalent to the construction of tens of millions of stūpas. The text belongs to the tradition of uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇīs, a family of texts concerned with the purifying and spiritually potent qualities associated with the crown protrusion of a buddha, and it promises that practitioners who engage correctly with its rites will ultimately attain full awakening. It is Toh 602 in the Kangyur, catalogued among the dhāraṇī and tantra-related works of that collection.

title: The Dhāraṇī Called Supreme Compassion
explainer: Toh 603 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in English as "The Dhāraṇī Called Supreme Compassion," in Sanskrit as the Karuṇāgra-nāma-dhāraṇī, and in Tibetan as Snying rje mchog ces bya ba'i gzungs. It belongs to the class of dhāraṇī literature, presenting a sacred mantra together with its accompanying liturgical framework and the spiritual and healing benefits conferred by its recitation and ritual use. The text is devoted to Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion described as the Lotus-Bearer who rouses beings mired in suffering, and it promises benefits ranging from the recollection of past births to the curing of leprosy in all its forms. As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it sits within the broader collection of esoteric and quasi-esoteric scriptures preserved in the Kangyur, and it opens by paying homage to the omniscient one before proceeding to reveal what it calls the supreme secret mantra of the Tathāgata.

title: The secret tantra of the wrathful conqueror
The Noble Dhāraṇī of Vajrabhairava
explainer: Toh 605 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-vajra-bhairava-dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Pakpa Dorje Jikjé kyi Zung, meaning "The Noble Dhāraṇī of Vajrabhairava." It belongs to the genre of dhāraṇī literature, presenting a sequence of sacred syllables and mantra phrases associated with Vajrabhairava, a wrathful tantric deity whose name means "Vajra Terrifier" and who is regarded as a fierce manifestation of wisdom. The text opens with a hymnic homage to the buddhas and bodhisattvas before delivering the dhāraṇī itself, accompanied by teachings on the merits and protective benefits gained through its recitation. As a dhāraṇī sūtra connected to the tantric tradition, it is classified among the tantra-related works of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Great Staff Dhāraṇī
explainer: Toh 606 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in English as "The Noble Great Staff," in Sanskrit as the Āryamahādaṇḍanāmadhāraṇī, and in Tibetan as Phags pa be con chen po zhes bya ba'i gzungs. As a dhāraṇī sūtra, it belongs to the broader class of protective and ritual literature within the Buddhist canon, presenting a sacred formula endowed with apotropaic power. The text opens with a scene set on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, where the Buddha resides with a great assembly of monks, while the Venerable Rāhula finds himself in a charnel ground called the Cool Grove, surrounded by a vast array of spirits and supernatural beings. This setting establishes the context for the dhāraṇī's protective function, suggesting it was transmitted to guard against the many threatening forces enumerated at the text's opening.

title: The Noble Invincible Precious Garland
explainer: Toh 607 in the Kangyur, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-ratnamālā-nāma-aparājita and in Tibetan as the Phags pa gzhan gyis mi thub pa rin po che'i phreng ba, or in English as "The Noble Invincible Precious Garland," is a dhāraṇī-related text belonging to the broader category of such works collected in the Kangyur. The text opens with an extensive series of homages addressed to the Three Jewels, vast numbers of buddhas and their assemblies, bodhisattvas, various grades of noble practitioners from stream-enterers to arhats, and a wide range of divine and supernatural beings including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, suggesting its character as a liturgically rich protective or merit-generating scripture. Texts of this type typically present powerful formulas alongside invocations intended to confer invincibility or spiritual protection on those who recite or honor them. Its placement in the Kangyur situates it among the canonical scriptures regarded as the word of the Buddha transmitted into the Tibetan tradition.

title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Purification of All Obstacles
sanskrit: Ārya Sarva Antarāyika Viśodhanī Nāma Dhāraṇī
explainer: Toh 608 in the Kangyur is a dhāraṇī text known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Sarva Antarāyika Viśodhanī Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Phags pa bar du gcod pa thams cad rnam par sbyong ba zhes bya ba'i gzungs, meaning in English the Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Purification of All Obstacles. It belongs to the dhāraṇī section of the Kangyur and presents a sacred incantation concerned with the removal of all obstacles, including those arising from the approach of death and the exhaustion of one's karmic formations. The text is framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha at Rājagṛha, prompted by the god Śakra, lord of the devas, who in fear of his impending death and transmigration seeks protection and guidance from the Blessed One. As a noble dhāraṇī sūtra, it combines the narrative conventions of canonical scripture with the conferral of a powerful protective formula intended to purify hindrances for those who receive and uphold it.

Toh 820 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical text known in Tibetan as the Auspic
explainer: Toh 820 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical text known in Tibetan as the Auspicious Verses of the Thirty-Seven Deities, belonging to the class of Yoga Tantra. The text consists of a series of benedictory verses invoking the auspiciousness of the thirty-seven deities of the maṇḍala of the Yoga Tantra, organized around the five buddha families — Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi — along with their consorts, bodhisattvas, and retinue figures including Vajrasattva. Each verse calls upon the merit and blessings of a particular deity or group of deities and dedicates that auspiciousness to all beings in the present moment. Framed as verses requested by a divine interlocutor, the text functions as a maṅgala or auspiciousness prayer and is placed within the tantra section of the Kangyur.
